#1. Maeve Communications Launches New York-Based Communications Company (EXCLUSIVE)

Maeve Communications, co-founded by industry veterans Laura Puig and Michelle Ciciyasvili, announced Monday the launch of its new publicity and strategic communications company.

The New York-based company will focus on entertainment, media and talent services offering project-based consultation and executive coaching services.

“The conversation to start our own company began in 2019 while working together briefly at a PR agency, but we knew we needed more experience before confidently building something of our own,” co-founders Puig and Ciciyasvili said in a joint statement. “The time for Maeve Communications is now. In merging our complementary backgrounds and experience, we’re ready and eager to partner with our clients and deliver thoughtful strategy, creative ideas, and the straightforward counsel they deserve. We take our work seriously but believe in having some fun, keeping things real and breaking a few rules along the way.” Related Stories 'Club Kid' to Host Free Screenings for Nightlife Communities in 12 U.S. Cities (EXCLUSIVE) Ben Affleck's 'Animals' Cast Wants Him to Run for Office: 'Maybe They Hate Me'

Puig recently left Tubi to launch her own publicity and strategic communications company with business partner Ciciyasvili, who was most recently the senior director of comms at Betches. Puig is an experienced publicist with a history of clients across television, film, talent, creator and entertainment industries. Throughout her 13 years of experience, she has developed long-standing press relationships, and garnered media hits across broadcast, print, online, podcast, digital and radio. Popular on Variety

Michelle Ciciyasvili is a communications leader with 15 years of public relations experience across media, entertainment, lifestyle and fashion brands. She blends creative storytelling and strategic thinking with her knowledge of how entertainment, media and culture intersect with business.

Maeve is inspired by Hollywood legend Mae West who was an American actress, singer, comedian, screenwriter and playwright in the 1930s. The founders said West serves as a symbol of the company’s “no-nonsense approach” when providing direct, senior-level counsel on the basis of honest and targeted conversations for each client.

#2. Sony Pictures Lands Rights To Brett Bean’s Bestselling Comic Book Series ‘D’Orc’

EXCLUSIVE: Sony Pictures has acquired the live-action film rights to bestselling comic book series D’Orc. D’Orc author and illustrator Brett Bean is attached to adapt for the screen.

The film plot is under wraps, but the comic book series marries swashbuckling humor with sprawling magical mythology and unforgettable creatures, all wrapped in a grittier, more action-driven fantasy adventure Published by Image Comics, the series debuted earlier this year and became an instant best-seller, with its first issue selling out before its release. It is now on its eighth printing, with subsequent issues also going into multiple printings.

Bean is an author and illustrator. In addition to the best-selling D’Orc comic book series, he is the author of the graphic novel series Zoo Patrol Squad, and the Muk ‘n’ Honey‘ book series. Watch on Deadline

As an illustrator, his work has contributed to the Dungeon Crawler Carl comic series, puppet designs for Jim Henson’s Creature Shop, and Marvel’s comic book series Rocket and Groot. Bean is represented by ChengCaplan Company, InkWell Management, and Alexander Lawrence

#3. Tim McGraw’s Country Music Hall of Fame Induction Was One the Most Emotional in Its History

Tim McGraw couldn’t help but marvel at the interconnectedness of the biggest night of his career. Onstage at the CMA Theater in Nashville on Sunday, the brand new member of the Country Music Hall of Fame drew a clear line from his fellow inductees the Stanley Brothers and Paul Overstreet to his first day arriving in Nashville from his hometown of Start, Louisiana: May 9, 1989.

It was the same day that Keith Whitley, McGraw’s musical hero and a former member of Ralph Stanley’s band, had died at 34, just a year after scoring one of his five Number One hits with “When You Say Nothing at All.” The writer of that song? Overstreet.

“I don’t believe that’s coincidence,” McGraw said from the podium. “I believe that’s country music.”

It was hard not to notice more than a few of those magic country moments during the 31st annual Medallion Ceremony, which welcomed McGraw as the Modern Era Artist, Overstreet in the Songwriter category, and the late sibling duo Ralph and Carter Stanley as Veterans Era Artists. There was Billy Strings and his arena-headlining band bringing the old-timey mountain sounds of the Stanleys into the present. There was Ricky Skaggs, another onetime member of Stanley’s Clinch Mountain Boys, joining Vince Gill to perform “Rank Stranger.” There was Jamey Johnson singing Overstreet’s “Forever and Ever, Amen,” while the artist who made it a country cornerstone, Randy Travis, looked on. And there were the frequent tributes to 2000 inductee Dolly Parton, who died in August, from Hall of Fame CEO Kyle Young, from Molly Tuttle and a band of female bluegrass aces, and from Patty Loveless, who closed the evening with the traditional singing of “Will the Circle Be Unbroken,” ad-libbing lines about our “sister Dolly.”

This being a pinnacle, if invitation-only, event of the country music calendar, star power was ever present. Blake Shelton was in the house, singing the cheeky Overstreet composition “Some Beach.” The 2023 inductee Tanya Tucker, who claimed she had recently fallen down a flight of stairs, dropped one-liners about muscle relaxants during her speech inducting Overstreet. And Parker McCollum and Lainey Wilson both sang for McGraw, with Alabama’s Randy Owen hanging the ceremonial medallion around McGraw’s neck. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Even Faith Hill made a rare public appearance to literally cheer on her husband’s induction: Throughout the evening, Hill pumped her fists, shouted praise, and led standing ovations for the performers. The only thing that would have made the evening better is if Hill took the stage to sing, something country fans have been hoping for in general since 2020. (In his frequently tearful speech, McGraw looked ahead to a day when he’s in the audience, watching his wife being inducted.)

Still, there was one moment that stood above all the rest for the way it conveyed emotion, courage, and the power of a song. As Young finished his remarks about McGraw’s 2004 carpe-diem hit “Live Like You Were Dying,” written by Craig Wiseman and Tim Nichols, the Hall’s CEO introduced the artist who would be interpreting it onstage — country vocal group Lady A. Last month, the trio’s singer Charles Kelley revealed he was diagnosed with a rare blood cancer and that he’d be starting treatment, making his appearance on the Hall of Fame’s stage to sing a ballad about fleeting time immensely powerful. Kelley, in perhaps the most emotional performance of his own career, nailed the song.

It wasn’t coincidence, as the man he was honoring might say. It was country music.

#4. Banijay CEO Marco Bassetti Urges European Producers to Fight for Better Terms of Trade With Hollywood: Studios and Streamers Should Provide ‘Rewards for Creativity’

Marco Bassetti, CEO of London-based Banijay Entertainment, the world’s largest independent studio, called for European producers to hold their ground when it comes to negotiating terms of trade with the U.S. studios and streamers during a fireside chat at Rome’s MIA market titled “What does it mean today to be a ‘European champion’ in an increasingly competitive global content market?”

“Who invests in creativity? It’s us independent producers,” said Bassetti during the chat with veteran Italian producer Marco Chimenz. He went on to point out that “the major debate currently taking place in Europe — and this is my own personal view — regardless of the different legal systems, across different countries we live under, is about recognizing and providing compensation for creativity,” he added. Related Stories Inside Omega’s James Bond Exhibition, From 007’s Toothbrush to His Passport and Mini Car Bombs Jamie Foxx Boards Indie Crime Thriller ‘East of the River’ as Producer (EXCLUSIVE)

The Italian executive went on to point out that “the current battle [in Brussels] over [investment] quotas is instead entirely pointless.” He was referring to contentious rules – known as Europe’s Audiovisual Media Services Directive – that force foreign streaming services to invest a portion of their revenue into local productions, but leaves the modalities of this obligation to each individual country. Popular on Variety

But Bassetti sees the rules of engagement as being crucial.

“The real fight should focus on studios and streamers recognizing and providing rewards for creativity” in the form of retention of IP rights on the part of producers, Bassetti added. “Yet that is not what is happening.”

At least not in continental Europe. “But when I work for a TV network — especially in countries like England — I retain ownership of the intellectual property,” he noted. “If I sell a series, the rights eventually revert to me after three years and there’s a built-in incentive for the creator.”

“Here in Europe, we’re accustomed to a system like that,” Bassetti said. “If the streamers just treat production companies as mere service providers it’s a problem,” because you don’t provide an incentive for creators to work with you.

“The reality is that we have no ownership, and it’s extremely difficult to secure any, though things are starting to open up a bit. There’s some movement regarding ‘windows’ (the sequence of release platforms)—but it’s only a partial shift. Ultimately, they [the studios and the streamers] still have total control,” he said.

Since taking the helm of Stéphane Courbit’s media powerhouse Banijay in 2013, Bassetti has firmly steered the company through some major transformations, from the takeover of production powerhouse Endemol Shine in the thick of the pandemic in 2020 to the diversification of the banner’s activities in live entertainment through Balich Wonder Studio and the Independents, all the while ramping up both scripted and unscripted business, and bolstering new and existing IPs.

It was only two months ago that Banijay Entertainment and RedBird IMI officially completed the $8 billion merger of Banijay and RedBird IMI’s All3Media, which is headquartered in London, U.K. The deal saw All3Media CEO Jane Turton take on the role of deputy CEO of the combined company, which boasts over 265,000 hours of content and some of television’s most recognizable franchises.

While the company is best known for its unscripted IP, thanks to “super brands” like “The Traitors,” “Big Brother” and “MasterChef,” Banijay also makes plenty of top notch scripted TV series and movies such as “Peaky Blinders,” “Black Mirror” and “Hamnet.”

Last week, speaking at the Mipcom TV market in Cannes, Bassetti said he saw an opportunity for the company to grow its presence in scripted production and hinted to an expansion into the U.S. scripted space.

That might help improve terms of trade for Banijay.

#5. CNN's Christiane Amanpour Announces Exit From Network After 43 Years

Christiane Amanpour shared that she would be leaving CNN next year after more than 40 years at the network, expressing her excitement to focus on "interesting new projects down the line."

More than four decades after the Chief International Anchor joined CNN, she confirmed that she will step away from the network in June.

"After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years," Amanpour said in an Oct. 19 statement. She added that she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism."

The 68-year-old, who has hosted her eponymous show on CNN International since 2009, thanked everyone she worked with, especially her "beloved show teams and field crews."

"It's the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much as we together battled to seek the facts," she shared, "the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor."

Amanpour also shared a message for her fellow journalists, "Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."

Meanwhile, CNN chief executive Mark Thompson shared insight into the network's future, telling newsroom employees in a letter obtained by NBC News that there are plans to scale back the show to once a week in early 2027.

"The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June," he wrote. "Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months."

"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go," he added, "but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally."

Her PBS series Amanpour & Company, which she's hosted since 2017, will also conclude in December.

Since joining CNN—whose parent company Warner Bros. Discovery was formally taken over by David Ellison's media corporation Paramount Skydance earlier this month—in 1983, Amanpour has covered major world events, starting with the First Gulf War. She also went on to report on wars in Bosnia, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and more.

"In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team,” Thompson concluded, “I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."

#6. ‘You Can See Everything’: Nathan Fielder Was So Skeptical He Could Break New Ground in Elizabeth Holmes Story, He Negotiated a Kill Switch with A24

Lance Oppenheim had been searching for a project to collaborate on with his cinematic idol Nathan Fielder. The two had become fast friends after Oppenheim reached out to Fielder about his first film “Some Kind of Heaven” — he knew Fielder had received a screening link, but when Oppenheim logged into the screening service, he could see the “Nathan for You” creator had only watched a portion of the 85-minute documentary.

“I saw [Nathan’s] email on this screening service, and I just decided to cold-email him,” said Oppenheim while a guest on this week’s Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast in support of the duo’s “You Can See Everything.” “I said, ‘Hey, I’m a huge fan of yours. You know, there’s another 40 percent of this movie left. It’s not that long. It’s probably 20 minutes — that’s all you have [left] to finish it.’” Related Stories Yet Another Netflix Stunner: Dan Lin Out as Film Chief Breakout ‘Behemoth!’ Musician Lukas Frank Reveals What It’s Like to Give Tony Gilroy a Rewrite

Fielder wrote back saying he had actually finished and enjoyed the then-24-year old director’s Sundance breakout film, and from that point forward, whenever Oppenheim was in Los Angeles, the two future collaborators would get together.

“We’d have these really long hangs, and I was just like, ‘What? Are we becoming really good buddies, a bromance or something?,’” Oppenheim said. He credits “Nathan for You” and Fielder’s early Canadian sketch work on YouTube with making him want to make documentaries. “We’d be out for several hours just talking about life and random things, and I started to realize, ‘Oh, maybe he wants to work with me on something.’ So I started just pitching him ideas.”

A couple of the projects Oppenheim brought to Fielder reached the early planning stages, but nothing took hold. Then, in early 2023, when Oppenheim was in town to shoot a commercial, Fielder — who grew up wanting to be a magician — took him to the Magic Castle.

Recalled Oppenheim of the fateful evening, “The magician asked for a celebrity name, just a random name to the group, and someone raised their hand and said ‘Elizabeth Holmes,’ and a light bulb went off in my head.” Earlier that day, Oppenheim had heard a rumor that Holmes had reached out to A24 about shooting a documentary with her before May 30, 2023, the day the disgraced Theranos founder would begin her 11-year prison sentence for defrauding investors of her medical testing device. “From what I had heard, A24 was interested and then backtracked because they got a little nervous and just didn’t have a director.”

Assuming the universe was speaking to him when Holmes’ name was injected into their Magic Castle hang, Oppenheim told Fielder about the rumor he’d just heard, and argued, if true, the project could be intriguing for two very different reasons: “First off, why A24? Did she watch ‘Ex Machina,’ or something, and liked it?,” he recalled.

And the second, more substantial, reason: Holmes hadn’t done an on-camera interview since Theranos imploded. The details of said implosion were unearthed by the Wall Street Journal, only to become a fascination for the general public, who couldn’t get enough of the story of the young CEO who conned Silicon Valley out of billions, via a popular podcast, best-selling book (“Bad Blood”), an Alex Gibney documentary, and a scripted Hulu limited series (“The Dropout“) starring Amanda Seyfried as Holmes.

Fielder agreed, but, according to Oppenheim, worried “that the story been told so many times already.” Regardless, Oppenheim nudged Fielder to call A24 in the morning, and he confirmed the rumors — a deal with Holmes had fallen apart, with only weeks left before she had to report to the Federal Prison Camp (FCP) in Bryan, Texas. It was against this backdrop that Fielder pitched A24 a highly unusual arrangement.

Explained Oppenheim, “Nathan [said to A24], ‘Well, do you think if Lance and I were to go and see if there was something there, would you be comfortable with giving us money and essentially just leaving us alone, and giving us a provision in our deal, whatever the money was, that we could just kill it at any time? If we didn’t find something, we could just throw it all away, we could throw it in the garbage can. And they thankfully agreed.”

Oppenheim said Fielder negotiating a “kill switch” on the project “changed everything.” Fielder remained skeptical there was a movie to be made with Holmes and her partner Billy Evans, who were holed up with their two small children in a Del Mar, California beach cottage with only 34 days — by the time Fielder and Oppenheim arrived — remaining before reporting to the Bryan FCP, but gone was the pressure to figure any of that out.

“This was the first time where I’ve ever been like, ‘Oh, we actually have room to explore something without any pressure of anyone looking [over us],’” said Oppenheim. “ I wish I could have that for every project, because then it really feels like you’re just operating purely out of curiosity. You can essentially fish.”

Regardless of the kill switch, fishing was Fielder and Oppenheim’s only option — there was no time to prep, let alone figure out the movie ahead of time. “All we really had time to do was call the people in our respective lives that we trust with our lives,” said Oppenheim. “We basically brought our individual Avengers into this thing.”

The small “You Can See Everything” team included Oppenheim’s longtime cinematographer David Bolen and production sound mixer Richard Carlos, while Fielder called up his “Nathan for You” and “The Curse” camera operator Jonathan Mitchell, and editor Adam Locke-Norden, who he’d been working closely with since high school.

“It was seven people that [just] went into that house in Del Mar, where Elizabeth and her partner Billy were living, and we didn’t know what we would find,” said Oppenheim. “Nathan was so skeptical about this being anything, and obviously I’m coming at it from the other side, ‘I’m working potentially with one of my cinematic heroes, so I want this to work. I want this to be great.’”

Once on the ground, Oppenheim worried he and Fielder were not on the same page. After 14-to-16 hour days filmming, they had wildly different interpretations of what each had observed of the couple’s domestic life, in which they mixed parenting with trying to launch their new venture, an AI-powered Theranos 2.0-like medical testing device.

“There were things that we were seeing that we could not agree on. Things that we were observing that should have been super simple and very mundane and very boring,” said Oppenheim. “We’d wrap shooting for a day, Nathan and I would talk about it, and he’d be like, ‘That’s not what happened,’ and I’m like, ‘That is what happened. I was watching it on three different monitors. I was watching it with distance. I wasn’t in the conversation [Fielder was the one engaging with Evans and Holmes].’”

The co-directors turned to their trusted crew to settle their debates, but Bolen, Mitchell, and Carlos each had interpretations of their own. Everyone had a different point of view on the isolated domestic life they were laser-focused on capturing.

“It felt like we were suddenly in this zone, almost like the zone in [Russian director Andrei] Tarkovsky’s ‘Stalker,’ it felt a little bit like [another Tarkovsky movie] ‘Solaris,’ it felt like we were in this place that the laws of reality and what we were seeing, no one could agree on anything, and that was the first time where Nathan, I think [started to see a film]” said Oppenheim.

Fielder and Oppenheim realized these divergent interpretations weren’t a problem between the collaborators; rather, the questions they were asking, and disagreeing over, were the film’s concept itself, something they could sink their teeth into.

“There’s these moments that are happening before us that feel extremely layered and dense. Like, ‘Is this a performance? Is it not a performance? Is this a real thing that’s happening? Is it possible to observe an authentic moment with someone who is known for being a master deceiver?,’” said Oppenheim. “I was definitely like, ‘I’m energized by this. I think the cognitive dissonance of this experience is cinematic. I think we can do something with this.’ And I think Nathan saw it and was like, ’There’s something rich and ripe within these moments that are extremely ambiguous, but as simple as someone whisking eggs.’”

According to Oppenheim, it was after this discovery that discussion of the kill switch dissipated: “That was the moment we were like, ‘OK, we have to commit to this. We have to make this work. Let’s just keep going with this process.’”

#7. Hugh Jackman's Gritty 126-Minute Thriller Is Officially HBO Max's Biggest Streaming Hit

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Hugh Jackman plays an old, violent man living in the shadows of a legendary past as he protects a young girl representing the hope of a future of which he'll have no part. No, I'm not talking about "Logan," but "The Death of Robin Hood," "Pig" director Michael Sarnoski's latest film that premiered in theaters earlier this year.

Everyone knows Robin Hood, but his actual cultural purchase is low. (Video essayist Patrick Willems has argued this is why there are so many failed Robin Hood movies out there.) That makes right now an odd time for a film titled "The Death of Robin Hood," which is all about not just ending Robin's journey but tearing down the folk hero's legend. Alternatively, perhaps that's exactly what makes it a perfect time for such a story. "The Death of Robin Hood" appears to have finally found an audience, as it currently sits as the No. 1 streamed film on HBO Max after grossing less than $10 million during its theatrical run.

Unapologetically indebted to "Logan" and Clint Eastwood's "Unforgiven," "The Death of Robin Hood" finds Robin living as a recluse. He's hunted by the friends and family of all the people he killed, and he kills them in turn. Injured while helping his old friend Little John (Bill Skarsgård) retake his farm and family, Robin convalesces on an idyllic island under the eye of Sister Brigid (Jodie Comer).

But this isn't the swashbuckling Robin played by Errol Flynn (to see how that Robin Hood might have grown old, watch Sean Connery and Audrey Hepburn's 1976 "Robin & Marian"). The poster for "The Death of Robin Hood" declares that "[h]e was no hero," and the film suggests his past as an outlaw was about killing for fun and profit.

As Hugh Jackman narrates in a promotional video recorded for "The Death of Robin Hood," the Robin Hood stories that became ballads and then myth changed a lot over the centuries. Gradually added elements like Robin's rivalry with the Sheriff of Nottingham or his romance with Maid Marian got away from the earliest recorded tales that cast Robin as a "wicked and murderous bandit."

The idea that Robin Hood "robbed from the rich and gave to the poor" isn't present in those early stories, either, and is born more from romantic ideas about the outlaw life. Jackman's Robin and Skarsgård's John, having killed so many people that their exploits have blurred together, have trouble remembering which parts of the stories are fact or fiction. There are no flashbacks to Robin's youth as a brigand, so we have only his word to go on.

But it's less that Robin finally realized "wait, killing is wrong???" in his old age, and more that he's had to live his years killing more and more people coming to kill him because he previously killed someone they cared about. The movie is about the practical consequences of living a violent life as much as the spiritual ones. At the beginning, Robin isn't guilty per se, he's simply tired, both of killing and having to explain he's not the man of whom songs were sung. His thoughts only grow into true guilt as he sits at the priory with Brigid, and with John's little daughter, Margaret (Faith Delaney).

There's almost no violence in the movie after Act 1, and for anyone expecting Robin to die with his bow in his hand, "The Death of Robin Hood" has a more melancholic climax and conclusion.

The insistence in "The Death of Robin Hood" that Robin was a monstrous thief and murderer has earned some raised eyebrows. Wealth inequality soars higher everyday — higher than it was in the Middle Ages — and now is the time to insist the folk hero famed for robbing the rich to give to the poor was actually a villain? After going in with these hesitations, I was able to get on Michael Sarnoski's quiet wavelength and enjoyed the movie. But critic Richard Brody of the New Yorker dismissed "The Death of Robin Hood" as "crude cynicism" for this very reason.

"The Death of Robin Hood" will not be the end of the character's time onscreen, either. "The Uprising," director Paul Greengrass' historical epic about the 1381 English Peasants' Revolt, is also another abridgement of the Robin Hood myth even if Andrew Garfield's unnamed "Ploughman" isn't actually called "Robin." "The Uprising" (read /Film's underwhelmed review here) centers on the class war elements of the Robin Hood myth that "The Death of Robin Hood" disregards.

But I'd contend the most striking reimagination of Robin Hood for 2026 was not in film at all. Many equate superheroes with older folk heroes — even "The Death of Robin Hood" itself does that by borrowing from "Logan." Regardless of whether you believe that comparison or not, DC Comics' archer hero Green Arrow is undeniably inspired by Robin Hood. New comic series "Absolute Green Arrow" by Pornsak Pichetshote and Rafael Albuquerque recasts Green Arrow as a serial killer who targets billionaires to the public's adoration. The book's tagline? "We need a Robin Hood who's less Errol Flynn and more Michael [Myers]."

2026 gave us "The Death of Robin Hood," but also proof there may be new life in this legend yet.

#12. Every 2026 Video Game Movie, Ranked

Video game films are the new comic book movies in Hollywood. Indeed, after years of being abhorred or treated as something to be ashamed of or ridicule, these types of films have recently become a gold mine. For years, though, video game movies were infamous for distorting their source material's lore, featuring cheaper costumes than a Spirit Halloween, or outright looking at their audience and mocking them for liking video games in the first place. These are things the worst video game movies ever made all have in common.

Cut to the present-day, and that's no longer the case (mostly). Instead, we tend to get video game adaptations that actually understand how to translate games to the medium of film or TV (revising and changing them to fit a different format), along with creators that actually have something to say about the source material. From "Arcane" to "Castlevania," "Fallout," "Sonic the Hedgehog," and "Detective Pikachu," there's no shortage of great adaptations that understand what it is people love about video games while offering something fresh in a different medium.

In 2026 alone, we've gotten an abundance of movies based on video games, ranging from bad to truly excellent. So, it's about time we ranked them to determine what these films manage (or fail) to fully capture about their source material and translate to the big screen.

Without further ado, here's our ranking of all the Hollywood-backed and/or American video game movies released in 2026. (You can also read our review of "Exit 8," the Toho-distributed, Japanese-language film version of Kotake Create's video game "The Exit 8.")

The first "Super Mario Movie" was a monumental success in every sense of the word (save for the film's critical response, anyway). It captured audiences' attention around the world with a blend of nostalgia, bright and colorful animation, and a whole lot of needle drops.

Its sequel, however, does things a little differently. Titled "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie," it's still flashy and colorful, and it features an incredible cast of actors voicing famous Nintendo characters like Mario (Chris Pratt), Luigi (Charlie Day), and Yoshi (Donald Glover) as they travel across the stars in a new adventure. The only problem? It spends too much time introducing characters from the larger Nintendo world like it's a late-stage Marvel Cinematic Universe entry. To be sure, it goes full Nintendo Cinematic Universe by bringing in the likes of Fox McCloud (Glen Powell), even if a "Super Smash Bros." movie isn't in the cards just yet.

On the whole, "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie" leaves a lot to be desired as a film. "Super Mario Galaxy" is a phenomenal video game loaded with visually striking worlds and innovative new gameplay mechanics. The movie adaptation, on the other hand, rings hollow and lifeless. It's simply way too concerned with referencing other (better) films than providing great scenes for viewers to remember long after the credits roll.

Compared to the 2021 "Mortal Kombat" movie, which inexplicably skipped the tournament that gives the original games a reason to exist and focus on a disappointingly bland original character, "Mortal Kombat II" is a massive improvement. Unlike its predecessor, this film understands the appeal of the fighting game franchise and centers on a big, violent tournament where powerful warriors face off in bloody combat. It also carries over the lore and aesthetic of the games without being overly faithful, serving up fights that feel like they came straight from the games yet are distinctly cinematic in their design.

What's more, "Mortal Kombat II" manages to weave some actual storytelling into the action, giving us memorable and grounded characters that nevertheless all have supernatural powers and fight in impossibly gory battles. With the addition of Karl Urban as the delightful Johnny Cage, plus visuals that capture the minutiae of the games' style (with certain fights being framed like they're stages in a video game, complete with floating platforms), this is the Platonic ideal of what "Mortal Kombat" can be on the big screen.

We got not one but two movies this year based on fighting games, and they both take very different approaches to adapting their respective games. Where "Mortal Kombat II" embraces the imagery of its source material, "Street Fighter" goes for more traditional action. In point of fact, the film often feels indebted to Stephen Chow in the way that it mixes humor and violence, bringing its thrilling fights to life through kinetic choreography and dynamic camera movements while at the same time integrating physical comedy into its stunts.

Without question, 2026's "Street Fighter" is a tongue-in-cheek movie inspired by 1990s action films, serving up ridiculous character designs and campy performances that are presented with a straight face. It can even be visually stunning, particularly during the animated flashback sequences that fill in the backstory for leads Ken Masters (Noah Centineo) and Ryu (Andrew Koji). With imagery straight out of an ultra-violent direct-to-video anime from the '90s, these scenes are by far the highlight of "Street Fighter," providing stunning visuals, hard-hitting action, and a genuinely emotional narrative.

While it doesn't quite capture the ethos of the best "Street Fighter" video games, this movie certainly understands their appeal, as well as the relationship between their characters. It's why, at the end of the day, "Street Fighter" works better as a movie than "Mortal Kombat II."

"Iron Lung" proved to be one of the biggest surprises of the year. It's a highly inventive indie sci-fi horror movie that was made by first-time director and YouTube sensation Markiplier, yet it ended up becoming a box office sensation. The film adapts the 2022 video game of the same name by David Szymanski and takes place after some mysterious catastrophe (known as the "Quiet Rapture") wiped out most of the Earth's human population. From there, it follows a prisoner named Simon (Markiplier) as he's forced to pilot a submarine through an ocean of blood.

Thanks to its simple premise, "Iron Lung" is able to be economical in its storytelling, with the entire film taking place in a single, impressively claustrophobic location. Markiplier proves adept at amping up the horror slowly, too, building up to a Lovecraftian threat that reveals the movie's true ambitions. More than that, the movie is able to be faithful to its source material (building an eerie atmosphere and an expansive world without over-explaining things) while still taking enough liberties to work as a satisfying standalone watch.

As a whole, "Iron Lung" makes for a brain-melting and, again, quite literally bloody horror movie full of terrifying and nightmarish imagery — the kind that encapsulates the experience of playing a horror video game alone on a laptop late at night.

After decades and many attempts, we finally have a fantastic "Resident Evil" film, and it only took a horror director superstar who understood how to approach the universe of the games without being restricted by their reputation to do it. Yes, Zach Cregger's "Resident Evil" ignores the exact plot from the games and doesn't include any known characters from them, but it understands the true appeal of the best "Resident Evil" games. It's why watching Austin Abrams' hapless medical courier go through absolute hell during the movie feels closer to playing a "Resident Evil" video game than, say, having a fan-favorite like Leon Kennedy show up.

From the growing look of desperation on Abrams' face to the alarmingly limited options his character has to stay alive (or even just small things like annoyingly indestructible padlocks), the name of the game in this movie is frustration, desperation, and knowing that you're up against forces beyond your understanding or capacity to defeat. But maybe the best thing about the film is how much it recalls one of the journal entries you find in a "Resident Evil" game, telling the story of some poor schmuck who turned into a zombie. Even if the movie doesn't mirror anything from the games in terms of plot or characters, the feeling it evokes is the same as the long-running Capcom franchise. And, at the end of the day, isn't that what we want out of all video game adaptations?

#13. The ’60 Minutes’ Overhaul Was Said to be Driven by New Ideas — You Can’t Tell That from Watching

When CBS News’ editor-in-chief Bari Weiss formally introduced executive producer Nick Bilton to steer “60 Minutes” into the future, the former writer on HBO’s “The Idol” sent a letter to his staff promising to “lead this show, not preserve it under glass.”

“I have a notebook full of ideas,” Bilton said. “Some are about the show itself. Some are about the next generation of correspondents. Some are about the strange fact that we produce one extraordinary hour for one night a week in a world that consumes content around the clock. I’m excited to share them.”

That excitement has not materialized onscreen. Not through five episodes, anyway. Related Stories ‘Dirty Dancing’ Sequel Will Honor Patrick Swayze, as Producers Work with Jennifer Grey to Write Baby’s Next Chapter Netflix Stunner: Bela Bajaria Out as Chief Content Officer, Former Disney Exec Peter Rice Steps in

For all the posturing around America’s No. 1 news program for 52 straight years needing a new direction, the latest season has shown scant evidence of what that new direction might be. The initial few months of Weiss and Hilton’s “60 Minutes” look a lot like the last 50 years of the classic “60 Minutes.” Perhaps that uniformity stems from pushback faced by the new regime, internally and externally, which led to assurances from the co-founder of The Free Press and her chosen EP that the show would “stay exactly like it is for now.”

But as ratings plummet and controversies rise, one has to wonder when these grand ideas to save “60 Minutes” might manifest. If the series wasn’t an “ice cube that is melting” before, it’s certainly feeling the heat now. So what’s being done to cool things down?

Using Bilton’s own blueprint — his “notebook of ideas” — let’s start with the changes we can see so far, which aren’t that easy to spot. Do you think many returning viewers clocked the alterations to the opening stopwatch? The cropping is tighter. Less of the watch-face is shown. And instead of “60 Minutes” appearing in a white font on a red background, it’s now in a red font on a white background.

Another brazen shift comes in how stories are introduced: Before, the lead reporter sat in front of a rectangular digital backdrop that looked like an open book. Now, the lead reporter sits in front of a rectangular digital backdrop that looks like… nothing. It’s just a screen. Or maybe an e-reader?

To be fair, a segment in the third episode kicks off with an attention-grabbing switcheroo: An AI-generated version of contributor Jon Wertheim gives the intro, before the real reporter walks out to explain the reason behind the stunt. (Their story, titled “Who needs humans?,” covers AI’s impact on the workforce.) But anyone fooled by Wertheim’s CGI avatar either wasn’t watching closely or thought the host had suddenly grown mutant fingers and a developed a wobbly eye.

Wertheim’s report also featured walk-and-talk shots, a standard technique (on “60 Minutes” and elsewhere) used to liven up static interviews, but one that Bilton said he wanted to avoid this season. Elsewhere, Bilton revived a retired series staple: the hidden-camera interview, which was used in the premiere’s report on President Trump’s “Pardon Economy.”

A lot of the old and less of the new doesn’t add up to significant change, let alone a surefire way to avoid purported extinction. Perhaps Weiss and Bilton are drawing from Jack Donaghy’s idea notebook, and the grand plan is to “make it 1997 again through science and magic.” Or maybe it’s not about altering the package as much as who’s delivering it, like Bilton mentioned in his second “idea.”

New correspondent Ross Douthat earned some of the show’s rare positive headlines when he landed an interview with Patrick Clancy. But where others may have heard pensive, sensitive questions fashioned for a man who’s been put through the ringer, online and off, I saw a reporter without the requisite patience and attentiveness to push a much-hyped interview beyond expectations. While sitting in a playground built as memorial for his dead children, Clancy chokes up recalling recurring dreams of his ex-wife. Douthat, meanwhile, can be seen tapping his leg and smiling.

Active listening is a skill, and Douthat rarely feels present. He’s awkward and terse, stilted and inexpressive. If his smile is meant to be reassuring, it comes off as clumsy, and the tapping is just plain rude.

No matter how you read Douthat’s comportment (his garbled narration, slouched posture, and rumpled suit don’t exactly scream “professional”), there’s no reason to assume he’s why “60 Minutes” — once the most respected name in news — booked a sought-after subject like Clancy, just as there’s no reason to believe his addition to the team is the trollish stewardship needed to court younger viewers or retain older ones. (There is reason to believe handing him a position on “60 Minutes” helped transfer his popular conservative print column from The New York Times to the Weiss-run Free Press — the reason being, that’s exactly what happened.)

As for the other new contributors, only one has issued a report: Ariel Levy, whose profile on Sacha Baron Cohen capped the latest episode. In five weeks, Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni, and Trevor Phillips have only appeared during “The Last Minute,” the closing segment that typically updates old stories or teases new ones. Their seconds-long spiels have touched on topical news instead, providing brief summaries of subjects like the protests in Europe and the war in Ukraine, as if long-form journalism is incomplete without a quick nod to the daily headlines.

That just leaves Bilton’s last idea: the “strange fact” that “60 Minutes” only airs “one night a week in a world that consumes content around the clock.” What he means by this is vague, even compared to his other unspecified ideas, which makes it even more difficult to imagine how it might be realized.

No spinoffs or extensions of “60 Minutes” have been announced, and its social media pages are comparable to previous years. YouTube features individual segments, full episodes, and archival content. TikTok hosts similar footage, albeit clipped for vertical video and treated with title cards. X is filled with a handful of videos every day, just as it was before Bilton’s hiring. (Based on a cursory scroll, previous social posts led with popular contributors like Anderson Cooper, whereas current stories — now without those popular contributors — tend to lead with the subjects.)

Perhaps pioneering new media strategies and must-see additional programming are still on the way, but for now, Bilton’s notebook of ideas has yet to yield appreciable results. The ratings, spun positively, are dependent on a good NFL lead-in.

Seen plainly, they’re setting record lows. Meanwhile, “60 Minutes” still looks like “60 Minutes”: No changes in these first five episodes could be expected to entice fresh viewers to tune in or convince alienated viewers to reconsider.

So, as a CBS senior staffer put it, “Why did you have to fire everyone to get a vaguely passable facsimile” of the original show?

Enter the 800-pound gorilla in any article about a Weiss-run “60 Minutes,” aka what really worries longtime viewers, true-blue journalists, and any honest supporter of the First Amendment: Rather than superficial changes to how the newsroom’s stories are shared, will there be an ideological shift in how those stories are reported — or what stories are reported at all?

Weiss, who’s nearly as proud of her conservatism as she is of her Zionism, validated those fears from the jump. The David Ellison-appointee (who has a fan in Donald Trump) reportedly introduced herself to “60 Minutes” producers by asking, “Why does the country think you’re biased?” Then she spiked a story critical of the Trump administration and, six months later, fired the venerated contributor Scott Pelley after he accused her of “murdering” the program. Her tenure is only possible because Ellison acquired CBS’ parent company, Paramount, which, in turn, only seemed possible because the network settled a controversial lawsuit against “60 Minutes” brought on by President Trump.

And yet “60 Minutes” — the country’s highest-rated news program for five decades — is what Americans consider biased?

Perhaps there’s an argument for bias now, when the only framing of the president’s “deeply unpopular” war in Iran is under the flattering guise of saving a soldier from behind enemy lines (Episode 1, “Shot Down Over Iran”). Or when Douthat helped Republican Senator Thom Tillis sell copies of his book by praising him for voting along party lines while “talking and maneuvering like a maverick” (Episode 3, “The Thom Tillis Tightrope”). Or when the best, most substantial story of the season (Episode 4, “Lost Sheep”) led to reports of interference that pushed Lesley Stahl to “the brink of quitting.”

These are the only biases, the only changes, viewers can see. Maybe more are coming. Or maybe the steady, unobtrusive creep of conservatism has been the idea all along.

#14. Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won’t Fix Hollywood’s Ills

A coalition hopes to build on momentum behind a U.S. tax incentive to restore a version of 'fin-syn' rules

It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.

The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And ever since the FCC did away with fin-syn 30 years ago, producers and agents have been longing for its return. Related Stories Julia Stiles Is 'Crying' at 'DWTS' Rehearsals Ahead of Heath Ledger Tribute: 'Bringing Back So Many Memories' Law Roach Wants to Try Acting: ‘If I’m Terrible at It, at Least I Tried’

Now, with momentum building behind a U.S. film incentive, they are hoping the moment is ripe to recreate fin-syn for the streaming era. They argue it would bring a jolt of creativity and a spirit of enterprise to a business stuck in a creative slump. Popular on Variety

The major agencies — WME, CAA and UTA — announced last week that they are forming a coalition with production companies including Imagine Entertainment and Legendary to push for legislation that would force streamers to buy at least 50% of their original content from independent producers. The legislation would also limit the length of licensing terms, reviving secondary markets that have largely withered away.

Their message is that Hollywood ails not only from runaway production, but also from a consolidated ecosystem that limits creativity and makes it harder for producers, writers and actors to profit from their labor.

“The tax incentive may change where the production shoots, but it doesn’t change who owns and profits from it,” argued Ken Ziffren, co-founder of Ziffren Brittenham LLP, who has been campaigning for a restoration of fin-syn for decades. “We think the tax legislation only goes so far to help our industry and it’s not a complete effort, and it can’t be a complete effort, unless it’s paired with a modernized ownership framework.”

Jeff Sagansky, a producer, investor and longtime fin-syn supporter, argued that overseas incentives are not the only reason that U.S. production jobs are going away.

“They’re also going away because of the way the streaming business has consolidated around four players,” he said. “They act as an oligopoly. They’ve got incredible pricing power,” saying the streamers are ordering 30-40% fewer hours of programming than they were a few years ago.

Getting the idea through Congress will be an uphill battle, and will face adamant opposition from Netflix, Amazon and the other streaming platforms. The effort also has the potential to sow division within an industry that has united behind the goal of passing the first-ever federal film incentive.

Supporters wanted to some version of their ideas into the tax credit bill that was introduced to much fanfare in September. But while they had some positive meetings, they were ultimately rebuffed. They are now aiming for 2027, when Democrats are expected to take control of at least one of the houses of Congress.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a co-author of the tax incentive as well as a former producer, said in a statement that she sympathizes with producers’ concerns about industry consolidation and the threat to diverse voices in entertainment.

“My focus right now is on passing our bipartisan national film tax credit bill to put film and television workers back on the job, but I look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to ensure the industry is vibrant for the future,” she said.

The Streaming Innovation Alliance, which includes Netflix and other streamers, issued a statement on Thursday calling the proposal a package of “blunt government mandates” that would “only dampen production and discourage creative risk-taking.”

The Federal Communications Commission adopted the fin-syn rules in 1970, when there were only three TV networks. The rules prevented networks from owning syndication rights in their shows, and later, from owning shows that aired in primetime. The rules are credited with leading to an era of groundbreaking TV, including “All in the Family,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “The Cosby Show.”

The repeal of the rules in the mid-90s spurred a wave of vertical integration, as Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC and Viacom acquired CBS.

Arguing that the end of fin-syn had killed off independent production, a group called the Coalition for Program Diversity urged the FCC to reinstate a version of it. In 2002, the coalition — led by Ziffren — sought a new regulation that 25% of primetime programming come from independent producers. In a deregulatory era, such pleas fell on deaf ears.

Nowadays, streamers typically either make shows themselves or buy from the handful of other major studios. When they do buy from indie producers, they typically take all rights for 10-20 years, locking the producers out of the option of selling into secondary markets.

Mark Vahradian, producer of the “Transformers” franchise and other films, argued that streamers are so powerful that they can dictate those terms, and that dynamic ultimately hurts consumers.

“There’s no incentive for the creators to go out and build something brand new,” said Vahradian, a founding member of Producers United. “That’s why they’re only making sequels and franchise titles. They own those and have no motivation to say ‘Why don’t we do something new?’”

For years there wasn’t much opportunity to do anything about it. But with President Trump vowing to “save” Hollywood from a dramatic downturn, fin-syn supporters see an opening.

The initiative would require an act of Congress, as the FCC’s ambit is limited to the public airwaves.

Andrew Long, a senior fellow at the Free State Foundation, a free-market think tank, argued that the streaming marketplace is far more diversified now than the three-network era of the 1970s.

“It’s hard to find factual predicate that would justify this kind of government intervention in the video distribution marketplace in 2026,” Long said, adding that it could raise First Amendment concerns. “I think there would be high scrutiny, and I think that given the state of the marketplace and the options available, it might not pass muster.”

But Rich Shuter, head of business affairs at UTA, argued that consolidation leaves his agency’s clients without much leverage — and viewers without much choice.

“We’re going back to a situation where you have these streaming conglomerates controlling all the content the country is viewing,” Shuter said. “They’re determining what is being produced.”

Shuter said that more risk-taking will lead to a more vibrant ecosystem.

“We don’t want to stall the federal tax credit from being passed as quickly as possible,” he said. “We hope the administration and Congress recognize this is a supplemental benefit.”

If there’s one thing to know about Taylor Swift (as far as her personal life goes), it’s that she enjoys supporting her husband, Travis Kelce. The Kansas City Chiefs tight end is currently in the middle of his 14th NFL season, and Swift continues to pop up at games here and there. It would seem that in the process of doing that, the singer still can’t avoid the spotlight. This past weekend, while Swift attended a game, she was apparently recorded by a spectator, leading her to apparently call them out. And the whole situation was captured on video.

The Chiefs took on the Los Angeles Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City this past weekend. Amid the event, Taylor Swift was not only on hand but also joined by musician Este Haim, Indiana Fever player Caitlin Clark and mother-in-law Donna Kelce. Swift and co. were in a suite when someone below them pulled out their phone and appeared to start recording. As captured by a TikTok user, Swift saw the fan and seemingly gestured to them to stop recording her and watch the game. Check it out:

Based on the clip, the “Willow” singer wasn’t too pleased with the spectator trying to capture footage of her during the game. Fans on social media weren’t too happy about the situation as well, as many took to the comment section to express disapproval of the onlooker’s actions. Per the responses, many couldn’t seem to fathom how the fan could openly record Swift under that particular set of circumstances. In many ways, the “Bad Blood” singer has become something of a staple at the games at this point. Just weeks ago, Swift also went viral for attending a game with Tom Cruise in September, at which point Kansas City took on the Denver Broncos. Funny enough, Kelce later told Cruise during an interview on his New Heights podcast that Swift had become a football expert since dating him.

Jason Kelce Asked If Taylor Swift Has Halloween Songs, And 3 Tracks Came To My Mind

Since then, there have been questions about the logistics of their union, including their living situation. Insiders allege that the two will have several homes, including one in New York, but that their primary residence is currently Kelce’s house in Kansas.

During their relationship, Swift and Kelce have sought privacy, and that’s especially seemed to be true since they exchanged vows. To that point, Kelce even shut down his brother, Jason, when he inquired about how he spent his birthday with Swift. It’d be an understatement to say that both stars try to shy away from the buzz that surrounds them, so it tracks that Swift would apparently scold an onlooker for recording her.

Regardless of any distractions Taylor Swift may or may not endure moving forward, it wouldn’t be surprising to me if she were to continue attending Chiefs games this season. Such events are special experiences, whether someone’s a general fan of the team or linked to a player like Swift is. Time will tell if she ends up having any more less-than-ideal run-ins with fans in the coming months.

#16. Nathan Fielder Didn’t Want to Be on Camera Until Elizabeth Holmes, Billy Evans Changed His Mind

The 'You Can See Everything' co-director on how he was persuaded to be on screen.

Nathan Fielder says he “definitely” didn’t want to be on camera in his groundbreaking Elizabeth Holmes documentary You Can See Everything.

The co-director and very much on-camera participant in the buzzy A24 film says when he showed up at the beach house rented by Holmes and her husband, Billy Evans, the original plan was to stay in the background — similar to how he’s shown in the film’s early lurking shots.

“I started this thing being like, ‘I’m definitely not gonna be on camera in this,'” Fielder told Wired. “The situation was very intense. She was going to prison … I was very aware this is the final month that she’s gonna have for a decade with her kids and her family.” Related Stories Movies 'You Can See Everything' Triumphs With $15M as 'Street Fighter' Wins Weekend Reporter's Notebook How 'You Can See Everything' Exacts Hollywood's Revenge on Big Tech

Holmes and Evans started asking him questions, drawing him into conversation, and he also realized that he couldn’t just give the duo free rein on camera without any pushback on their narratives.

“Firstly, because I was there, they would keep engaging with me,” Fielder recalled. “So they would be talking to each other, but then they would be like, ‘Nathan, what do you think?’ And I would chime in from off camera. Or if nothing was really happening, I would ask a question to see what they would say about something. But I was off camera, and it was more to prompt a discussion or something like that. Or they would start talking to me, and conversations would go on for long enough that the operators started panning over to me.”

Fielder continued: “But also, they would say stuff that tickled a part of my brain that was like, ‘Something’s off about this.’ Or I feel like this is them trying to do some sort of propaganda. So I would wanna interject to be like, ‘Well, actually, I read this,’ or ‘I thought this was the case.’ We realized, ‘Oh, someone has to push back, and we can’t just let them run whatever show they kinda wanna do.'”

You Can See Everything opened on Friday to $15 million from just 855 North American theaters, blowing away expectations and marking the biggest nonconcert documentary debut since Michael Moore’s 2004 hit Fahrenheit 9/11.

#17. June McDoom Makes Folk Music With the Bass Turned Up

The leaves are a vibrant mix of greens and auburn, casting a warm glow over Greenpoint, Brooklyn, where I meet singer-songwriter June McDoom at her studio. The space, on a scenic block near the water, looks something like a dentist’s office. McDoom shares it with musician Nick Hakim and her partner, Evan Wright; dance music from next door bleeds into the room where they record drums and vocals. “Yeah, it’s definitely a New York situation,” she says.

Her self-titled debut EP, released in 2022, introduced her hushed brand of folk to indie rock spaces. Her recently released debut album, Follow the Light, brings the deep bass of Jamaican dub into McDoom’s intimate productions. McDoom says she knew the sound she was after before she understood what her debut album would say. She imagined the Jamaican records she grew up hearing, plus the harmonies she loved in Joni Mitchell and Judee Sill.

“I knew that before the project started, I wanted to do some sort of fusion between the genres, but I wasn’t really sure how,” she says. “And that was what the album became, just a puzzling process of me trying to put together my different influences.”

Born Alyssa McDoom, she grew up in Florida, where her parents, who moved from Jamaica to the U.S. as children, filled the house with Jamaican music. Her father, a carpenter, built speaker boxes and kept multiple DJ setups around the house.

“They would just build the biggest speakers and see how loud they could get,” she says. She wonders whether his fascination with sound helped shape her own. “I’m naturally, for some reason, attracted to the way that something is recorded, and I listen for it in records. I don’t know why. It could be the fact that my dad was DJing.”

She discovered other kinds of music through films like The Sound of Music and The Graduate. Her family supported her, even when her tastes surprised them; school could be lonelier. “In school, I didn’t have that many friends. I didn’t have a community of musicians until college that I could talk to about music. And I kind of found folk music on my own.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

Returning to Alton Ellis records while developing her own music, she heard new possibilities in something familiar. “I didn’t really know the term rock steady until two years ago,” she says. “I knew the music, but I didn’t know the terminology of the genre.”

McDoom studied voice in New York, initially focusing on jazz. She graduated in 2019, having begun writing the songs for her first EP. She and Wright taught themselves how to record.

“I wanted the record to feel kind of handmade even if it sounded not-perfect,” she says. “I didn’t want it to be like I have my first album and I’m going to change my process completely and make my music sound differently, because I’m not really trying to make it sound perfect. I’m just trying to see how I can grow and see how my music can evolve.”

There was pressure, too, in trying to honor the musicians she loved. “A lot of the artists that I listened to are underground artists that never really had much of a career beyond making a couple projects. And they had lives where they did music but also did other things. I felt a lot of pressure to honor those things, and that made it really hard.”

She did want to change her approach to lyrics. On the EP, the excitement of recording had sometimes carried her past words she wasn’t satisfied with. “So with the album, I just made a really strict rule that I wanted to be really intentional about the lyrics and feel really strong about them before any other process.” Related Content How Reggae Icon Jimmy Cliff Put His 19 Children First Jimmy Cliff Was Reggae’s Humble Hero ‘It’s a Bad Situation’: How Ziggy Marley and His Family Are Working to Help Jamaica Shaggy, Sean Paul Lead Jamaica Strong Benefit Concert for Hurricane Relief

McDoom produces her own projects. She and Wright write separately, then help with each other’s recordings. “So I’ll be like, ‘I really want this bass line,’ and I sing it and then he’ll play it. We understand each other kind of well. We’ve been together for 10 years, so we’ve been growing slowly together, and I feel like we have this pretty good chemistry now.”

Around us, an eight-track reel-to-reel sits above a pair of Ampex preamps, their meters glowing orange. There’s a Roland Space Echo RE-201 on the rack beside it, with a mess of cables trailing down to the wooden floor. A microphone lies across the Sound Workshop mixing desk, and a Roland Jupiter-8 synthesizer is reflected in the studio window. The sill holds a beat-up VHS copy of Boogie Nights alongside a jar of tools. Above the window, a program for D’Angelo’s celebration of life is propped between a record sleeve and two little Sony speakers.

“I think because we went to music school, it kind of messed us up,” she says. “So when we’re working together, we’re pretty technical and we’re pretty analytical.” The two can spend an hour trying to find a particular microphone sound. “We both are in love with finding textures with recording, which takes time.”

She works with tape and a computer, finding uses for old preamps and digital reverb. “I feel like digital has texture too,” she says. “If I’m adding a violin part, should we record it and should it be brighter or should it sound darker and have a lot of reverb on it? I feel like that’s a part of the process that I’m really excited to think about.”

Her family also helped make the record. On “Grandpa,” she brings in her grandfather, who plays banjo and guitar in a band devoted to mento, a form of Jamaican folk music. She considered covering an older song before writing something for him herself.

“Growing up, I would go and see them play at parties and stuff,” she says. “But I felt kind of removed because again, I didn’t fully embrace Jamaican music until recently, and now I’m just like, ‘He’s the coolest person ever. I really want to be in his band.’”

He had played at her college senior recital, but this collaboration happened remotely. “My dad recorded his vocal on his iPhone and sent it to me,” she says. By the time we speak, she has also filmed a version of “Get Out of My Life” with her grandfather’s band.

That song came from a less welcoming relationship. Moving to New York, she had expected to find friends who understood her. “And I was making friends with people that reminded me of the people that I was around when I was a kid that I could tell didn’t really actually like me, and I was kind of the outcast again.”

The song’s title carries some relief. “It’s kind of freeing to realize that someone’s not for you, and it doesn’t have to be this negative, ‘Fuck you, you suck,’” she says. “It was just a message for myself that I don’t need to hold onto people in my life that don’t accept me completely…. The things that are right for you are when you are around people where you can just completely explore and be free. I didn’t even realize I wanted to say that with this record, but all the songs ended up being about that.”

“Without You” is a love song, whatever its title might suggest. “I can’t live without this person because I’ve realized how important they are to my life,” she says, describing the song’s sentiment.

She hears something similar in Judee Sill’s “Emerald River Dance,” which she has covered. “That song feels really sad, but it’s actually a similar sort of message where she’s talking about the pain of life and how you have to experience pain to understand the beauty of life,” she says. “But she says it in the most beautiful way, and she’s referencing nature and grass growing through concrete and stuff.”

She came to understand her album more fully after finishing it. “Even while I was working on it, I wasn’t like, ‘Oh, this is a positive record about finding yourself.’ I still wasn’t even really thinking about it until the record was done and then I could really take in what I made.”

That discovery extended to the sound. “Even with the sound of the record, I feel like it became this dreamy sort of sound that I didn’t intentionally try and do.”

On “Follow the Light,” a reggae groove gives way to a choral passage written by a friend. The song began with an image of McDoom on a dark, rainy road, following a light. Its encouragement has practical applications. “If you’re having a really hard day, just think about the family member that you really want to call that always gives you really good advice. Just put that stuff in front of you instead of the thing that’s driving you crazy.” Trending Stories Miley Cyrus Responds to Criticism of Hollywood Bowl Show: ‘I Am Fully Present’ Bob Dylan Unveiled Yet Another New Guitarist, Covered Randy Newman at Tour Launch Pharrell Trying to 'Rewrite History' and 'Erase' Chad Hugo from Neptunes, Producer Claims Cindy Crawford, Kaia Gerber Pay Tribute to Presley Gerber: ‘Til We Meet Again Our Sweet Boy’

Making the record required a similar trust in what mattered to her. “I’m trying to find myself through my music by including different parts of myself. I hope to encourage people to do that too, because we’re just living in this crazy echo chamber of content. I think people are confused. I’m confused.”

She knows the temptation to make something whose success seems easier to predict. With Follow the Light, she let herself find out what would happen. “I just made it because I thought it could be a special thing for people to hear,” she says. “I wasn’t sure how it would turn out.”

#18. Josh Duhamel Breaks Silence on Ransom Canyon's Surprise Cancellation

Ransom Canyon star Josh Duhamel revealed his "bummed" reaction one month after Netflix shocked fans by canceling the hit drama after just two seasons.

Josh Duhamel was ready for another rodeo.

Over a month after Netflix canceled Ransom Canyon following the release of season two, the actor shared his candid thoughts, admitting he was "bummed" by the unexpected decision.

"I was pretty surprised, if I’m being honest," the 53-year-old told Us Weekly in an interview published Oct. 19. "I thought [it was safe] because the show was No. 1 for almost two weeks and the numbers looked really, really good and people really loved the show."

"I was a little upset with Netflix for not giving the audience another season, because people really did love the show," the Las Vegas alum told the outlet, "but that’s the business. At the same time, I get it. They have their reasons for why things stay and why things go. I don’t always understand those reasons, but it’s not my job to question."

Still, Duhamel—dad to 13-year-old son Axl with ex Fergie as well as 2-year-old son Shepard and newborn daughter Rocca wife Audra Mari—sympathizes with heartbroken viewers. Especially those wanting to see whether his rancher character Staten Kirkland and Minka Kelly’s Quinn O’Grady would officially find their happily ever after together.

"I’ve just gotta move on," he lamented. "I just feel bad for the fans who are really invested in it, and that’s it, unfortunately."

But while Staten may by hanging up his saddle for now, Duhamel is certainly open to reprising the role of a cowboy in the future.

"I really loved playing that character," he reflected. "It was in my wheelhouse, because I remember when I first got the job, I was actually out of my cabin, which isn’t a ranch. But I’m always doing ranch-y type things."

As for his costar Kelly's honest reaction to Ransom Canyon's abrupt cancellation?

"All good things must come to an end. And so it is," the Friday Night Lights alum wrote on Instagram Sept. 11. "Thank you all for giving us two beautiful seasons! I love you forever my Ransom Canyon family!!"

#19. Dan Lin Axed As Netflix Film Boss; Streamer Set To Unveil Earnings Tuesday Amid Stock Slump

UPDATED with statements from Netflix and Lin: Dan Lin is out as film boss at Netflix in a move that has been largely speculated for weeks. Insiders at the streamer have denied that Lin and even Bela Bajaria were on the chopping block, but here we are.

Lin is meeting with his feature staff this morning for a post-mortem.

Ted Sarandos, Netflix co-CEO said this AM: “I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear. Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigor around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.” Related Stories Acquisitions Netflix Strikes Deal With Globo For Brazilian Fare Including 'I'm Still Here' & 'India - A Love Story' Cancellations and Renewals Ju Ji-hoon & Choo Young-woo Return To 'The Trauma Code: Heroes On Call' With Seasons 2 & 3 In Production At Netflix

Lin added, “It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg and Bela for the opportunity.” Watch on Deadline

At Saturday night’s Academy Museum Gala cocktails, we caught up with Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos and asked if more cuts were coming. In what seemed like a polite dodge, he just winked and stepped away. Interpret that as you may. Sarandos was in great spirits at the Gala despite Netflix’s gloomy clouds, chatting up 2x Oscar winner Adrien Brody, Jessica Lange and former Paramount and 20th Film Boss Jim Gianopulos. While this was going, we hear that Lin was informed of his firing over the weekend.

Lin’s firing comes in the wake of Netflix making 1,000 pink-slips given their recent slow growth, and minimal overall viewership spike. Wall Street is bracing for what is expected to be a downer quarter from the OTT service. At the time of this post, Netflix shares were trading at $69.76, -1% at the time of this report. The 52-week share high on Netflix was $124.86. The company-wide town hall this Wednesday at Netflix with Sarandos and co-CEO Greg Peters will certainly be an interesting one.

Many were shocked when the ax swung last week and it missed Lin’s head, landing on his lieutenant co-head of film, Doug Belgrad. It was seen that Belgrad was an extra layer at the top of Netflix’s film brass that could easily be let go, dollar wise. Lin was expected to be safe until Bajaria’s replacement arrived on Oct. 26, Peter Rice. It was at that point in time that the exec was going to assess the situation.

All of this boils down to: Netflix, what is it you exactly want? All of streaming has turned into basic cable as we get farther away from Covid. They looked to Lin in April 2024 post Scott Stuber in order to ratchet down the quantity of features and at a lower cost. Lin arrived to Netflix after being a producer at his own hub, Rideback. Also from 2008-2024, Lin produced movies which minted $6 billion at the global box office. Lin did exactly what Netflix asked, steering away from overpriced $200M-plus, non-downstream features like Red Notice, The Irishman and The Electric State. However, he had a no-nonsense approach to filmmakers. He had no problem reportedly pushing back on prestige content creators like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck. During the Lin regime, one source told us that relationships with filmmakers were fraying. Recently, The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth filmmaker David Fincher opted not to renew his longtime exclusive contract with the streamer. That said, we’re also hearing there was never any bad blood between Fincher and Lin.

During Lin’s run Netflix saw their most viewed movie of all-time, Sony’s Kpop Demon Hunters (325.1M global views). However, that was greenlit under the previous Stuber administration. Lin and Belgrad’s bragging rights include War Machine ($80M production cost, 147M views), animated movie Swapped (144.9M views, which broke into the streamer’s top 10 of all-time), The Rip ($100M production cost, 136M views), Happy Gilmore 2 (135.1M), Apex (129M), Thrash (100M views) and People We Meet on Vacation ($14M production cost, 77.1M). Still there wasn’t a consistent reseeding of the Top 10 Most Popular list like there was during the Stuber era. Also during the Lin regime, he acquired 2x Oscar winner Emila Perez in addition to the streamer’s current awards contender, Cannes winner La Bola Negra.

Just as Lin is being shown the door, Netflix is finally embracing theatrical with respectable window releases and the reporting of grosses with select Q3, Q4 and Q1 titles, i.e. next year’s $200M+ Greta Gerwig directed Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew. In the four theater NYC and LA launch of La Bola Negra this weekend, Netflix done good on a small scale as the pic notched the best opening per screen average for a Spanish movie of $69,3K and the second best overall for a non-English movie after Parasite‘s $131K.

If Netflix wants their movies to be a gong around the world, then they need to embrace theatrical. That’s an ironic maneuver for them, because Wall Street doesn’t want them to be a traditional motion picture studio. In the streamer’s pursuit of Warner Bros, Sarandos began to drink the Kool-Aid on theatrical, conceding to a 45-day exclusive theatrical window (but to streaming, not PVOD; still not an ideal situation for exhibitors or filmmakers).

Now that Netflix is reporting grosses, will they spend for the weekend win? Before they would shove films into limited theaters to qualify for Oscars, which also doubled as an in-theater advertisement for the service. So far Netflix’s No. 1 movie at the weekend box office was late August 2025’s Kpop Demon Hunters Singalong with $19M.

It’s interesting to note that at a presser earlier this year, Bajaria and Lin were not in lockstep when asked about the streamer’s future with theatrical after losing the Warner Bros. bid. Following Sarandos’ public campaign to guarantee an exclusive 45-day theatrical window, Bajaria took Netflix’s standard line about theatrical: it’s not what the company is about; it’s there for stunting purposes. Lin was more optimistic saying “Give us time.”

After being passed over by Skydance for top jobs at the new Paramount Warner Bros. post-merger, we hear that former WB Motion Picture Bosses Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy are in the home stretch this week of finalizing the payout of their WB contracts by David Ellison. Until they’re closed, they can’t entertain any job offers. Those close to De Luca tell us he’d have no problems reporting into Rice if offered the job, however, Netflix would need to make a fire-breathing commitment to theatrical. The notion of a 45-day theatrical window to streaming isn’t a prospect that De Luca (and Abdy) could make to the filmmakers they’ve worked with, i.e. Ryan Coogler, Paul Thomas Anderson, Ridley Scott. The notion that the duo are bound to raise capital for their own feature operation seems like the more practical future for them.

All this smoke over De Luca and Abdy heading to Netflix came about due to a friendly lunch with Sarandos. This has morphed into gossip that Sarandos was full-on courting the duo.

If Sarandos and Rice bring the filmmaker-friendly duo in, the question is whether they’ll put any guardrails on them. When it came to De Luca and Abdy justifying the lofty costs for Anderson’s One Battle After Another, Coogler’s Sinners, Tom Cruise’s Digger and so on, David Zaslav didn’t blink an eye. Will Sarandos allow them the same greenlight independence he granted Stuber? Or will he expect them to count coins like Lin? Riddle us that, Mr. Sarandos.

“Netflix isn’t a place where they talk about film,” says one creator who has worked with them, “They’re all about the process, the algorithm and breaking the code, which still makes Lin a good workhorse for them as he’s also about process.”

There’s a rumor out there, and that is despite the notion that De Luca and Abdy are always joined at the hip, historically they haven’t been. Some believe there’s a world that Abdy could entertain an offer sans De Luca from Netflix once her WB contract is paid out. “Sure, there is a world where that could happen,” says one source with knowledge of the situation.

Still, there’s no solid definite word out there as to who might fill Lin’s vacancy. No interview process going on as of yet.

A rival studio boss complimented over the weekend, “I think you’ll be surprised as to who Peter Rice selects.”

Meanwhile, we hear that Lin will not be headed back to the label he created, Rideback, though he still has an interest in the company. Rideback and Netflix have a production deal.

But still, no matter how the greenlight process is improved at Netflix, there’s a new sign of the times for the streamer.

“If you want to know where the young crowd is looking, Meta just introduced Muse. People are heading back to cinemas, and streaming has become basic cable,” said one Netflix vet, “They can change shuffle as many executives as they want, and it still won’t make a difference.”
