Why is Netflix bringing in executives from studios that failed to lead their previous companies out of a rut? If they were able to successfully lead Fox and WB out of their problems, those studios would still be here today. What is the rationale of bringing them in? Is plan to execute a slow decline to be bought and rolled into another company down the line?

I watch a lot of movies, at least one a day, and I haven’t seen any of the movies you mentioned as being hits for Lin. I’m not sure the movies he green lit have had much of a cultural impact. And if I had to cut back on streaming services, Netflix would be one of the first to go. Our family hardly ever watches it anymore.

Netflix should fire their HR and PR team for handling layoffs like this. They are beyond incompetent.

#20. Watch Cardi B Bring the Brash & Beauty to NPR for Unapologetic Tiny Desk Concert

Her debut for the popular series was long overdue.

Cardi B’s Tiny Desk Concert has been one of the most anticipated in recent memory, and she delivered on the hype with an energetic set on Monday (Oct. 19).

The Bronx native brought her arena hits to the intimate setting of the NPR offices in Washington, D.C., for a boisterous run through her decorated catalog.

Rocking a suit jacket and latex pants, Cardi was flanked by a complete live band, and the dress code was all black because they were dressed to kill their performance.

The Grammy-winning rapper fittingly introduced her set with “Hello” from Am I the Drama? and moved into another standout from her sophomore album, “ErrTime.” “Let me get some water. You know I be smoking cigarettes,” Cardi quipped during a brief intermission.

Cardi B slowed down the pace for “Man of Your Word” as she ruminated on the deceit and cheating from a previous relationship.”You never loved me, f–k n—a,” she spewed.

Invasion of Privacy‘s “Be Careful” followed, and by that point, Cardi was sick of being in her feelings and the emotions tied to the last couple of tracks. “Change the vibes,” she ordered.

It was time for the hits, as the room immediately felt lighter as Billboard Hot 100 No. 1 hit “Up” led into her 2026 single “AH HA,” and then Cardi’s 2017 breakout anthem, “Bodak Yellow.”

The rapper can bring comedic relief to any room, and she joked about being hungry and not having any Maryland crab cakes or celery sticks in her rider. Even in the latex pants, Cardi could still move her hips as she swayed into her Tiny Desk closer and Diamond-certified Hot 100 No. 1 hit “I Like It” to finish things off.

It’s been a busy October for Cardi B, who turned 34 years old on Oct. 11. She surprised the Bardi Gang with a single on Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, which arrived earlier this month and is titled “Don’t Chart.”

The “WAP” rapper will also be the first artist to ever accept the Global Woman of the Year award at Billboard Canada Women In Music 2026 on Nov. 24.

#22. You Can See Everything Deserves An Oscar Nomination It Probably Won't Get

Spoilers for "You Can See Everything" follow.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's new three-hour documentary "You Can See Everything" is generating more buzz than seemingly any doc in recent history. A secretive project that obtained almost mythical status when we learned about it a few weeks ago, the documentary looks at Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster behind Theranos. The filmmakers were granted unprecedented access to Holmes in the days leading up to the start of her 11-year prison sentence, and Fielder is our guide as he spends countless hours with Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans.

A jaw-dropping saga unfolds, resulting in a film that really does live up to the hype: This is one of the best movies of the year, and one of the most fascinating documentaries I have ever seen. The reaction to "You Can See Everything" has been so resoundingly positive that many are wondering if the film could do something historic and become the first documentary nominated for Best Picture at the Oscars.

But that's not what I want to talk to you about. While no doc has been nominated for Best Picture before, I could actually see the Academy finally making an exception here. But there's another Oscar nomination I think the film deserves that it has absolutely no chance of nabbing: Best Supporting Actress for Amanda Seyfried.

Amanda Seyfried played Holmes in the Hulu series "The Dropout," and one of the many twists and turns "You Can See Everything" has in its back pocket is a brain-breaking appearance from Seyfried herself. About an hour into the movie, after the real Holmes heads to prison, Nathan Fielder brings Seyfried into the narrative. And this isn't a cameo, either: Seyfried has a significant role in the film. I'd argue the film wouldn't be as successful without her.

Seyfried engages in elaborate re-enactments to play Holmes once again to recreate moments Fielder and company didn't or couldn't capture on camera, but she also becomes Fielder's co-investigator, looking at the footage he shot of the real Holmes and offering invaluable feedback. One of the running themes of the film is how sympathetic the real Holmes can come across to some people, and indeed, Fielder seems to genuinely like her and care about her. Seyfried, however, seems to the voice of reason, able to look past Holmes' huge blue eyes and her potentially manipulative presence. She's also quick to clock that Billy Evans, who ends up serving as the film's villain, is bad news (although to be fair, you'd probably have to be blind to miss that).

Documentaries do not get acting Oscar nominations — how could they? They're meant to be showing us the truth, so we don't tend to think of them as having "acting." Yet one of the many themes of "You Can See Everything" is the nature of documentaries themselves, and how you can't always believe what you see on screen. As Seyfried herself says near the end of the film, "It's complicated."

Other than Fielder, who has great instincts when it comes to getting people to open up on camera, Seyfried has the toughest part to play in "You Can See Everything." Not only does she deliver an uncanny performance as Holmes in the re-enactments, but she essentially drives the narrative further by helping Fielder get to some semblance of the truth. I found her presence to be enchanting and brilliant, and the way she's able to seemingly cut through all the B.S. underscores how sharp Seyfried is, like a great private detective cracking a case.

"You Can See Everything" would be a good movie without Seyfried's presence, but adding her to the story elevates the film to a whole other level. She's essential to making the film work, and she deserves some sort of awards season recognition for that (and it would be only fair since the Oscars previously snubbed her incredible work in "The Testament of Ann Lee"). Do the right thing, Academy: Nominate Amanda Seyfried.

#23. Yet Another Netflix Stunner: Dan Lin Out as Film Chief

It looks as if those Netflix cuts and trims are not over just yet.

Netflix’s head of film, Dan Lin, has been let go from the gig after less than three years at the streamer, a source with knowledge of his exit told IndieWire. Lin is the latest big name cut, joining the firing of chief content officer Bela Bajaria last week and a large-scale set of layoffs that have so far impacted about 1,000 Netflix employees. The layoffs also impacted high-ranking members of Lin’s team, including Doug Belgrad and indie film head Sheroum Kim.

Variety adds via multiple sources that Lin was let go at the start of the weekend and will address his teams throughout the day Monday. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, and rumors have abounded that ousted Warner Bros. film chiefs Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy could be in the running, but Netflix is clearly in the midst of a major restructuring that goes beyond layoffs. Lauded film and TV executive Peter Rice has already been tapped to replace Bajaria. Related Stories Breakout ‘Behemoth!’ Musician Lukas Frank Reveals What It’s Like to Give Tony Gilroy a Rewrite Léa Seydoux Became Fearless After the Controversies of ‘Blue Is the Warmest Color’ — She’s Doing It Again with ‘Gentle Monster’

IndieWire has reached out to Netflix for comment.

Lin joined Netflix in February 2024, replacing longtime film chief Scott Stuber. He came over from his own production house, Rideback, which built the “LEGO” film franchise, Stephen King’s popular “It” adaptations, and the “Sherlock Holmes” movies. During his time at the streamer, Lin greenlit and acquired over 85 movies, including “Apex,” “Emilia Pérez,” and “Train Dreams,” plus the upcoming titles “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” and Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew.”

As IndieWire noted earlier this year, “One of Lin’s hallmarks since taking over has been to organize his film team leaders based on genre, so individual executives are focused on producing 3-4 films a year each within distinct genres like comedy, drama, horror, sci-fi, etc.,” and it’s unclear if the streamer will continue with those distinctions as it continue to re-organize its business.

Though he did champion some ambitious foreign films and art house indies that were awards darlings, Lin had a reputation as being more interested in commercial fare rather than auteur-driven films than his predecessor Stuber. Some of his hits have included “War Machine,” “The Rip,” “People We Meet on Vacation,” and “Remarkably Bright Creatures.” And though it originated as a Sony Animation film, he was at the helm when Netflix’s biggest title of all time came out, “KPop Demon Hunters.”

And yet Netflix across the board, not just on the film side, has struggled with engagement as it tries to compete with the likes of YouTube for total hours spent viewing. Lin’s approach has been to soften its position on theatrical, starting this weekend with reporting box office data for “La Bola Negra” for the first time in Netflix’s history, and it hopes to reach an even larger audience when next year it releases Gerwig’s “Narnia” in wide release with a healthy theatrical exclusive window before it premieres on Netflix.

Variety first reported the news of Lin’s exit.

#24. Collage, a New Management and Investment Company, Launches as a Bridge Between AI-First Studios and Hollywood (EXCLUSIVE)

As Hollywood continues to navigate the plethora of questions surrounding AI and its place in the industry, one former talent agent hopes to be the link between everyone involved.

Enter Collage, a new management and investment company aimed at helping AI-first production companies navigate the Hollywood pipeline. Founded in July by former UTA agent Dante DeSario and media investor Michael Lambert, who worked within the talent agency’s independent film group before leaving in March, the company has completed a seed funding round — the amount of which DeSario would not disclose — backed by a suite of investors and advisers: Black Bear and Fundamental Films, Dennis Miller, Blue Deer Media, GOAL Ventures, AGC Studios, Roy Lee, Marty Bowen, Todd Lieberman, Todd Garner, Barry Porter, George Huber, Max Michael and Ric Roman Waugh, among others. The firm, based in Beverly Hills, currently has five full-time employees and roughly a dozen part-time staffers. Related Stories 'La Bola Negra' to Receive Gotham Vanguard Tribute at Gotham Film Awards (EXCLUSIVE) Inde Navarrette on Meeting Pamela Anderson, Hosting ‘SNL’ and X-Men Stunt Training

The earliest inklings for Collage came in February 2024, after DeSario got his hands on an early demo of OpenAI’s short-lived video generator Sora. After meeting with — and signing — some filmmakers who played with the generator and seeing them build their own companies focused on AI productions, DeSario realized that his own venture could “support these artists in a way that they needed help in various degrees” while helping “Hollywood navigate this, frankly, incredibly sensitive time over AI.” Popular on Variety

Much of DeSario’s work includes aiding the initial batch of companies — which includes AI studios like Asteria, Native Foreign, Obsidian, and Jason Zada’s Secret Level — as they navigate Hollywood guilds, “studio bureaucrats,” copyright issues and demonstrations of the technology’s capabilities. DeSario’s firm also acts as an investment company, though he would not disclose which companies he’s invested in. “We’re here to offer the menu of things to what this new category needs,” he says.

On the Hollywood side, DeSario wants to demonstrate to studios which companies are making human-led work and “who to stay away from” in an era of seemingly never-ending upstarts.

Collage’s model comes as legacy Hollywood companies figure out how to engage with AI at a time when consternation persists among both creatives and audiences over issues surrounding jobs, slop content and the impact on creativity. DeSario hopes Collage can act as “infrastructure,” a bridge between the various stakeholders in the industry that allows more stories to be told while encouraging acceptance of the technology.

“I’m an independent film guy,” he said. “I just want to help filmmakers get their projects made. That was my whole intention, and realizing that this is something that is unlike what a lot of people think. There’s a lot of fallacy. It’s not pushing a button. There’s real craft and real differentiation between those who can have taste and want to tell stories and helping them get out there.”

He’s also hoping that, as more of these companies emerge, they’ll be able to compete with and complement the companies that have maintained footprints in Hollywood through their traditional filmmaking offerings. “The legacy system should be inviting them because they’re incredible craftspeople to work with all of the various people who are already working on films,” DeSario says.

A goal for him, he says, is to help audiences witness the AI version of a “Toy Story” moment, or a film developed with AI that breaks through with general moviegoers.

“I’ve personally seen work that has made me feel something,” he says. “You want to feel something. I’ve had that experience. I think a lot of people haven’t had that experience, and because it’s hard to feel something when there’s so much fear in the air. I want to help show the general audiences and help facilitate what I’ve seen to everyone else because it’s pretty potent.”

Michael Che’s Netflix special, Michael Che: Shot in Minnesota, debuted on the Top 10 list this weekend. The comedian’s pretty proud of the fact, though he feels like he may have set himself up for some uncomfortable moments by taking press in the days leading up to its release. In fact, in a new post, he said he believes the grassroots initiative was the thing that brought eyeballs to his new special… and not the brouhaha surrounding what happened with a recent SNL guest host on the air.

To be clear, Michael Che has told some hairy jokes on SNL before, particularly whilst doing joke swap with Colin Jost. Regardless, he was not the subject of attention during the NBC sketch comedy series’ October 10th episode. Instead, it was host Shane Gillis who shocked audiences, the Internet and even some people previously involved in the show with commentary about women’s gym clothing during his monologue. His use of the word “whores” to describe women getting their workout on garnered more headlines than his f-bomb.

Che was seemingly a little mad this whole thing went down because it happened right before his SNL special dropped. He’d (likely) already committed to press for the special, and knew deep down that people would want to talk about Shane Gillis. Indeed, there was a very uncomfortable exchange when he appeared on NBC’s Today.

Now, in a new post on his Instagram, he seems to be implying he should have skipped the press and let word of mouth do its thing.

A post shared by Michael Che (@chethinks)

Now, by the time of this writing Monday morning, Che’s special had fallen out of the Top 10. Intriguingly, other special Mojo Brookzz I Know You Lying has been going strong in the Top 10 since it landed on the Netflix release schedule on October 6th. Netflix has a tendency to do really with comedy specials and has developed a loyal fanbase when it comes to that type of content on the streamer, so I would have liked to have seen Che’s special stick it out on the list a little longer, and maybe it could have used a bit more word of mouth.

I’ll also just mention, I only heard about his special because Che started commenting on how Gillis’ joke would impact his press for Shot in Minnesota. It hit the 2026 TV schedule on October 13th -- three days after Gillis' SNL episodes, and Netflix started recommending the special to me over the weekend after I started researching the topic. So, there’s certainly different ways to get the word out there.

#27. Amy Helm Was Ousted From Levon Helm Studio in ‘Illegal Takeover,’ New Lawsuit Claims

Levon Helm‘s daughter Amy has filed a new lawsuit claiming she was improperly ousted from Levon Helm Studio earlier this year in what she describes as an “illegal takeover” of the Woodstock venue.

The lawsuit centers around the alleged actions of Brian Parillo, a local musician and friend of Levon Helm’s, who was given a 10 percent shareholder stake in Levon Helm Studios (also known as the Barn), when it was incorporated in the mid-2000s. Parillo was put in charge of the Barn earlier this year with the backing of both Helm’s widow (and Amy’s stepmother), Sandra “Sandy” Helm, and Levon’s former manager, Barbara O’Brien (another minority shareholder).

According to the new lawsuit, Parillo’s “illegal takeover of LHS was achieved through a series of invalid corporate acts.” First, in June 2025, the suit claims that Parillo convinced Sandy and “another shareholder” to join him in signing a shareholder consent to remove Amy as director of LHS. Then, in late May and early June, the suit claims Parillo got Sandy to step down as director of LHS and assign Parillo her voting rights. (Sandy is not named as a defendant.)

“Every one of these corporate acts is void,” the lawsuit claims. It states that LHS’ Certificate of Incorporation “does not permit shareholders to act by written consent of fewer than all shareholders,” and Amy “never signed any of the consents.” A shareholder meeting was never “noticed or held,” the suit adds.

Reps for Parillo and Levon Helm Studios did not immediately return a request for comment.

The lawsuit further alleges that these moves should be considered void “because Parillo produced them through undue influence over a vulnerable person who lacked the ability to understand the nature and consequences.” Specifically, the lawsuit claims Parillo “coerced” Sandy into signing the 2025 shareholder consent agreement after Amy alleged, in a separate matter, that Sandy had “misappropriated… hundreds of thousands of dollars” in Levon Helm estate assets. Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

With the new lawsuit, Amy said she is seeking to “reassert control of LHS,” asking for an order that would remove Parillo and recognize her as director and president. She also wants the court to declare Parillo’s actions void, and state he had no authority to bring a federal lawsuit that was filed against Amy in August.

The new lawsuit marks a significant escalation in the dispute over the Barn, which burst into public view earlier this year. In previous court filings related to the Helm estate matter, Amy claimed that Sandy was susceptible to manipulation and accused Parillo of “financial exploitation and elder abuse.” She also suggested that, during a confrontation at the Barn after the shareholder meeting, Sandy expressed regret over backing Parillo and said she’d been “conned.”

Sandy has denied Amy’s claims and has continued to voice support for Parillo. Parillo has also denied this, accusing Amy of denying him and other LHS shareholders access to corporate records.

In August, the Barn’s new management team sued Amy, accusing her of financial mismanagement during her tenure as president between 2017 and 2026. The suit claimed that a recent review of LHS’ financial records “uncovered millions of dollars of self-dealing transactions apparently authorized by Amy, or for her benefit.”

According to the suit, Amy charged $400,000 to LHS to cover everything from touring expenses to “personal tax repayments, her health and life insurance, her driver, her personal lawyer’s fees,” and more. Of this $400,000, the suit claims that $167,000 was “apparently so unrelated to the company” that Helm’s accountant (also named as a defendant) couldn’t “justify them as legitimate expenses” and categorized them as “Due from Amy.”  Trending Stories Miley Cyrus Responds to Criticism of Hollywood Bowl Show: ‘I Am Fully Present’ Bob Dylan Unveiled Yet Another New Guitarist, Covered Randy Newman at Tour Launch Pharrell Trying to 'Rewrite History' and 'Erase' Chad Hugo from Neptunes, Producer Claims Cindy Crawford, Kaia Gerber Pay Tribute to Presley Gerber: ‘Til We Meet Again Our Sweet Boy’

At the time, Amy released a statement saying, “I unilaterally deny any and all of these baseless, spurious allegations.”

After Amy’s ouster from the barn, many artists canceled shows at the venue, citing solidarity with Helm’s daughter. Since then, the Barn only hosted a pair of concerts from guitarist and singer, Laith Al-Saadi, in late September.

#28. Sony Pictures Television Names Lauren Glaubach EVP Distribution, Digital & Social Platforms

Sony Pictures Television has tapped Lauren Glaubach for the newly created role of EVP, Distribution, Digital and Social Platforms.

Reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, Presidents of Distribution & Networks, SPT, Glaubach will help drive Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and digital platform for both film and television content, “while building connections with audiences and creating opportunities for sustained engagement and revenue.”

The hiring of Glaubach follows news earlier this month that SPT distribution and networks co-president Mike Wald would be retiring at year-end after 32 years with the company, and the naming of Spivak and LIttman as Presidents of Distribution & Networks, Related Stories Executives Sony Ups Tim Erickson To CEO Of Peanuts Worldwide, Appoints Ken Ohtake As Chairman News 'Beyond The Spider-Verse' Director Bob Persichetti On "Limitless" Fan Expectations And "Never Saying No"

Leading Sony Pictures’ global strategy on social and digital platforms, Glaubach will shape and drive a comprehensive growth and monetization strategy that balances long-term brand stewardship with revenue generation, per SPT. She will oversee efforts to deepen audience engagement, extend the reach of the studio’s marketing and promotional initiatives, and unlock new opportunities across the company’s film and television library. She also will lead the continued growth of Sony Pictures’ digital channel portfolio, maximizing the value of the studio’s extensive collection of franchises, brands, and intellectual property across social and digital platforms. Watch on Deadline

“Lauren has spent her career working at the intersection of content, platforms, and audiences, and has a proven track record of building and growing digital businesses,” said Spivak and Littmann. “We’re very pleased to have her join SPT and are excited about what we can accomplish together.”

Glaubach joins SPT from Pinterest, where she served as Vice President, Head of Global Content Partnerships, leading an international team responsible for overseeing the platform’s content producer network and growing creator communities. Prior to Pinterest, she spent more than a decade at YouTube in senior strategy, programming, partnerships and operations roles, most recently serving as Director, Global Head of Kids & Family Content Partnerships & Programming. During her tenure at YouTube, Glaubach managed a partner portfolio of more than 500 channels spanning traditional media and YouTube-first creators, and built a creator ecosystem across YouTube Kids, Supervised Experiences and the main YouTube app.

“The ways audiences engage with entertainment continue to evolve, creating meaningful opportunities to extend the reach and impact of the stories and franchises they love,” said Glaubach. “I’m excited to join Sony Pictures and work with this talented team to develop digital experiences that meet audiences where they are, deepen their connection to our content, and open up new possibilities for our iconic brands.”

Her appointment comes at a time of significant momentum across Sony Pictures Television’s digital business. Recent initiatives include the announcement of Jeopardy! YouTube Edition Volume 2, the launch of Reading Rainbow on YouTube, and a newly announced partnership with Professor Brian Cox to develop premium original content for global digital audiences.

Earlier in her career, Glaubach held strategy, brand management and marketing roles at The Walt Disney Company and BloomSpot. She earned an MBA from Harvard Business School and a B.A. from Princeton University.

#29. Marshals' Most Shocking Deaths: From 'Yellowstone' Alums to Country Stars

Marshals is only two seasons in, but there have already been numerous character deaths.

Before CBS picked up the show centered on Kayce Dutton (Luke Grimes), the Paramount+ franchise started with Taylor Sheridan‘s hit series Yellowstone, which premiered in 2018. Fans got to know the Duttons — including Kayce and Monica (Kelsey Asbille), who remained at the center of the show until the finale.

The original show came to an end in 2024, later expanding its universe with Marshals and Dutton Ranch. Marshals quickly found success when it premiered on CBS in 2026 — but it also shocked existing fans with the reveal that Monica had died.

Puck reported at the time that Marshals ran into issues when plotting out the new CBS show centered on Kayce’s life after Yellowstone. To avoid making the new series too identical to its flagship, Marshals chose to remove Monica from the narrative and shift the voice of the show to be more of a fast-paced procedural.

According to the newsletter, Paramount allegedly worked with lawyers for months on how to successfully feature other Yellowstone leads Beth Dutton (Kelly Reilly) and Rip Wheeler (Cole Hauser) in their own Dutton Ranch spinoff without facing potential legal issues over their story being too similar to the OG show.

CBS and Paramount have not publicly addressed the Puck report.

Marshals also built out the world with stars Arielle Kebbel, Ash Santos, Tatanka Means, Brett Cullen and Logan Marshall Green. To keep the audience on their toes, Marshals managed to kill off three characters within two seasons.

Keep scrolling to see who has died on Marshals — so far:

The series premiere revealed that Monica died after being diagnosed with cancer. Her death resulted in Kayce becoming a single father to their son, Tate, while mourning the loss of his wife.

Cal’s and Kayce’s former Navy SEAL teammate — who was played by Riley Green — was involved in a fire in season 1. He initially seemed to be on the mend despite sustaining second-degree burns and inhaling a lot of smoke, but when Kayce, Cal and Andrea (Ash Santos) returned to the hospital at the end of their shift to check on Garrett, they were informed he had died.

Kayce’s love interest Dolly (Ellyn Jameson) was killed after a standoff between him and her dad, Tom Weaver (Chris Mulkey).

#30. 10 Best Superhero TV Shows Not Made By Marvel Or DC, Ranked

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While DC and Marvel are the biggest names in the superhero genre across virtually all media, there have always been other companies with their own superhero properties. Just as there are fantastic superhero movies not made by Marvel or DC, there are television shows in the genre from companies other than the Big Two. These can be other original superhero concepts while others are based on established comic book properties from different publishers. Sometimes the stories are parodies and postmodern takes on the genre, while others are more conventional narratives.

We're taking a look at the superhero television series beyond the usual fare from the Big Two multimedia companies. These shows all feature main characters using their extraordinary abilities to protect the world, often against bona fide supervillains. From hit animated series to ambitious live-action shows in the streaming age, there is no shortage of superheroes beyond the usual suspects. These are the 10 best superhero TV shows not made by Marvel or DC ranked, highlighting just how diverse the genre truly can be.

In between recording My Chemical Romance albums, frontman Gerard Way and Gabriel Bá launched the moody comic book series "The Umbrella Academy" in 2007. The show centers on a group of adopted siblings who were raised as superheroes by the eccentric Reginald Hargreeves (Colm Feore). Reuniting years later as adults following Reginald's death, the group contends with their unresolved trauma just in time to defend the world against a new threat. Later seasons feature the ensemble exploring the consequences of tampering with the timeline, leading to an adventure with reality hanging in the balance.

With Hargreeves as a clear pastiche of Professor X, "The Umbrella Academy" offers its own commentary on found family superhero teams. Like its comic book source material, this comes with a visibly quirky sensibility to its storytelling, with the work of filmmaker Wes Anderson influencing the "Umbrella Academy" aesthetic. But more than being kooky just for the sake of it, the show excels when it leans into its family dynamics and distinct trappings. A breezy four-season watch, "The Umbrella Academy" runs off the rails during its final season but its character arcs and interplay earn it a place here.

For many a millennial who grew up in the late '80s and early '90s, one of the defining superhero series of the era was "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles." Based on the hit indie comic book by Kevin Eastman and Peter Laird, the first animated adaptation premiered in 1987 with an undeniably catchy and propulsive theme song. The show centers on its titular quartet of anthropomorphic reptilian martial artists defending New York City from the shadows. In between battling various supervillains menacing the Big Apple, the heroes in a half-shell enjoy pizza and skateboarding around town.

The number of pastiches that flooded the market, like "Biker Mice from Mars" and "Street Sharks," really underscores how big a deal "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" was at the time. While certainly not always the case in the industry, the decision to turn the gritty, violent comic into a family-friendly cartoon was a smart one that paid significant dividends. The show went on to run for an impressive 10 seasons, outlasting the live-action movie series that it helped inspire by several years. Of all the superhero cartoons to surface in the '80s, "Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles" is the one we're still talking about the most four decades later.

One of the most underrated Netflix original series is "Raising Dion," a two-season postmodern take on the superhero genre. The show is named for protagonist Dion Warren (Ja'Siah Young) raised by his single mother Nicole (Alisha Wainwright) after the death of his father. This is complicated by Dion developing superpowers, leading him to be targeted by those looking to exploit his abilities. By Season 2, Dion grows into his role as a young superhero, only for a sinister entity linked to Dion's origins, escalating their feud with the world in the crossfire.

A more grounded take on the superhero genre than its contemporaries, "Raising Dion" mixes in family drama and coming-of-age stakes for good measure. Those elements coalescing magnificently comes largely from strong performances by Young and Wainwright, giving the story a firm emotional foundation to build from. At the same time, the show builds a taut conflict that involves possession and shadowy figures that maintain the thrills. Perfect to binge over the course of a long weekend, "Raising Dion" keeps its action more grounded but no less exciting in its execution.

While there is no shortage of anime shows with super-powered characters like "Dragon Ball" or "Jujutsu Kaisen," series with more conventionally superheroes are a bit rarer. One anime above the usual super sentai fare is the action comedy "One-Punch Man," based on the manga by ONE and Yusuke Murata. The show follows an unassuming aspiring superhero named Saitama who possesses the ability to defeat any opponent with a single blow. However, Saitama remains under-appreciated due to a number of circumstances, even as the League of Monsters attack humanity.

"One-Punch Man" is a hilarious anime parody of superhero stories from the ridiculous costumed personas that heroes come up with to its subversion of super-powered spectacle. While its core premise may seem like a one-note gag, the sight of Saitama effortlessly obliterating enemies never gets old. In fact, whenever the series tries to move away from Saitama's comedically overpowered strength, the less effective it becomes. While later seasons aren't on par with the show's inaugural run, "One-Punch Man" remains good enough overall to earn a spot on this list.

Among the best '90s cartoons is "The Powerpuff Girls," Cartoon Network's hit action comedy that debuted in 1998. The titular trio are three sisters created from sugar, spice, and everything nice along with a healthy dose of the super-powered compound Chemical X. This makes them the best-suited to defend their hometown from a whole host of supervillains, as long as they can do it before bedtime. The ensemble is led by Blossom (Cathy Cavadini), joined by her precocious sisters Bubbles (Tara Strong) and Buttercup (E.G. Daily) as they keep their city safe from harm.

The charm in "The Powerpuff Girls" is that it mixes requisite superhero action while keeping the fact that its main characters are still young children very much in sight. Conflicts stem primarily from childhood struggles like being afraid of the dark or dealing with boys, punctuated by a supervillain showdown. The action usually aren't throwaway sequences either, but infused with a vibrant, almost punk rock, energy to them as the girls make short work of their enemies. A self-aware celebration of the superhero genre, "The Powerpuff Girls" remains one of the best Cartoon Network originals.

British television offers its own deconstructionist take on the superhero genre with the 2009 series "Misfits." The show revolves around a group of young delinquents sentenced to complete community service for various crimes. Caught in a freak electrical storm, the ensemble emerges with differing superpowers, which they try to keep a secret. This is complicated by others using their newfound powers for more twisted ends, including the formation of a sinister cult, and the group's own rambunctious nature.

There was talk of an American remake of "Misfits" on Freeform but the show really works because of its British perspective on the genre. This includes a dark sense of humor but also a bleaker depiction of consequences stemming from the show's central premise. Try as they might, when mistakes are made, and they're made often, there are lethal repercussions that punctuate the characters' journey. Viciously brutal and sharply funny, "Misfits" never gives its main characters the easy way out, especially after they receive their powers, and it's all the better for it.

One of the marquee titles for Image Comics when the creator-owned comic book publisher launched in 1992 was "Spawn." Created by Todd McFarlane, the comic's titular superhero is a former assassin who is revived as a demonic avenger. A smash hit with readers, Spawn starred in his own HBO original animated series "Todd McFarlane's Spawn," which premiered in 1997. Running for three seasons, the show took advantage of its premium cable platform to include more mature content in line with its comic book source material.

With a level of animation on par with contemporaries like "X-Men: The Animated Series," "Todd McFarlane's Spawn" was the most intense animated superhero show of its time. McFarlane himself hosts the episodes, setting the stage for the story to come, many straight from the pages of the comics. Elevating the whole production is Keith David lending his commanding voice to bring the character to animated life with a real sense of gravitas. With the long-gestating Blumhouse Spawn movie featuring a particularly cursed production history, "Todd McFarlane's Spawn" remains the best adaptation of the hellish superhero.

One last anime series to include on this list is "My Hero Academia," poised to become your next superhero obsession. Based on the manga by Kōhei Horikoshi, the anime adaptation takes place in a world where gifted individuals are born with powers, known in-universe as Quirks. Protagonist Izuku Midoriya is seemingly born without a Quirk but is allowed to enroll in a private high school for superheroes in training. As Izuku develops friendships and rivalries among his classmates, he becomes a pivotal figure in a shadowy plot involving the world's most nefarious supervillains.

If "One-Punch Man" examines superhero tropes under the lens of power-scaling parody, "My Hero Academia" does so as a coming-of-age drama. The costumed action is definitely in abundant supply but the high school premise really does drive the emotional stakes. Canonical to the events of the main series, there were also four theatrically released anime movies set between various seasons. An anime superhero epic that ran for eight seasons, "My Hero Academia" celebrates the genre while introducing the ultimate super-powered teenage feud.

Comic book creators Garth Ennis and Darick Robertson teamed up to launch their pitch-black parody of superheroes with their comic series "The Boys" in 2006. This was adapted into a Prime Video series in 2019, retaining the source material's penchant for crude gags and over-the-top violence. The story features a group of misfits led by the unhinged Billy Butcher (Karl Urban) who keep super-powered individuals in line. The ensemble's primary conflict is with the Seven, a corporate-backed superhero team led by the psychotic ubermensch Homelander (Antony Starr).

"The Boys" sands off the rougher, more misanthropic elements from the comic book, without compromising its brutal nature and dark humor. The Prime Video series leans more into a commentary on corporate and celebrity-run culture, which fuels much of its laughs, while keeping its antagonistic focus on Butcher and Homelander. A popular draw throughout its run, "The Boys" Season 5's viewership numbers stayed strong as a testament to its continued appeal. "The Boys" revels in the gory possibilities of the superhero genre but not without embracing some of its tropes along the way.

To Prime Video's credit, the streaming service boasts being the home of the two best superhero shows on this particular list. "Invincible" is based on the comic book series of the same name by Robert Kirkman, Cory Walker, and Ryan Ottley, faithfully recounting the long-running tale. The story centers on Mark Grayson (Steven Yeun), whose father Omni-Man (J.K. Simmons) is the world's greatest superhero, with Mark developing powers of his own. However, as Mark becomes increasingly involved in the superhero community, he learns how dangerously unpredictable it can be, especially when it comes to the true nature of Omni-Man's extraterrestrial heritage.

More than just topping this list, "Invincible" is one of the best Prime Video shows of all time, whether superheroes are involved or not. This comes from the show, like its source material, visibly celebrating the possibilities of the genre while offering its own postmodern approach. The animation is richly rendered while the all-star voice cast really gets us invested in this colorful ensemble of heroes and villains. And though a largely faithful retelling, "Invincible" makes major and welcome changes from the comics to tell the ultimate superhero coming-of-age story with an ambitiously cosmic scope.

#31. Tim McGraw, Paul Overstreet & Stanley Brothers Inducted Into Country Music Hall of Fame

Billy Strings, Lainey Wilson, Jamey Johnson, Blake Shelton and more were on hand to honor this year's inductees.

On Sunday night (Oct. 18), the Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum inducted its 159th, 160th and 161st members, as Tim McGraw, Paul Overstreet and the Stanley Brothers were awarded country music’s highest distinction, during the 31st Medallion Ceremony, held at the Hall of Fame’s CMA Theater in Nashville. Explore Billy Strings Lainey Wilson Tim McGraw See latest videos, charts and news

Members of the Country Music Hall of Fame, including Vince Gill, Randy Travis, Alabama’s Randy Owen, Ricky Skaggs and Dean Dillon, were also in attendance to usher in the Hall’s newest class members. Related Wolfmother, Ball Park Music and Yothu Yindi to Headline Sydney's Aloha Festival Taylor Swift Joined by Caitlin Clark at Sunday's Chiefs Game Fans Choose Tate McRae's 'Housewife' as This Week's Favorite New Music

CMA CEO Sarah Trahern, who will retire at the end of the year after leading the CMA for more than a decade, spoke during her final time helping to lead the Medallion Ceremony.

“Telling 40 people or their loved ones they are going into the Country Music Hall of Fame is one of the biggest honors of my career,” Trahern said.

Before the inductions began, the evening paused to remember two Country Music Hall of Fame members who had passed away in the past year: Dolly Parton, who died in August at age 80, and songwriter Don Schlitz, who died in April 2026. Country Music Hall of Fame and Museum CEO Kyle Young called Parton “country music’s ambassador to the world,” and Schlitz was a frequent co-writer on current Hall of Fame inductee Overstreet, including co-writing songs such as “Forever and Ever, Amen” and “On the Other Hand.”

Bluegrass trailblazers the Stanley Brothers, Carter and Ralph Stanley, were inducted in the veteran era artist category. The brother duo, influenced by the works of Bill Monroe and Flatt & Scruggs, became one of the most influential duos in bluegrass. Carter wrote bluegrass standards including “The Lonesome River” and “The White Dove,” and was the duo’s main vocalist, while Ralph offered up precise banjo playing and high lonesome tenor harmony. The duo’s career was cut short when Carter died in 1966 at age 41, but his brother Ralph continued touring and releasing music for another half-century, including lending his unmistakable voice to “O Death” on the soundtrack to the 2000 film O Brother, Where Art Thou?. Stanley’s performance earned a Grammy for best male country vocal performance. Ralph Stanley died in 2016 at age 89.

“It is time,” Trahern said in honoring the Stanley Brothers. “I hope tonight you feel the love of the entire industry.”

During the Medallion Ceremony, Billy Strings feted the Stanley Brothers with a version of “How Mountain Girls Can Love,” while Gill and Ricky Skaggs teamed for “Rank Stranger” and the First Ladies of Bluegrass (Alison Brown, Missy Raines, Becky Buller, Sierra Hull and Molly Tuttle) sang “Bound to Ride.” Gill formally inducted the Stanley Brothers as members, with family members Ralph Stanley II, Ralph’s daughter Lisa and Carter’s daughter Jeanie accepting on their behalf.

“Ain’t nobody happier than I am to see this day finally arrive,” Skaggs said. “We love Ralph and Carter and all they gave to mountain music. They raised it out of the clay… so all the world can hear it.”

Gill noted that the first song he ever learned was a Stanley Brothers song, saying, “I tried my whole life to sound like Ralph Stanley.”

Overstreet was inducted in the songwriter category. He has co-written songs including The Judds’ “Love Can Build A Bridge,” Whitley’s “When You Say Nothing At All,” Kenny Chesney’s “She Thinks My Tractor’s Sexy,” and several of Travis’ signature hits. He’s also a member of the Nashville Songwriters Hall of Fame, and was named BMI’s country songwriter of the year for five years. Beyond his many hits as a songwriter, Overstreet also earned several of his own hits, including “Seein’ My Father in Me,” “Daddy’s Come Around” and a collaboration with Tanya Tucker and Paul Davis on the 1988 No. 1 Billboard Country Songs hit “I Won’t Take Less Than Your Love.” Overstreet was also part of the group SKO, known for the Country Songs No. 1 “Baby’s Got a New Baby.”

Songwriter and Country Music Hall of Fame member Dean Dillon performed “If I Could Bottle This Up,” while Jamey Johnson sang “Forever and Ever, Amen” and Blake Shelton sang his 2004 Overstreet-penned song “Some Beach.” Tucker inducted Overstreet into the Hall of Fame. “Congratulations big boy, welcome to the party,” Dillon told his longtime friend and songwriting colleague.

Shelton recalled seeing Overstreet perform while Shelton was still in high school, and getting Overstreet’s autograph after the show. “I wanted to be Paul Overstreet, and hoped to get [to record] a Paul Overstreet song,” Shelton said.

Taking the stage, Overstreet told the invitation-only crowd, “You don’t get here by yourself… I thank you all for voting for me and believing my contribution to country music is deserving of this honor.”

McGraw was inducted in the modern era artist category. Since first entering the Billboard country charts in 1992 with “Welcome to the Club,” McGraw has become known for hits including “Live Like You Were Dying,” “Where The Green Grass Grows,” and “Humble and Kind,” as well as such duets with his wife and fellow country star Faith Hill as “It’s Your Love.” McGraw was named the CMA’s entertainer of the year in 2001. Beyond music, McGraw has cemented himself as a multi-faceted creative force, starring in films like Friday Night Lights and The Blind Side, as well as the television series 1883.

During the ceremony, Parker McCollum honored McGraw with a rendition of “Don’t Take the Girl,” while trio Lady A turned in one of the night’s most well-received performances, with a version of his “Live Like You Were Dying.” Lainey Wilson, who grew up one parish over from where McGraw was raised in Louisiana, spoke about McGraw’s influence on her career and performed “Just to See You Smile.”

Lady A’s Hillary Scott spoke of how meaningful it was “to honor one of the most influential artists… that we have admired for so long and gotten to be the recipient of your generosity and kindness by joining you on tour two times… thank you so much for just the way that you lead and the way that you have given artists like us inspiration and a stage to stand on.”

“You know you’re my hero,” the group’s Charles Kelley told McGraw.

“A lot of people say, ‘Don’t meet your heroes’ — but you and Faith [Hill] are both more than I could have ever imagined,” Wilson said. “You are who you say you are and that means a lot to me… you were my very first concert, the Down on the Farm Tour… I feel like a seed was planted that night. And I want to say thank you for making me feel like I could do it, too.”

McGraw was inducted by Alabama’s Owen. Taking the stage, McGraw offered an emotional, heartfelt and inspiring acceptance speech.

“I’m a little overwhelmed right now,” McGraw said, before reflecting on arriving in Nashville the day that Keith Whitley passed away. “Some people might call that a bad omen. I’ve come to believe it was something else, that Nashville was telling me the truth on my very first day, that this music costs something. The people who make it give everything that they’ve got. And if you’re lucky enough to make it down the road, you owe it to the ones who didn’t and the ones who paved it… I can’t tell you what it means to walk into this Hall on the same day as the men whose fingerprints were on my very first day. I don’t believe that’s coincidence; I believe that’s country music.”

Whitley, who was posthumously inducted as a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame in 2022, was a thread tying each of this year’s inductees together. Before finding country music stardom, then-teens Whitley and Ricky Skaggs had been part of the Clinch Mountain Boys band, which Ralph Stanley had continued with after the passing of his brother Carter. When Tim McGraw moved arrived in Nashville on May 9, 1989, it was the same day that Whitley passed away; one of Whitley’s final country radio hits at the time was “When You Say Nothing At all,” written by Overstreet and Don Schlitz.

McGraw also honored his fellow inductees, and said that country music “was in my blood from the beginning.” He recalled the familial struggles of his early childhood and how, at age 11, he discovered that his biological father was Major League baseball player Tug McGraw.

“Seeing what he had done with his life, I knew that there was something in me that was going to help me make something of mine,” he said. He recalled moving to Nashville, signing early on with Curb Records and striking out with his first record. “What I learned was the rules weren’t going to save me, but my instincts might,” he said, recalling he decided on his second album to take a different approach to making music; that resulted in hits including “Indian Outlaw,” “Not a Moment Too Soon,” “Down on the Farm” and “Don’t Take the Girl,” launching a career that has earned McGraw 26 Country Songs No. 1s.

He also thanked many of the people who have supported him on his own journey to enduring country music stardom — most notably, his mother, Betty D’Agostino Trimble, and his wife Faith Hill, who were both in attendance, as well as McGraw and Hill’s daughters.

“You have been my rock through it all,” McGraw told his mother. “You nurtured, you provided, you endured. You are the one who stayed. You sacrificed more than any of us understood at the time, and the pain you carried was real, and now, so is the joy we share in this room.” Of Hill, McGraw told the audience, “You know our story, but what you don’t know is she is the most loving, compassionate and the best person I know. She’s so solid, and I am more solid because of her… she is for many, many reasons, why I am standing here.” He added, “The only thing that can beat this night, is when you’re standing here and I’m sitting there.”

The evening traditionally concludes with a performance of The Carter Family’s “Will the Circle Be Unbroken,” and this year, Country Music Hall of Famer Patty Loveless did the honors, turning in a stellar performance, while also slightly changing some of the lyrics to honor the late Country Music Hall of Fame member Parton.

The evening’s music was spearheaded by a top-notch Medallion All-Star Band, including drummer Mark Beckett, keyboardist Jen Gunderman, vocalist Tania Hancheroff, bassist Alison Prestwood, fiddler/mandolinist Deanie Richardson, steel guitarist Scotty Sanders, band leader/acoustic guitarist Biff Watson, guitarist/vocalist Jeff White and electric guitarist/vocalist Charlie Worsham.

#32. Dan Reynolds Steps Out With Chantel Jeffries After Minka Kelly Split

Imagine Dragons’ Dan Reynolds, who recently broke up with Minka Kelly, stepped out at Miley Cyrus’ Hollywood Bowl residency alongside Chantel Jeffries.

If Dan Reynolds is the lightning, then Miley Cyrus is the thunder.

So, it makes sense that the Imagine Dragons frontman didn’t want to miss the Disney Channel alum’s latest residency at the Hollywood Bowl Oct. 18.

And while the performances mark Cyrus’ first return to the stage since her Attention tour in 2022, Reynolds also turned heads by stepping out alongside Chantel Jeffries, just days after his apparent breakup from Minka Kelly.

Reynolds, 39, and Jeffries, 34, arrived at the concert together, according to videos shared on social media, and later sat side-by-side inside the venue.

The “Radioactive” singer kept it casual, sporting a brown leather jacket, a white T-shirt and jeans, while Jeffries—who was previously linked to Justin Bieber in the mid-2010s—opted for a beige quarter-zip sweater and jeans. The pair appeared friendly, chatting and intently taking in the concert.

E! News reached out to reps for Jeffries and Reynolds but has not yet heard back.

Reynolds—dad to four daughters with ex Aja Volkman—and Jeffries’ low-key outing comes just days after multiple outlets reported the “Thunder” singer and Friday Night Lights alum had ended their relationship after four years together. E! News previously reached out to reps for the former couple regarding their split, but did not hear back.

For Kelly’s part, she also appears to be embracing a new chapter. The 46-year-old shared a photo dump to Instagram Oct. 18, proving she’s using the autumn season to start anew.

Alongside photos of Kelly taking part in some home renovations as well as indulging in some fall activities like watching horror movies, the Champagne Problems actress also included a cryptic quote about soulmates in her latest dump.

“Soulmates or partners of destiny can be people that come into your life and change your life,” the quote read. “And ideally, it’s not about holding onto it, but understanding what they brought into your life—what did you learn and how did you change? It’s about seeing these people and situations as a gift, as steps in your own personal development.”

Prior to their breakup, Reynolds and Kelly had appeared to be going strong, even making their red carpet debut earlier this year at the 2026 MOCA Gala in June.

And for Reynolds’ birthday in July, Kelly had emphasized their bond in a sweet birthday post.

“Thank you for making ordinary days feel extraordinary,” she wrote at the time, “for making me laugh until I can’t breathe, and for loving so deeply and so freely.”

For more couples who have called it quits this year, keep reading…

#33. Breakout ‘Behemoth!’ Musician Lukas Frank Reveals What It’s Like to Give Tony Gilroy a Rewrite

Though he is the designated newcomer of the “Behemoth!” Music Collective, composer and songwriter Lukas Frank has a level of familiarity with its director that makes him one of the few people that can say they did rewrites on something two-time Oscar nominee Tony Gilroy wrote.

Speaking at the Middleburg Film Festival after a Sunday morning screening of the Pedro Pascal vehicle that features music from nine different composers, Gilroy said, “Lukas and I have a relationship that goes back like 10 years. His father [Scott] and I are very good friends and Lukas was a real touring drummer.” Over the years, the filmmaker had stayed in touch with the burgeoning musician, and became a fan of Frank’s band Storefront Church, “so we had a real relationship. I know his music inside out.” But even then, as Gilroy began working on “Behemoth!,” he said that Frank “wasn’t really going to be part of it originally. It wasn’t like he was an obvious choice.” Related Stories Léa Seydoux Became Fearless After the Controversies of ‘Blue Is the Warmest Color’ — She’s Doing It Again with ‘Gentle Monster’ ‘La Bola Negra’ Earns $277,500 in Limited Release as Netflix Reports Box Office Results for the First Time in History

As Gilroy developed ideas for what music could be featured in the film in order to avoid an underscore, from Oscar winner Michael Giacchino writing the theme to a fictional classic cartoon to music icon Alan Silvestri scoring a blockbuster titled “Open World,” the biggest challenge actually became what music represented the character Viviana, a young woman who Pascal’s professional cellist character Alan Serian takes interest in.

“It says on the page, oh, it’s this transformational [requiem], this woman beyond a prodigy, a proto-Mozart,” describing one of the pieces that first showcases the young musician’s talent. “It’s like when a writer says, ‘Oh, the greatest sunset ever.’ The director goes, ‘Fuck you. Really?’ So I’m on both sides of that equation, but I know that I have to have this thing, and I just know intuitively that this is going to be the hardest thing to do. So I started very early on.”

Gilroy cast a wide net that finally came back around to a piece that his primary music collaborator, nine-time Oscar nominee James Newton Howard, wrote. “We picked a lock on the Viviana thing,” said the director. “At that point I said, ‘Oh, my God, James, you know what? Now that you have the genetics of this, now that we know who this is, you should take the rest of the Viviana cues.’ He destroyed them. I love what he does with Viviana.”

One of those cues was an original song called “Your God Is Sleeping,” an experimental pop song that Pascal’s Alex sees Viviana perform at a packed music club in Los Angeles. “I wrote a version of it and brought it to James. He tweaked it up and had all the lyrics. We’re like ‘Wow, this is kind of good. We should take it over to Lukas and have him make a hit,’” said Gilroy. “Lukas listens to it and goes, ‘It’s really good, but it’s really old.’”

Seated next to the “Behemoth!” helmer, Frank said “Tony wrote this great song, it felt like a ‘70s protest song.” “It wasn’t that lame,” replied Gilroy.

“It was a good song. It did not feel like something a 16-year-old girl could write was my complaint about it,” said the songwriter. The director said, “‘OK, you can have the title. Do whatever you want.’ And then a couple of days later the song came out.”

“Your God Is Sleeping” served as redemption for Frank who had sent Gilroy several pitches for the aforementioned pivotal piece of music that a younger Viviana performs in the film. “All along the way, Lukas is like, ‘What are you doing? What happened? What’s going on? Let me try.’ He tried a bunch of Viviana requiems and kept sending them to me, but our relationship is different. I can just say ‘No, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. Don’t stop, but no. Forget it. I don’t see how this is going to happen,’” said the director.

“Someday I’m going to release my four projected piano requiems. I got such great feedback,” joked Frank. “My favorite one, the piece was called ‘My Mother.’ Tony had the title for me, he wanted me to call it ‘My Mother.’ So I sent him one of them. I’m so proud of this piano requiem I sent. I sent it over to him. He goes, ‘I mean, it’s great. I’m sure your mother will love it.’”

After laughter from the audience, the composer continued, “I sent him another one over and he goes, ‘This is the definition of interesting for interesting’s sake.’ I then put that song [and melody] on my record. I don’t tell him. I send it to him. He goes, ‘Track four is great.’ I go ‘Motherfucker! That’s the one that you said wasn’t that good.’”

“Behemoth!” is a cornucopia of engrossing, original music, and Gilroy said Howard, the victor in the hunt for who would write music for Viviana, “was obsessed with what Lukas was doing after ‘Your God Is Sleeping.’” He added that part of the fun of the film’s musical experiment was “all the composers on this movie wanted to hear what the other ones were doing,” and they all thought Best Original Song contender “Your God Is Sleeping” “is the dopest. It’s really hard to be that simple and that effective. It’s really cool.”

Sony Pictures Television hired Lauren Glaubach, a former YouTube and Pinterest content exec, in the newly created role of executive vice president, distribution, digital and social platforms.

Glaubach will head up Sony Pictures Entertainment’s continued expansion across YouTube and other digital platforms, reporting to Jason Spivak and Paul Littmann, presidents of distribution and networks at SPT. Miley Cyrus addresses online criticism towards her Hollywood Bowl show this past Friday: “It is hard for me to stand up here and do this show. It does not come as natural as it once did…. “I have never heard that I don’t put my heart into something,” Cyrus told the crowd early on in the show on Sunday, labelling some of the the commentary that had surfaced after night on as “clickbait.” She further said that the Bowl shows were not “an experiment of you, this an experience for me.” Related Stories Music Miley Cyrus Returns to the Stage With Emotional and Cathartic Hollywood Bowl Show Music Miley Cyrus Tearfully Pays Tribute to Dolly Parton With "Jolene" Performance at Hollywood Bowl: "Me and Dolly, We Are Eternal"

Cyrus acknowledged to the crowd that playing shows doesn’t come “as natural as it once did,” and that she’d even considered not coming out Sunday but that “never would I leave you all sitting in these seats, unfulfilled from a show.”

Before the “Jolene” performance, Cyrus told a funny and touching story about playing a video of “Jolene” to a Parton mannequin Parton had given Cyrus as a Christmas gift, putting a flower down and asking Parton’s spirit to flicker the lights if she was there.

“I didn’t say anything out loud but the entire hallway started flickering,” Cyrus said. “Max can vouch, he was there but he didn’t know what I said. So I know she’s here with me tonight, and I’m feeling some of the feelings that I’m most afraid of, but having her here with me is getting me through. And having you here with me is getting me through. So no matter what it takes, this show is for you and for Dolly.”

#39. I Just Found Out A Disney World Attraction Inspired Robin Williams' Casting In Aladdin

Over the course of his career, Robin Williams starred in some of the best movies, transforming himself into unforgettable characters like Mrs. Doubtfire and Sean Maguire in Good Will Hunting. However, one of his most beloved roles remains the voice work he did for Genie in Disney’s Aladdin, and for good reason. Believe it or not, he apparently had a Disney World attraction to partially thank for landing the part.

As a Disney nerd, I thought I knew all the lore there is to know about Williams ' participation and complicated history with Aladdin. One of the most famous stories is that the animation team frequently had to reanimate entire sequences starring the Genie because Williams regularly improvised lines that didn’t fit what they had. Apparently I was wrong, though, because I had no idea that the Dead Poets Society actor landed the role largely because of the former Disney World attraction, The Magic of Disney Animation — not to be confused with the newly opened Animation area of Hollywood Studios under the same name.

Co-director Ron Clements recently sat down with People to discuss the Disney's classic 1992 animated film. During that chat, Clements finally set the record straight on why they tapped Williams for the role:

He was a big movie star at the time, but that wasn’t at all why we cast him.

By this point in his career, Williams had appeared in over two dozen film and TV projects and was famous for playing beloved alien Mork in Mork & Mindy and for starring in films like Good Morning, Vietnam and Dead Poets Society. Even with all those big credits, he'd yet to star in Good Will Hunting, for which he won an Academy Award. However, it wasn't Williams' A-list status that led Clements and his co-director, John Musker, to reach out to him. Instead, it was Williams ' involvement in the short film “Back to Neverland,” which was featured at the start of the animation tour at the former Disney-MGM Studios:

This combination live-action and animated film, starring Robin Williams and Walter Cronkite, took you behind-the-scenes of how Disney animation was produced at the time.

Back when Disney-MGM Studios, now known as Hollywood Studios, first opened, its goal was to offer its guests a glimpse into what a real film studio looks like. This was easier at the time since Florida did have its own animation division creating hits like Mulan and Lilo & Stitch.

Much like the Studio Tour at Universal Studios Hollywood, The Magic of Disney Animation tour took guests into the halls of the animation studio, but not before showing them the short that starred Williams playing a tourist sporting a Goofy hat. Clements explained the short in his own words in his book Making Disney Magic… from a Mermaid to Moana, writing:

Robin is turned into a cartoon character in the style of one of the Lost Boys from Peter Pan and joins an animated adventure. As part of this, there’s a little tour de force black-and-white pencil test where Robin’s character goes through multiple transformations accompanied by Robin’s vocal histrionics.

Unfortunately, the short is not streamable with a Disney+ subscription, but there are some videos and clips of the short on YouTube. If you watch it, it’s easy to see how the short served as a de facto audition tape for the Genie. Clement also said:

Without question, this was a major inspiration for John and me in wanting to use Robin, as well as for what we hoped to do with the animation of his character.

"Back to Neverland" turned out to be so impactful that at the end of Aladdin, Genie sports a near-identical tourist outfit to the one Williams wore at the start of the short as an homage.

Now that Hollywood Studios once again has a The Magic of Disney Animation building, this time themed after the Walt Disney Studios building in Burbank, maybe the “Back to Neverland” short will play in the Once Upon a Studio Theater on rotation with the centennial short film “Once Upon a Studio,” which Williams' Genie does appear in despite his passing. At least, that’s what I’m hoping will happen so I can see the short the way its creators intended it to be watched!

#40. The Best 2026 Horror Movies To Watch At Home For Halloween

It's the most wonderful time of the year: Halloween season. The weather is getting cooler, you're already eating the candy you bought to give out to trick or treaters, and it's the perfect time to watch horror movies. Sure, you can watch horror movies any time of the year — lord knows I do. But there's something special about watching a scary movie during Halloween season. It just hits different, ya know?

Horror continues to thrive as a genre, and 2026 has unleashed several strong horror movies upon us, many of which are now available to watch from the comfort and safety of your home. Below, I've rounded up some of the best 2026 horror movies you can watch at home for Halloween. So carve a pumpkin, stuff some candy corn in your face, and get ready to get scary.

Two 2026 horror flicks just hit digital (meaning you can rent or purchase them via Fandango, iTunes, and other such sites) and they're both worth checking out. "Buddy," from "Too Many Cooks" filmmaker Casper Kelly, is a darkly funny and surprisingly disturbing film about children trapped in a Barney-like TV series, where the host — an orange unicorn named Buddy — is a demonic monster willing to kill to get his way. The idea is fun, but it also feels like it would be hard to sustain through a feature film. And yet Kelly pulls it off, creating an engrossing, upsetting film that goes to extremely dark places.

"Insidious: Out of the Further" is the latest entry in the seemingly never-ending "Insidious" series. These films can often be hit or miss — I love some of them, and think others are completely disposable. But "Out of the Further" is pretty successful as it takes the franchise lore to new places and brings in even more ghouls to freak us out. There's also a delightfully twisted scene set in a dentist's office that made me want to throw up, and I mean that as a compliment.

"28 Years Later: The Bone Temple" came out at the beginning of the year and underperformed at the box office, which has unfortunately erased the film from many people's minds. Thankfully, it's now on Netflix, and absolutely worth checking out as it takes the "28...Later" franchise to strange new places, anchored by an incredible, heartfelt performance from Ralph Fiennes. Please, give us the proposed third film in the new trilogy.

Meanwhile over on HBO Max, two of the year's best horrors await you. First is a film that needs no introduction: Kane Parson's "Backrooms" was one of the biggest hits of the year, taking the creepypasta phenomenon and grafting it onto a haunting liminal space nightmare. On the opposite end of the spectrum is the nasty, brutal, but frequently funny "Evil Dead Burn," loaded with gore, gore, and more gore. Fans seem a little mixed on how mean this movie is, but I dug it.

And then on Shudder, you can find "Faces of Death," one of the year's biggest surprises. Inspired by the infamous mondo movie of the same name, this smart meta slasher is about a serial killer drawing inspiration from the original "Faces of Death" to upload murders online.

The streaming horror keeps on coming. Over on Hulu, you can check out two different 2026 titles. First is "Hokum," a slow-burn ghost story that has the added bonus of being set during Halloween. Adam Scott plays a rude, troubled writer investigating a haunted hotel room, with creepy results. Sam Raimi knows a thing or two about giving you the creeps, but he also loves to make audiences laugh, and that's what he does with his delightfully crazy "Send Help," the second Hulu-streaming movie here. The always-welcomed Rachel McAdams is delightful as a mousy office drone who finds herself trapped on a desert island with her rude boss, played by Dylan O'Brien. A bloody power struggle ensues.

Of course, no list of 2026 horror would be complete without "Obsession," Curry Barker's funny, terrifying indie hit that made a star out of Inde Navarrette (who is destined for an Oscar nom; bookmark this for later). Navarette plays Nikki, who has long been the dream girl of her friend Bear (Michael Johnston). When Bear makes a wish for Nikki to love him, it goes horribly wrong. But Nikki isn't the monster here — Bear is. Believe the hype: "Obsession" is the real deal.

Finally, we have "Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma," streaming on Mubi. This extremely meta slasher from Jane Schoenbrun stars Hannah Einbinder as a filmmaker hired to remake a horror classic. She meets with the star of that film, played by Gillian Anderson, and an unexpected passion blooms. "Camp Miasma" is definitely a love letter to folks who grew up obsessed with the horror section in video stores, as well as horny freaks (complimentary).

Okay, so I know this is supposed to be devoted entirely to movies from 2026, but I wanted to give a special shout-out to the brand-new Lionsgate Limited release of "The Blair Witch Project," which includes a filmmaker-approved restored theatrical cut and festival cut newly restored from the original Hi-8 videotapes and 16mm film elements as well as the original 35mm theatrical exhibition version.

A phenomenon when it hit theaters in 1999, "The Blair Witch Project" changed movies forever and also experienced some backlash from those who felt it was overhyped. But history has judged the film kindly, because it absolutely rules. The film is lightning-in-a-bottle-stuff that's been often imitated, and yet it still maintains its power for inducing a genuine feeling of dread as a trio of amateur filmmakers slowly realize their impending doom after they get lost in the woods. Halloween season is the best time to revisit the film, and this new physical release gives you a perfect excuse to do so.

#43. Léa Seydoux Became Fearless After the Controversies of ‘Blue Is the Warmest Color’ — She’s Doing It Again with ‘Gentle Monster’

While accepting the Middleburg Film Festival Achievement in Acting Award this weekend, Léa Seydoux told the crowd that her parents sent her to summer camp in Middleburg. “The first time I came to the United States,” she said, “I flew on my own, and I was eight years old, and I didn’t speak a word of English, which is true. I knew how to say ‘yes,’ ‘no,’ and ‘sorry, I don’t understand.’ So it was it was difficult, but also rewarding. I discovered a new culture. I didn’t know then that I would become an actress, and that this would be my life: traveling, discovering new cultures, and exploring human nature.”

That has become the 41-year-old Seydoux’s hallmark, as she accompanied her Cannes breakout “Gentle Monster” (Netflix) to Middleburg with Austrian filmmaker Marie Kreutzer. Seydoux is in the running for the Best Actress Oscar. Related Stories ‘La Bola Negra’ Earns $277,500 in Limited Release as Netflix Reports Box Office Results for the First Time in History How Titmouse Animation Gave ‘Street Fighter’ Its Secret Sauce

Kreutzer grabbed the germ of an idea for the film from a 2020 newspaper article about pedophiles. “The article made it clear to me how close [to us] the perpetrators mostly are in most cases,” she said. “And that I must certainly also know not only victims of child sexual abuse but also perpetrators myself.”

When Seydoux first heard about the film from her agents, she was hesitant. As the mother of two children, “I was a bit scared of it,” she said. “I read the script, and I fell in love with the character. The script was so well-written, so intelligent, and that was it.”

In the film, when Lucy Weiss, a French pop singer living with her Austrian husband (Laurence Rupp) and young son in the country, finds out that her husband is accused of abusing children, “she’s in a state of shock,” said Seydoux. As the revelations about his behavior keep coming, “It’s a shock after another shock. It’s all these contradictions. This is what I loved about the character. It’s through her perspective that the story unfolds. It’s not through the victim’s perspective, not through the traitor’s perspective, but through her. I was able to bring a lot of different emotions that are not explainable with words.”

Seydoux is often silently reacting. “I used my facial expressions,” she said. “I try to to express internalized emotions with my body and my face. That was extremely interesting for me as an actor.”

Kreutzer structured a script that starts off with an intimate relationship with the husband, then evolves as Lucy finds out one thing after another, terrified that she might discover that her son was a victim of her husband’s predatory behavior. “After doing research and learning more about the subject,” said Kreutzer, “I became aware that I had had so many stereotypes in my head about pedophile criminals, so I really wanted to show a man and a couple that could feel like friends to an audience, a guy who would never have any suspicions of that kind. I like to get the audience to like them, to feel close to them. And then when all of this unfolds, also being in Lucy’s shoes and not wanting this to be true, and hoping for her and hoping for him that it’s not true, and that there will be some explanation, because that’s very human. When it comes to someone we know and have trusted, it’s much harder to accept that they have done awful things.”

Added Seydoux, “When it’s someone we know, that’s way harder to to accept because everyone has different sides to them, and also monstrous people have likable sides.”

Seydoux had to speak three languages on this film: English, French, and German. “Of course the German language is difficult in the pronunciation,” she said. “I found it difficult to play the emotions with the language you don’t speak. But then I had to be, emotionally speaking, in a strong emotion. There was a word that I struggled to pronounce, and at some point I remember that I burst into tears. Lucy can’t really express herself, and she doesn’t speak the language either, and so she’s even more isolated.”

The great Catherine Deneuve, who plays Lucy’s mother, points out that she’s supposed to be in the city, not in the country, because she’s a performer. “Yes,” said Seydoux. “The hardest part for me was the piano and the technical aspects. We spent some time in Vienna with Marie and a piano teacher who helped me. I had to press the right keys. The singing is my voice. I’m proud of it, and I’ve always loved singing. So that was for me also a dream come true.”

After 20 years in the business, Seydoux has learned many lessons, but none as heart-wrenching as shooting Abdellatif Kechiche’s “Blue Is the Warmest Color,” which won the Palme d’Or in 2013 for the director as well as his two actresses, Seydoux and Adele Excharpoulos.

“That was thirteen years ago,” Seydoux said, “at the time before the #MeToo movement. I’ve spoken already a lot about how disrespectful the director had been with us. We shot for six months, and we just discovered the movie in Cannes. The scenes were graphic, let’s say. So I discovered them during Cannes, which is absolutely crazy, and I didn’t have any approval on these scenes. We won the Palme d’Or, which makes us in a way co-writers of the film, which was true. True, because there was a lot of improvisations, and the story is based on both of us.”

It was after that award that things got complicated when Seydoux started to speak out about “the bad conditions,” she said. “The producers came to me and said, ‘You better shut your mouth, because if you want to be nominated for something, if you want to do the award season, you better stop.’ And I said ‘no, I want to explain how mistreated we’ve been on this film,’ and I didn’t say half of what happened. Really, it was horrible. And so I got fired. They fired me for promotion. It was difficult because then the director started to bully me. He said that if I was speaking, it’s because I come from this privileged family.”

Seydoux has never revealed the promo firing before. At a Golden Globes Q&A, Seydoux was challenged by some of the HFPA members, who said she was speaking out because of her family. “This was so humiliating,” said Seydoux. “Even now I could cry, but I’m not doing it. But I burst into tears and it was hard.”

“Since “Blue,” Seydoux has worked steadily with directors in France and Hollywood, from Wes Anderson (“The Grand Budapest Hotel”) and Woody Allen (“Midnight in Paris”) to Mia Hansen-Løve (“One Fine Morning”).

After #MeToo, her director has not returned to his previous station in international cinema. And Seydoux demanded final approval on any scenes involving her naked body. “When you work hand in hand with a director,” she said, “as I as I did with Marie, she showed me the scenes. I need to have the approval of that because it’s so intimate.”
