#50. Wildwood Review: LAIKA's Stunner Makes Fantasy Feel Fresh Again

Travis Knight's new stop-motion fantasy epic "Wildwood," based on the novel by Colin Meloy and Carson Ellis, is one of the most dazzling films I have seen in a long time. I've never seen an animated film that looks quite this alive, bursting in every frame with vivacious detail. There is a tactile quality to stop-motion animation that allows the medium to breathe and jitter to life, and Knight has filled his film with expressive characters, quivering plants, and windblown leaves that make "Wildwood" a beauty to behold.

"Wildwood" is so visually astonishing, so textured and vivacious, that it makes the old fantasy clichés in its script feel new again. After a generation of "Harry Potter" knockoffs, YA fantasy tropes became a reliable road map, usually suffused with boring "chosen one" and "special child" narratives that became as predictable as any slasher movie.

"Wildwood," however, manages, through its wilful visuals, to shed its genre's staleness. It is free of Harry Potter-style YA self-grandeur, free of the tiresome Peter Jackson "Lord of the Rings" portent, and definitely beyond insufferable Disney hyperkinetic semi-comedic cheekiness. Too many animated films, even great ones, lean into a type of chaotic CGI visual busyness, clearly aimed to distract the kiddies with movement and noise.

"Wildwood," perhaps because stop-motion animation is so labor-intensive, settles into a more natural pace. Characters aren't "witty" chatterboxes who scream eight lines before you get a chance to think. The action is deliberate and focused. The frame isn't stuffed full of too many details; many films require a Blu-ray release and a pause button for some scenes to be fully appreciated. Not with "Wildwood." Finally, finally, we can breathe and take in the beauty of it all.

/Film posited that "Wildwood" could be one of 2026's best films. It is.

"Wildwood" tells the story of Prue McKeel (Peyton Elizabeth Lee) a 12-year-old girl with a one-year-old brother who lives in Portland with her hippie-dippie parents (Jake Johnson and Maya Erskine). The attention to Portland is impeccable, with Prue riding her bike past Powell's Books and buying herself one of those Cap'n Crunch donuts from Voodoo Donuts. Her parents have warned Prue not to take her little brother outdoors, but, being a defiant tweener, she does it anyway. This attracts a Hitchcockian murder of crows that whisk away the infant, and lead Prue, along with an accumulated friend named Curtis (Jacob Tremblay), to the edge of the Oregonian woods.

Prue manages to break the seal between worlds (there is something eerie about her blood) and treks into the greenworld of "Wildwood." There, she encounters a pack of talking coyotes dressed like Colonialist soldiers. Delving deeper, and becoming separated from Curtis, Prue encounters noble talking birds, led by a regal eagle played by Angela Bassett, and eventually runs aground in the magical state capital, run by a corrupt mayor and his sniveling Roy Brocksmith-like assistant. She also is astonished to find that animals and humans live side-by-side, filling out paperwork together.

Curtis, meanwhile, finds himself in the company of the Dowager Governess Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), an imposing sorceress who commands the coyote army, and who has a scheme of her own. Also involved in the narrative is a colorful band of angry bandits led by the enormous Brendan (Mahershala Ali) and a group of tree-worshiping druids, represented by the elderly Iphigenia (Tantoo Cardinal). All of this results in the most visually creative fantasy movie since "The Dark Crystal."

The bandits and the mystics give a lot of grave warnings about Alexandra and her plan. Alexandra, meanwhile, has no issues with indoctrinating Curtis as a child soldier; she gleefully murders people right in front of him.

For sensitive parents, be warned: "Wildwood" features scenes of actual death and on-screen blood (it's rated PG-13, uncommon for animated films). This is a fairy tale that ends in a fiery battlefield conflagration with swords, bayonets, and arterial spray. In a weird way, it's refreshing to see a fantasy film lean into the more unpleasant aspects of war, depicting it as horrifying and bloody. Not a single character is a kung-fu-trained badass who backflips and slashes at enemies bloodlessly.

There is a tendency in fantasy films for human protagonists to react to the extraordinary with a flippant "whatever," or, at the very least, a brief bout of panic before settling into the fantastical with ease. "Wildwood" somehow manages to retain its awe, mystery, and fear throughout. Prue and Curtis understand the rules of the world, but they also never lose their outsider status. This is a small detail, but it's vital to maintaining wonderment and magic in your fantasy film. "Awesome" has become the antithesis of "awestruck." "Wildwood" leaves you feeling the latter.

The original "Wildwood" book was published in 2011, making it a direct descendant of the YA trend kicked off by Harry Potter. It's literary influences, however, aren't of that trend. "Wildwood" has more in common with the works of Philip Pullman ("The Golden Compass") than J.K. Rowling (boo, hiss). Its pastoral, mossy visuals seem to have been taken from folk horror tales like Arthur Machen's 1904 short story "The White People" combined with the poetry of Wordsworth.

Throughout "Wildwood," you may need to remind yourself that this was all stop-motion, and that you are watching real-world maquettes captured by real cameras. The movement is so smooth, and the characters are so expressive, you wonder why anyone bothers with CGI at all. "Wildwood" was photographed by the great Caleb Deschanel ("Being There," "The Right Stuff," "Fly Away Home," many others), which may go a long way to explain its visual appeal. Everything is clear, crisp, and cogent. And beautiful. It's all so beautiful.

The central criticism I have with "Wildwood" is its script. The story is, on paper, typical fantasy hooey, all about a brave sister entering a scary place to rescue a helpless relative. That's the plot of "Labyrinth" and a dozen others. The main themes of "Wildwood" are also familiar, with a young girl finding a sense of responsibility and becoming a young woman, all through the crucibles of adventure, friendship, and battlefield violence.

Too many fantasy stories climax with an actual war, which always feels uncreative to me. Is there no way to better settle an existential battle than to depict people waiting on each other for 20 minutes? But some great characterization and animation are more than enough to elevate "Wildwood" into something breathtaking. I felt like I was drinking a cool glass of water after a months-long heatwave, left in tears by something so gorgeous.

"Wildwood" opens in theaters on October 23, 2026.

ABC’s The View is currently in the midst of its 30th season, which has marked the return of some veteran panelists amid the 2026 TV schedule. Throughout this milestone year for the show, some of its current hosts have been reflecting on the daytime talk show’s history and their experiences on it. Veteran co-host Joy Behar also recently shared her recollections and in the process, mentioned “mean girls” having been on the daytime staple. This comes years after her disagreement with series alum Meghan McCain, but who’s in the right here?

Behar is one of The View’s original panelists, as she joined the Barbara Walters-created talk show when it premiered back in 1997. While she left the show in 2013, she made guest appearances until returning to her full-time duties in 2015. Behar opened up about her work on the series during a wide-ranging interview with Vulture. The article mentions Meghan McCain replacing Candace Cameron Bure as the show’s conservative pundit on the dais in 2017 and, afterwards, Behar is quoted as saying:

This group now is very good. They all have a sense of humor. Nobody’s mean over there. Over the years, there’s been a couple of little mean girls.

Of course, Behar doesn’t explicitly name McCain when discussing those alleged “mean girls.” It’s no secret, however, that McCain and Behar got into their share of on-air skirmishes due to their disagreements on different topics. For example, when McCain returned to the show in January 2021 following maternity leave, she and Behar got into a spat after the former mused that the latter missed her. Behar responded by saying, “I did not miss you. Zero.” In 2022, McCain would attribute that comment to her reasoning for leaving the show.

Whether or not Behar is actually talking about McCain during that recent interview is uncertain, and there’s always the possibility that Behar is referring to another former host or two. But, at the very least, it’s hard not to assume Behar is referring to McCain, given their history. That aside, though, McCain has also shared her own side of what went down when she was on the ABC show.

In July 2021, McCain officially announced that she’d decided to exit The View after four seasons. She confirmed the news on air, telling viewers and her co-hosts that it was a “difficult decision” but that she wanted to step away in great part to care for her baby girl, who was born in 2021. She went on to say that her time on the show was “one of the hands-down greatest” honor she’d had in her career. McCain also spoke about having had the “privilege to work alongside such strong brilliant, intelligent and credible broadcasters.”

The View Is Planning A Special 30th Anniversary, But It Sounds Like Shots Fired At Meghan McCain

By the fall of 2021, though, McCain shared very different thoughts about being on the show. The podcaster took part in a lengthy interview with Variety and shared candid details about alleged backstage problems. McCain accused the show of fostering a “toxic work environment” and said the experience “felt extremely isolating because of my political ideology.” She also alleged that “people were not comfortable around” her amid production and that a disproportionate amount of negative stories were leaked about her in comparison to her co-stars. ABC execs later denied McCain’s claims and accused her of stirring up drama on set.

The overall question seems to be whether Meghan McCain really was one of those “mean girls” being alluded to by Joy Behar or if the two simply have different takes on working as View panelists. It’s hard to say whether the public at large may ever get a concrete answer on that front. What appears to be crystal clear right now, based on other comments McCain has shared, though, is that she has no plans to return to the show for its 30th season.

New episodes of The View air weekdays at 11 p.m. ET on ABC, and they can also be streamed with a Hulu subscription.

#60. You're Not A Fantasy Movie Fan If You Haven't Seen This Cheesy '80s Relic

1980s video store denizens and serious explorers of schlock likely know all about Ruggero Deodato's far-out 1987 fantasy adventure film "The Barbarians." To be sure, it's a must-watch for fantasy fans of all creeds.

"The Barbarians" stars fraternal twins David and Peter Paul, famed bodybuilders already known at the time as the Barbarian Brothers. By 1987, the Pauls already had some acting experience under their belts, having had supporting roles in films like "D.C. Cab" and "The Flamingo Kid." Nevertheless, "The Barbarians" marked the first time the Pauls led a movie together.

"The Barbarians" was put out by the Cannon Group, a studio well-known to lovers of B-grade action films, ridiculous horror movies, and ninjas. Really, simply evoking the studio's name should give folks a good idea as to what to expect from a film like "The Barbarians." (For those unfamiliar with Cannon, we at /Film recommend checking out the documentary "Electric Booglaoo: The Wild, Untold Story of Cannon Films.") Indeed, it has all the silly jokes, clunky action, and scantily-clad/half-naked models (men and women alike) one might expect from any Cannon movie.

"The Barbarians" was clearly ripping off the success of John Milius "Conan the Barbarian," which was released five years earlier, just as the Barbarian Brothers themselves were aping the success of "Conan" star Arnold Schwarzenegger. Thanks to Schwarzenegger, you see, there was suddely a market for bodybuilders as movie actors not seen since the days of Steve Reeves, so the Pauls jumped on the bandwagon. "The Barbarians" was hardly a blockbuster, but it has become a cult favorite over the years, turning the Pauls into legit cult stars. It also starred B-movie luminary Richard Lynch as the vicious medieval tyrant Kadar and Eva LaRue from "All My Children" as an itinerant thief.

"The Barbarians" takes place in an unknown time in a fantasy kingdom that resembles the Dark Ages and concerns a tribe of nomadic circus performers called the Ragnicks. In the film's opening, the Ragnicks are attacked by the evil Kadar, who seeks a magical ruby possessed by the tribe's queen, Canary (Virginia Bryant). Two young twins, Kutchek and Gore, bite off some of Kadar's fingers in his raid, so they are enslaved by him. Meanwhile, Canary is forced to live in a cage in his harem.

Fast-forward a few years, and Kutchek and Gore have grown into Peter and David Paul, now greased-up beefcakes of the highest order. The Pauls, it should be noted, were not taciturn, scowling action stars like Arnold Schwarzenegger. They were, instead, smiling "big lug" characters, suffused with humor and charm. "The Barbarians" is not meant to be taken terribly seriously, as the Pauls are always mugging and grinning and getting into shenanigans.

The plot continues as Kutchek and Gore escape Kadar's gladiatorial arena and flee into the woods. From there, they find that their despondent tribe has kidnapped Ismene (Eva LaRue), a thief who ends up joining Kutchek and Gore on a mission to get revenge on Kadar. The film then becomes a biome-exploring picaresque wherein the Barbarian Brothers have to have an arm-wrestling contest, infiltrate Kadar's harem, and trek to the Forbidden Land to find Canary's magical ruby (something Sheeba Alahani's China, Kadar's chief sorceress, wants as well). But since the gem is guarded by a dragon, Kutchek and Gore are wise enough to set out and gather a few enchanted weapons before facing the creature themselves.

"The Barbarians," to reiterate, is a very nonsensical movie. Many lovers of schlock 1980s adventure films are well aware of it, and it has been discussed on YouTube shows like "Best of the Worst" (from RedLetterMedia). Many folks will also note right away that "The Barbarians" helmer Ruggero Deodato is the same director behind 1980's "Cannibal Holocaust," which ranks among the most infamous horror movies that even hardcore horror fans can hardly finish. "The Barbarians," in contrast, is more or less a live-action riff on the '80s cartoon series "He-Man and the Masters of the Universe."

Following its release, "The Barbarians" led to a series of low-budget films starring Peter and David Paul. In 1990, they starred in Jon Turteltaub's surprisingly solid trucker comedy "Think Big," followed by their work on the 1992 action comedy "Double Trouble." They even tried their hand at the "burly babysitter" sub-genre with "Twin Sitters" not long after and had small roles in Oliver Stone's "Natural Born Killers" (although their scenes were only included in the director's cut). In a weird coincidence, Stone himself wrote a gloriously outrageous early script draft for 1982's "Conan the Barbarian," itself the very film that led to "The Barbarians" happening in the first place (as mentioned earlier).

Basically, "The Barbarians" is for people who liked "Conan the Barbarian" but felt it was too big-budget and serious and violent. "The Barbarians," on the other hand, hits a fantasy sweet spot of low-budget silliness, coupled with an earnest need to entertain. It's the perfect movie to watch with friends while getting a little intoxicated. It's a classic for the ages. Well, for the '80s, anyway.

The new Nathan Fielder/Lance Oppenheim-directed documentary You Can See Everything finally hit the 2026 movie schedule after weeks of hype, and it did not disappoint. Some of the early hype for You Can See Everything even came from Elizabeth Holmes’ own X account. Now that I've seen the documentary, I feel confident in hedging it was almost certainly her husband, Billy Evans, who thought up the tweet and posted it, just as we saw him doing in the new A24 release. The reactions to the tweet made it clear that people don’t believe Holmes herself had anything to do with it.

It’s a simple one-sentence tweet, posted on October 5:

I really don't think you are ready for this docOctober 6, 2026

It’s worth noting that Evans had not seen You Can See Everything before posting that. Fielder confirmed in a Q&A after a screening in LA that Evans did not watch the film ahead of its release. Evans and Holmes were working closely with the filmmakers, during production, but Fielder added that “communication broke down” at some point because Evans was trying to exert too much control over the final product. If you've seen the movie, this is hardly surprising.

Having seen the movie, one of the best of the year, I might add, I have to wonder if it is actually Evans who was not ready for the documentary. It’s not like he gets the most glowing edit in the movie. In many ways, he is the villain. Or at least one of them. He is shown to be overly controlling of Holmes in the movie, as seen in one already-famous egg-beating scene in the movie. Just as he takes control of cooking breakfast, he’s also admitted to taking control of Holmes’ X account.

As Evans admits in the movie, before Holmes reported to prison in Bryan, TX, in May 2023, she signed over power of attorney to him. That includes control of her social media account. He has been posting on it ever since. Sometimes, he said in the doc, it's tweets that Holmes reportedly sends to him in an email, and he copies and pastes them. Other times it’s just things Evans wants to tweet, and often they can be confrontational. People have caught on now, as many of the replies to the tweet point out. Replies like “We know it’s you, Billy,” “Get off this account, Billy,” and “How’s it going, Billy?”

He does push back on a couple of things in the thread, including arguing the blood testing machine that Holmes’ company, Theranos, “invented” does indeed work, and that Amanda Seyfried’s performance in The Dropout, which you can watch with a Hulu subscription, wasn’t good, giving it a 3/10.

Evans hasn’t posted since that tweet on October 5th, and given both the success of the movie, finishing second in the weekend’s box office results, and the negative light in which he is portrayed in the movie, I wouldn't be surprised if he were to lay low for a little while.

#66. How Much Do the Angel Wings Weigh & More Victoria's Secret Show Facts

Here's one, er, secret from the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show: Those wings are heavy AF. And with Barbara Palvin working the runway weeks after giving birth, viewers witnessed many feats of strength.

No doubt Kylie Jenner was doing amazing, sweetie, as she made her Victoria's Secret Fashion Show debut in the brand's iconic $50 million diamond-studded bra.

But props should also be given to the 15 artisans who took on the task of ensuring the 29-year-old could literally rise and then shine at the Oct. 18 event.

Before the Kylie Cosmetics founder could get her f--king ass up and work the runway inside Sony Pictures Studios in Los Angeles—as boyfriend Timothée Chalamet and mom Kris Jenner screamed from the front row—those 15 skilled craftspeople spent upwards of 1,000 hours carefully placing 4,410 natural diamonds from Jacob & Co. including the literal crown jewel: The $22 million 75.54-carat natural fancy vivid yellow diamond.

And while those stats that make up the brand's most valuable Fantasy Bra ever are wild, they're trumped by another number: 41, as in the days Barbara Palvin had between welcoming daughter Sylvie with husband Dylan Sprouse and strutting down a runway in lingerie.

It's a feat that left her spouse floored.

"I don't know where she finds the energy," Sprouse marveled to E! News. "I'm a tired guy all the time, and obviously having a newborn makes you more tired. Barbara's just up and in super mom mode, and now she's walking the show. I'm like, 'Where does it come from?'"

The way he sees it, "Some people are just better than other people."

But for Palvin, 33, it was just another day at the office.

"I'm going to be six weeks postpartum tomorrow, which I think in the U.S. most people have to go back after six weeks," the Hungary-bred stunner detailed to People. "So it's not that big of a deal."

And despite the late nights and endless feedings, "I'm feeling great," she noted. "I think it’s very empowering that the Victoria's Secret team is having me at the show and we’re supporting women."

To keep the celebration going, we're going to let you in on a few more of the brand's, well, secrets, detailing everything from the literal weight of those wings to the hours they take to create. Allow us to run the numbers.

Jasmine Tookes may have made light work of the task, but she wasn't exaggerating when she dubbed the fringed wings she wore at the 2026 Victoria's Secret Fashion Show "so heavy." In 2024, Victoria's Secret revealed that their heaviest-ever wings to date weighed in at 40 pounds.

Though Bella Hadid estimated the following year that her oversized set tipped the scales even further. "OK we're going to pretend these wings weren't 50 pounds," she shared in an Instagram Story, "but HOW BEAUTIFUL."

Before the brand's angel can truly take flight, artisans spend literal days meticulously crafting each set of wings.

That's how long Barbara Palvin had to ready herself for her 2026 runway walk after she and husband Dylan Sprouse welcomed daughter Sylvie in September.

As he put it to E! News ahead of the show, "Some people are just better than other people. I'm extremely proud of my wife."

Admittedly, the Hungary-bred model had even less time to prep for the 2025 show after breaking her foot. "The adrenaline's gonna kick on and she's gonna walk just fine, but I am nervous at the same time for her," Sprouse admitted to E! News. Because someone has to be.

"She's very nonchalant about everything," the actor acknowledged. "She's just like, 'Ah, well, today's the day.' I'm like, 'But you've trained for months. Don't you get stage fright?'"

The dozens of hit-making stars that have taken to the Victoria's Secret runway includes Tate McRae, Halsey, Kelsea Ballerini, Shawn Mendes and Taylor Swift.

Though the $50 million Fantasy Bra that Kylie Jenner donned at the 2026 show—returning for the first time since 2018—was made up of 4,410 natural Jacob & Co. diamonds it was the more than 75-carat yellow stunner dangling from the center that truly allowed the cosmetics mogul to rise and shine.

The true secret behind the lingerie giant's fashion show is how much work the models put in before stripping down. Though Candice Swanepoel told Vogue in 2013 that her "lead-up to the show changes every year," for that go-round she committed to regular boxing, yoga, Pilates, cardio and other strength sessions with longtime trainer Justin Gelband.

Said the stunner, "On the whole, 100 minutes of nonstop action every other day does me well!"

#70. 2027 Oscars Best Picture Predictions: Winner, Runner-Up And Other Contenders

Every year, the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences gathers to pick the best movie of the previous year — and sometimes, the Best Picture Oscar winners are genuinely exceptional films like "Parasite" and "Moonlight." Other winners — including, but not limited to, "Green Book," "Crash," and "CODA" — send cinephiles into full-blown crashouts as "worthier" movies miss out on the top prize. (I'm as guilty of this as anybody else. Indeed, I'm still angry that Tom Hooper is walking around with the Academy Award for directing that he won for "The King's Speech" when that should have gone to David Fincher for "The Social Network" — a film that should have taken home the Best Picture Oscar to boot.) The Academy's track record certainly isn't perfect, but that doesn't stop movie lovers like me from tuning in every year to see who wins the top prize.

The 2026 winner, Paul Thomas Anderson's Americana triumph "One Battle After Another" — which also won Anderson his first-ever directing Oscar after years of great work — had a tough battle (sorry) to face on its way to victory, fighting tooth and nail against Ryan Coogler's equally excellent Southern Gothic film "Sinners." So, who's going to win at the 2027 ceremony? It's anyone's guess, but we've got some ideas ... and thoughts about what else might get nominated, with everything but the projected winner and possible upset in alphabetical order.

I'm not saying "The Odyssey" is going to cakewalk into a Best Picture Oscar win by any means. After all, Christopher Nolan just won in 2024 for "Oppenheimer," and conventional wisdom tells us that the Academy doesn't love giving the same person the big awards over and over again. Still, I think "The Odyssey" is so undeniable that it's still the one to beat for Best Picture. With Matt Damon as the arrogant but all-too-human hero Odysseus (who comes up with the infamous Trojan Horse trick to sack Troy and win a war, only to get totally lost on the way home because men will literally face off against witches and cyclops before asking for directions), "The Odyssey" is a triumph on essentially every level. Not only is Damon phenomenal and a clear front-runner for the Best Actor Oscar, but Anne Hathaway, Robert Pattinson, Samantha Morton, and John Leguizamo could all get recognized for their respective supporting performances as Odysseus' world-weary wife Penelope, Penelope's slick but slimy suitor Antinous, the solitary witch Circe, and Odysseus' loyal swineherd Eumaeus.

At the end of the day, "The Odyssey" seems destined to duke it out with "Dune: Part Three" (more on that in a moment) for a lot of below-the-line technical categories, but unless another movie sees a huge surge, I still think it's the clear front-runner. Between its luxuriously beautiful shots, seamless practical effects, and great performances, "The Odyssey" is filled with gorgeous movie magic, and Academy voters might be too seduced by its perfectly executed tricks to remember that Nolan won both a Best Director and Best Picture Oscar earlier this decade.

As of this writing, the general populace hasn't seen "Dune: Part Three" yet. However, based on the overwhelming critical and commercial success of Denis Villeneuve's first two Frank Herbert adaptations, I think it's a pretty safe bet that "Dune: Part Three" will be a big player when awards season kicks off properly. In this long-awaited threequel, we'll catch up with Timothée Chalamet's protagonist turned antihero Paul Atreides after the events of 2024's "Dune: Part Two," which saw Paul take over control of the Imperium, defeat Austin Butler's Feyd-Rautha of House Harkonnen, and kick off a holy war as he embraces his role as the messiah, aka. Lisan al Gaib. He also, in the process, drove away his one true love Chani (Zendaya) by not only taking power so bluntly but by simultaneously deciding to wed Princess Irulan (Florence Pugh), the daughter of Christopher Walken's Emperor Shaddam IV, who has surrendered completely to Paul.

Alongside Chalamet's tyrannical Emperor, we'll see several returning players from the previous "Dune" films in this movie, including Javier Bardem as the Fremen leader Stilgar, Josh Brolin as the Atreides family's weapon expert Gurney Halleck, and Rebecca Ferguson as Lady Jessica, along with newcomers like Robert Pattinson's wily Tleilaxu dancer Scytale. Again, "Dune: Part Three" has yet to prove that it can best something as massive as "The Odyssey," but don't rule it out.

Luca Guadagnino has made some incredible movies ("Challengers," "Call Me By Your Name," "Queer") and some duds ("After the Hunt" comes to mind) in recent years, and if early reactions to his 2026 film "Artificial" are any indication, he's got another hit on his hands. "Artificial" was originally set to be distributed by Amazon MGM Studios before the real Sam Altman allegedly, potentially, maybe interfered with the planned release. (He denies it.) Now that Neon is distributing the movie, though, we'll get to see Guadagnino's take on the real-life story of Altman, his company OpenAI, and his co-founder Ilya Sutskever ("Anora" standout and Oscar nominee Yura Borisov), who instigated a coup against Altman in 2023.

"Artificial" has a seriously star-studded cast that includes Monica Barbaro, Cooper Hoffman, Jason Schwartzman, Chris O'Dowd, Ike Barinholtz, Mark Rylance, Zosia Mamet, and Billie Lourd, just to name a few — but it's also an urgent, timely, and apparently jarring warning about the advent of massive AI corporations. The Academy loves a hyper-relevant project, and aside from the truly alarming fact that it ignored "Challengers" completely, I think odds are good that its members will recognize "Artificial" and include it in the Best Picture race.

In 2024, Jesse Eisenberg stepped behind the camera to make "A Real Pain" — and though his actual feature film debut came in 2022 courtesy of "When You Finish Saving the World," "A Real Pain" is the one that put him on the map as a director and screenwriter. Most importantly, it earned multiple Oscar nominations, with Eisenberg getting one for Best Original Screenplay and his co-star Kieran Culkin sweeping the entire awards season to emerge triumphant with a statue for Best Supporting Actor. (Was this category fraud? Yes, because Culkin is a co-lead, but I love my "Succession" slime puppy Culkin ... so, I'm at peace with the whole thing.) Now, he's back with his 2026 film "The Debut," and I think Eisenberg has a real shot at making it into the Best Picture race.

So, why will "The Debut" clinch a nomination that "A Real Pain" didn't get? Well, Eisenberg propelled his co-star to an Oscar win, for one ... but more than that, the cast of "The Debut" is wild. Oscar winner Julianne Moore leads the pack as Mona Friedman, an introverted suburban housewife who breaks out of her comfort zone by auditioning for a local theater production run by the extremely intense Jerry Blankenbuehler (Oscar nominee Paul Giamatti, who also has a pretty good chance of becoming Eisenberg's second Best Supporting Actor winner in a row). With Eisenberg playing a supporting role as well, "The Debut" co-stars Halle Bailey, Bernadette Peters, Lili Cooper, Bonnie Milligan, Patrick Fabian, Craig Bierko, Stephen Adly Guirgis, Havana Rose Liu, and Cara Buono, just to name a few. The Academy loves movies about acting, and I think "The Debut" is a strong enough pick to make it into the Best Picture category.

Every year, a different movie is marked as "Oscar bait." In the lead-up to the 2026 ceremony, that title fell to "Hamnet," a weepy literary adaptation about the loss of a child that earned a spot in the Best Picture category, won its star Jessie Buckley an Oscar, and partially focused on Paul Mescal's William Shakespeare writing "Hamlet" out of grief for his son. That's what's particularly "funny" about Simon Stone's 2026 movie "Elsinore," which I think is a near-lock to score a Best Picture Oscar nod and is also about a production of "Hamlet" ... and which centers around the art of acting. (Again, in a non-derogatory way, the Academy loves that stuff.)

In "Elsinore," Andrew Scott — known for Netflix's "Ripley" and playing the infamous "Hot Priest" in "Fleabag" — plays real-life actor Ian Charleson, who spent the final months of his life grappling with an AIDS diagnosis (and fairly severe symptoms, for that matter) while at the same time performing the title role in "Hamlet" at London's National Theatre. Scott, per usual, is transcendent as an artist choosing to spend the end of his time on Earth doing what he loves, and he's joined by unbelievable talents like Billie Piper (as a casting director who becomes a confidante and nurse to Ian), Joe Locke (a fellow patient in the AIDS wing at a London hospital), and Juliet Stevenson (as a fellow actor), just to name a few. "Elsinore" might fit the definition of Oscar bait, but it would nonetheless be a worthy inclusion in the Best Picture race.

No other 2026 movie has shaken me to my very core like Olivia Wilde's third feature film "The Invite," and I mean that as a compliment. My jaw dropped multiple times, I laughed, I cringed, and at one point, I even cried. Written by Will McCormack and Rashida Jones (who adapted it from Cesc Gay's 2020 Spanish-language movie "The People Upstairs (Sentimental)"), "The Invite" is a four-person film that feels like a play (partly because Gay's movie was itself based on a stage play he wrote), letting us into the apartment of the deeply unhappy married couple Joe and Angela (Seth Rogen and Wilde) as they prepare to host their upstairs neighbors, Hawk and Pina (Edward Norton and Penélope Cruz). Not only are Hawk and Pina unbearably cool, but there's an elephant in the room ... which is that their lovemaking is, if Joe and Angela are to be believed, so loud that they can hear every encounter clearly in their home.

Wilde's skills as a director are on full, gorgeous display here (while I don't think her last film, "Don't Worry Darling" was quite as bad as everyone says, "The Invite" blows it out of the water), and every performance is perfect as well, from Rogen's music teacher and perennially stoned Joe to Norton's cerebral and arrogant Hawk to Cruz's alluring and brilliant Pina to Wilde's twitchy, anxious Angela. Not only do I think "The Invite" should be invited into the Best Picture category, but I also think Wilde should make Academy history by being nominated for Best Director and Best Actress as well.

Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi, known for their work in their home country of Spain, might just snag a spot in this year's Best Picture category for their sprawling queer epic "La bola negra," which is loosely adapted by Calvo, Ambrossi, and Alberto Conejero from an unfinished work of the same name by Federico García Lorca as well as Conejero's own play, "La piedra obscura." Told across three narratives that take place in 1932, 1937, and 2017, respectively, "La bola negra" focuses on three men in those time periods.

1932 belongs to Carlos (Milo Quifes), the heir to his wealthy family's fortune who finds himself shunned from high society due to rumors about his queer identity. In 1937, we meet a young trumpeter named Sebastián (Álvaro Lafuente Calvo, who performs as singer-songwriter Guitarricadelafuente), who narrowly survives an attack in the Spanish Civil War and is forced into serving the Nationalists by guarding their prisoner Rafael Rodríguez Rapún (Miguel Bernardeau), all while he discovers a queer enclave courtesy of Nené Romero (Penélope Cruz). Then, in 2017, we're introduced to historian and writer Alberto López Azcuna (Carlos González), who receives a copy of Lorca's work as a sort of inheritance ... and wants to learn more about queer history in Spain.

"La bola negra" is ambitious, massive, and absolutely beautiful, thanks to its stunning performances and careful direction from Calvo and Ambrossi. Ever since "Parasite" took the top prize, more and more non-English language picks have found their way into the Best Picture race, and I'm betting we'll see "La bola negra" join the other nominees in 2027.

Before his narrative feature debut "Primetime," director Lance Oppenheim was best known for documentaries like the unexpectedly gripping "Ren Faire" — and when you watch "Primetime," you can see Oppenheim's instincts as a documentary filmmaker on display. I don't mean that as a bad thing — quite the opposite! In fact, I think "Primetime," which re-enacts key parts of the making of the "Dateline NBC" spin-off "To Catch a Predator" with a script from Ajon Singh, probably would have been sort of a dud with any other director at the helm. Oppenheim's vision is uncompromising, unflinching, and uncomfortable, and it's the perfect fit for an unsettling, disturbing, and often darkly hilarious movie about what happens when you make content out of criminal justice.

Robert Pattinson is absolutely perfect as a self-obsessed, self-important, and ultimately sad Chris Hansen, the infamous host of "To Catch a Predator" (his line read of Hansen's famous phrase "You know how this looks, right?" is absolutely astounding), but the performances found in "Primetime" are exhilaratingly great across the board. Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo should, by all rights, both get nominations for playing Chris' ruthless producer Andie Bender and the sensitive but ambitious decoy Dan Plum, respectively, but you'll also catch great turns from Alex Winter, Jonathan Lipnicki, Phoebe Bridgers, Tony Revolori, and Anna Faris throughout the film. "Primetime" is weird, urgent, and incredible, and if the Academy doesn't nominate it for Best Picture, its members will be overlooking one of the year's best movies.

Ever since "The Dark Knight" failed to make it into the Best Picture category at the 2009 Academy Awards (back when there were only five spots for nominees), a major blockbuster has pretty much always found its way into the expanded category, which now boasts 10 spots. (Recent-ish examples include "Avatar" and its sequel "Avatar: The Way of Water," "Barbie," and "Mad Max: Fury Road.") Here's the caveat: the blockbuster hardly ever wins. ("Oppenheimer" is an exception, but frankly, nobody knew in advance that an R-rated three-hour biopic about the father of the atomic bomb would become a near billion-dollar box office hit.) That's where Phil Lord and Christopher Miller's 2026 box office smash "Project Hail Mary," adapted from Andy Weir's best-selling novel of the same name, comes into play ... because if any non-"Odyssey" blockbuster is making it into the Best Picture race, it's this one.

Ryan Gosling would, in a less competitive year, be a lock for the Best Actor race for carrying nearly this entire movie on his back as biology teacher turned space-bound savior Dr. Ryland Grace. Meanwhile, Sandra Hüller could still snag a Best Supporting Actress nomination for her role as Petrova task force leader Eva Stratt, and James Ortiz, who voices and physically portrays the alien Rocky, is eligible for Best Supporting Actor. I worry that the worthy performances in this movie will get overlooked (which is frustrating, because this is ultimately a tricky film to pull off), but I also don't think there's any question that we'll see "Project Hail Mary" compete for Best Picture and perhaps take home some below-the-line awards in the process. ("Fury Road" was the most nominated movie in 2016 and took home six tech trophies while losing for Best Picture, to provide a precedent.)

Irish playwright and director Martin McDonagh won his first Academy Award in 2005 for his live-action short film "Six Shooter" and a Best Original Screenplay nomination for "In Bruges" at the 2009 ceremony. All the same, he didn't become a true Oscar darling until his 2017 film "Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri" snagged Academy trophies for its lead Frances McDormand and supporting actor Sam Rockwell. Then, in 2022, McDonagh returned to the Oscars with "The Banshees of Inisherin," which earned acting nominations for stars Colin Farrell, Brendan Gleeson, Kerry Condon, and Barry Keoghan. Now, McDonagh's 2026 movie "Wild Horse Nine" pairs his previous collaborator Rockwell with living legend John Malkovich, making it a pretty undeniable pick for the Best Picture contest.

"Wild Horse Nine" (which features Steve Buscemi, Parker Posey, and Tom Waits in supporting roles as well) casts Malkovich and Rockwell as, respectively, veteran CIA officer Chris Carlisle and his mentee Lee Chesterfield, a pair who are sent to Chile's Easter Islands right on the precipice of the 1973 coup d'etat in the country. Not only are Rockwell and Malkovich downright magical together (their easy chemistry really makes the movie sing), but McDonagh's sharp script and the story's twists and turns help make this one of the best films of 2026, without question. Yes, McDonagh is an Oscar darling, but this movie is just so good.

Oscar nominations will be announced on January 21, 2027 — and the ceremony will broadcast on March 14.

Presley began modeling as a teenager and worked with fashion houses including Burberry and Dolce & Gabbana. The Gerber family previously requested privacy as they mourn. Nothing written beneath a social media post can make losing a brother easier. Still, the response to Kaia's open letter shows how many people wanted her to know they were remembering Presley, too.

#79. Luke Bryan’s Son Bo, 18, Breaks His Collarbone During Football Game

Luke Bryan's son Thomas "Bo" Boyer Bryan broke his right collarbone during an Oct. 16 game between his school Battle Ground Academy and Pope John Paul II High School.

Thomas "Bo" Boyer Bryan, the country singer’s eldest son with wife Caroline Bryan, broke his right collarbone after being sacked during his team Battle Ground Academy's second possession against Pope John Paul II High School Oct. 16. Still, the 18-year-old doesn’t anticipate being kept off the field for too long.

"Broke my collarbone last night," Bo wrote on his Instagram Stories Oct. 17, per USA Today. “Thank you everyone for your thoughts and prayers. We will be back."

The quarterback, 18, later detailed the moment he hit the ground and two players landed on top of him, after which he went to his team's locker room before reemerging later in the first quarter with his arm in a sling.

"I thought it was just a stinger when I hit the ground," he admitted in an interview with The Tennessean published Oct. 16. "Once I got up I knew something was wrong. When I got to the sideline, I really knew something was wrong."

As for how long before Bo throws his next snap? Well, the severity of his injury had yet to be determined.

"I don't know what we're looking at yet," Coach Bobby Bentley told the outlet. "We'll have to figure this thing out. That's the challenge for us as a team and as coaches. What do we do? How do we do it? We're going to figure it out."

Earlier in the season, Luke—also dad to son Tatum, 16, with Caroline—declared that he was "super impressed" with Bo's form.

"This senior year, he’s learning as he goes,” he said in an interview with USA Today High School Sports in September. “This year is the first time he’s had all these pressure situations and ups and downs.”

“You see the hard work he puts in, and you just want the hard work to pay off," the country star continued. "Nights like tonight is when you get to celebrate that. The main thing is to see his hard work and his commitment and his love for the game. I’m just so proud of him."

#81. Marshals Season 2 Finally Introduces A Real Villain, But Doesn't Use Him Enough

"Marshals" has struggled with a few things since its March 2026 debut, and one of its biggest problems is the lack of a compelling villain. Thankfully, Season 2, Episode 3 "Falling Sky," introduces a new character that looks like a promising potential antagonist for Luke Grimes' Kayce Dutton and his Marshals team. Sadly, he's barely in the episode.

"Marshals" Season 1 wasn't really sure what it was about, which meant we got a bewildering number of storylines, some of which never went anywhere while others just sort of fizzled out. "Marshals" Season 1, Episode 3 introduced us to a powerful and previously unseen Dutton family rival in Michael Cudlitz's Randall Clegg and his family of sovereign citizen rebels. At the time, it appeared as though the show was setting up a major recurring villain who might even known some Dutton family secrets. Then, in Episode 9, Clegg was arrested and hauled away by the authorities, never to be seen again.

After that, "Marshals" pivoted, revealing that Chris Mulkey's rancher Tom Weaver had been the season's big bad the entire time. Unfortunately, it was all a bit too late, and when Season 2 began, Weaver was dealt with as swiftly as Clegg before him. Now, the show is without an overarching villain, but the introduction of a shifty little tech bro character named Gavin Escher in Season 2, Episode 3 suggests we might finally get what we've been waiting for.

Marhsals Season 2 started with a disappointing premiere, but "Falling Sky" is more promising. It begins with a military drone being shot at by three unidentified individuals on the Broken Rock Reservation. We later learn that the trio actually managed to bring down the drone, which crashed into the home of a Broken Rock resident, killing him.

Soon, Air Force Colonel Brooks arrives at Marshals HQ and introduces Pete Calvin (Logan Marshall-Green) and Kayce Dutton to Gavin Escher, CEO of Horus Avionics. His company is developing surveillance drones for the military, and testing them in the skies over Broken Rock. Turns out it was their drone that came down on the Res.

When Escher, Cal, and Kayce meet, the tension is immediately obvious, with the Horus CEO trying to undermine the Marshals. "You guys are really on the cutting edge here, huh," he says with a smarmy grin. "If I ever lose a cow, I know where to come." Escher seems more impressed after being told that Cal and Kayce are former Navy SEALs, but he continues to butt heads with Kayce, who plays down the loss of the drone and calls attention to the death of a Broken Rock resident. Escher then shows the group a video of the three shooters who brought down the drone and the colonel asks Pete and Kayce to bring them in. When Escher suggests the Marshals are "out of their depth," Cal assures the colonel he can complete the mission.

That's it for Escher, who soon disappears and isn't seen for the rest of the episode. That's a shame, as his clash with Cal and Kayce is one of the best moments in "Falling Sky," and is far more compelling than any scenes featuring previous villains.

The big villain reveal at the end of "Marshals" Season 1 highlighted the show's biggest weakness. Specifically, it reminded viewers that the series has far too much going on and simply doesn't have time to build up a compelling villain. With Season 2, the writers have a chance to rectify that, and Gavin Escher seems perfect for the job.

For one thing, his unearned tech bro confidence is all too familiar in 2026. That makes Escher feel like a far more relevant villain than the shady ranchers and off-grid fanatics of Season 1. What's more, as Pete Calvin says later in the episode, Escher has a direct line to the White House, which introduces real stakes to the equation. Meanwhile, his drones clearly pose a real threat to the Broken Rock Reservation that could make for an interesting ongoing battle between the Marshals, Broken Rock, and Horus Avionics. Then there's the fact that the actor portraying Escher does a solid job of projecting a slimy self-importance that has already rubbed Kayce Dutton the wrong way. It would be great to see more of him as the season goes on, but the show needs to devote the time to developing his character in order for this villain story to pay off.

For now, the show is clearly trying to keep things slightly more focused. "Marshals" Episode 2 suggested that overlooked "Yellowstone" alum Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill) might finally get a storyline this season, and Episodes 2 and 3 both make use of a "Yellowstone" tradition by featuring a Buffalo as a symbol of Kayce's ongoing struggles to keep Tate from following in his family's footsteps. If Escher plays a more prominent role as the season goes on, "Marshals" might start to resemble a decent show.

There are a number of trends dominating Hollywood fashion, including the sheer look and gowns that seem to defy gravity. Kim Kardashian has been wearing dresses that magically stay on, and Ana de Armas took a page from her book at the Academy Gala. She shared a photo dump of her look over on Instagram, check it out below:

A post shared by A N A D E A R M A S (@ana_d_armas)

I mean, how stunning is that? We've seen how good De Armas looks in black in projects like No Time to Die (which is streaming with an Amazon Prime subscription), and she once again crushed it in her signature color for this star-studded event. Although I have to assume I'm not the only one wondering how this strapless and plunging dress managed to stay on the 38 year-old actress.

While Kim Kardashian admits that her SKIMS shapewear can help her pull of looks where she looks like she's not wearing a bra, I'm not sure if that would work logistically for Ana de Armas' gown. I have to assume that plenty of fashion tape was used to keep the dress from exposing too much skin. Whatever the process was, those efforts seriously paid off as she rocked that Louis Vuitton and jewelry.

One of the major perks of being a celebrity is that legendary fashion houses are willing to dress you for high profile events. That includes the Oscars and the famous Meta Gala, as well as the Academy Museum Gala. Louis Vuitton might have a big advertising budget and fancy commercials, but sometimes seeing someone like Ana de Armas dressed head to toe is an even more effective way at getting the public's attention.

I can't help but think of Ana de Armas' truly iconic role in No Time to Die when seeing her in yet another chic black gown. Her character Paloma was a real scene-stealer during the movie, despite having a relatively small amount of screentime in the theatrical cut. It's unclear what's going to go down when Denis Villeneuve's developing Bond movie, but part of me is holding out hope that the Blonde actress will get to reprise that role sometime in the future.

No Time to Die is streaming on Amazon, and Ana de Armas is attached to a number of upcoming projects. But since they're not on the 2026 movie release list we're going to have to try and be patient until she returns to the big screen.

#90. Marshals Is Putting A Twist One One Of Taylor Sheridan's Yellowstone Traditions

"Marshals" Season 2 got off to a disappointing start, but at least the writers are trying to go beyond the show's procedural format by injecting some good old-fashioned Taylor Sheridan-style symbolism. The latest episode of Luke Grimes' "Yellowstone" spin-off confirms that the buffalo Kayce Dutton saw in Episode 2 was much more significant than it seemed. That essentially makes this stoic beast the "Marshals" version of the wolves that hounded Kayce throughout "Yellowstone."

Before his wife Monica Dutton (Kelsey Asbille) was killed off in the worst way possible and Kayce joined the U.S. Marshals, he was struggling to figure out his place in the Dutton Dynasty. Throughout "Yellowstone," his conflict was symbolized by wolves, who showed up at numerous points throughout Sheridan's neo-Western and seemed to portend dark days ahead for John Dutton's (Kevin Costner) youngest son.

Now, however, we have a new animal symbol. The buffalo first appeared in "Marshals" Episode 2, wherein Kayce looked over his East Camp land and he spotted the beast grazing in the distance. He then left to find his son, Tate Dutton (Brecken Merrill), reflecting on recent events by John Dutton's grave. We got the sense the buffalo was supposed to represent something, but it was too fleeting a moment to really mean much. Now, Episode 2 has seen the return of this single creature, and it seems Kayce is just as confused as we are.

In "Yellowstone" Season 3, Kayce and Monica Dutton encountered a wolf watching them while they camped. Kayce later saw the same animal outside his tent and approached it, saying, "I am not your friend. I'm your enemy. Whether I like it or not, I am." In that instance, the wolf seemingly represented the tension at the heart of the Duttons' determination to keep their Montana land. Nobody can truly own the natural world, and if anything, the land really belongs to nature itself, as represented by the wolf. The fact Kayce and his family's presence on the land puts them at odds with these rightful residents, whether Kayce likes it or not, highlights how something is deeply wrong with the Duttons' multi-generational enterprise.

Later, at the end of Season 4, Kayce takes part in an Indigenous ritual known as Haŋbléčeyapi, during which he has a vision of a girl in white — a human representation of his spirit animal, the wolf. The girl takes him to a cliff edge, where he sees two paths ahead of him, neither of which are revealed. Kayce later tells Monica he "saw the end of us." All of which is to say that wolves were hugely significant for the character in "Yellowstone," and now, despite the fact Taylor Sheridan is hardly involved in "Marshals," the spin-off's writers are continuing the tradition with the buffalo.

In Season 2, Episode 3, Kayce finds Tate Dutton doing some target practice and is immediately concerned, as his son has never shown any interest in guns. After trying and failing to connect with Tate, Kayce looks off into the distance only to see the buffalo watching him from afar. Again, we get the sense it's supposed to mean something, but what?

In "Marshals" Season 2, Episode 3, Kayce Dutton talks to Mo (Mo Brings Plenty) about seeing the buffalo, telling him. "I'm not sure it's even real." Mo then tells him that the buffalo "symbolizes self-sacrifice," adding, "But you already lost everything, except for Tate. The buffalo could be here to make you confront your shame. Spur you to take action."

"Marshals" has never been subtle, frequently having characters reiterate plot developments to hold the audience's hand as the narrative progresses. In the scene between Kayce and Mo, we once again have things blatantly spelled out. In that sense, the "Marshals" take on Taylor Sheridan's animal symbolism is far more on the nose, but it's at least nice to see the show calling back to "Yellowstone." "Marshals" has faced major criticism for failing to maintain the same tone as the mothership series (at least fellow spin-off "Dutton Ranch" fixed that major issue). But this animal-watches-from-afar motif is a small way of bringing some "Yellowstone" energy into Luke Grimes' offshoot.

What's interesting is that the buffalo comes with very different connotations to the wolf. Though Mo seems to think it symbolizes self-sacrifice, it's also clearly emblematic of resilience and the quiet power of nature. That's a very different thing than the more obviously predatory aura of the wolf, which highlighted how precarious the Duttons' hold on their land really was. It will be interesting to see how the writers continue to use this buffalo imagery as the show goes on — though no doubt multiple characters will tell us exactly what it's supposed to mean.

#91. NFL's Jalen Hurts Out Indefinitely After Clots Discovered in Lungs

Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is likely out for the remainder of the NFL season after doctors discovered bilateral blood clots in the 28-year-old's lungs, his agent confirmed Oct. 19.

The Philadelphia Eagles are huddling up in support of Jalen Hurts.

The NFL quarterback has been sidelined—likely for the remainder of the season—after doctors discovered life-threatening blood clots in his lungs due to deep vein thrombosis, his agent Nicole Lynn shared.

“Jalen was initially diagnosed by specialists in London with a left calf superficial vein thrombosis,” Lynn wrote in an Oct. 19 statement. “After further testing and monitoring, the current diagnosis is a deep vein thrombosis, as well as bilateral pulmonary emboli. He is clinically stable and has no significant functional limitations. His treatment should only involve anticoagulation (i.e. "blood thinners").”

However, she added, “During this time, he will not be allowed to participate in any contact activities, including football.”

Thankfully, she affirmed the 28-year-old’s prognosis is good and that Hurts is expected to make a full recovery.

“We anticipate that he will have the opportunity to resume contact football activities when off the blood thinners,” Lynn added. “In the meantime, he will remain active around the team and continue to condition. More importantly, we anticipate that he will have no long-term effects.”

While Lynn’s statement didn’t share insight into the timeline of Hurts’ recovery and his return to football, NFL Network’s Ian Rapoport reported the quarterback’s recovery will take an estimate three months—meaning he’s likely out for the remainder of the season.

The update comes after Hurts was placed on the injured reserve ahead of the Eagles’ game on Oct. 18, with an Oct. 15 statement from the team confirming the NFL player had been struggling with a calf injury since early in the month.

“On Thursday, October 8th, Jalen visited the training room after practice requesting treatment for his calf,” the statement shared to the Eagles’ website read. “He informed the medical staff he had been cleated during the Rams game on October 4th. This was his first treatment session for the calf injury following the game.”

The message noted Hurts had undergone an ultrasound “out of an abundance of caution” after the team landed in London for its Oct. 11 game against the Jaguars. At the time, the scan revealed what was believed to be a superficial blood clot and Hurts was cleared to play.

“Jalen played without limitation in the game Sunday, received treatment on Monday and Tuesday, and practiced in full on Wednesday, as reflected in the practice report,” the statement noted. However, “On Wednesday night, a follow-up ultrasound revealed movement in the small blood clot. Jalen will be out for Sunday's game vs. the Panthers as we determine the appropriate course of treatment.”

While Hurts focuses on recovering, read on for more celebrities who have navigated harrowing health challenges.

The Jessie alum opened up about her "hellish" migraines, sharing how they've worsened after suffering five concussions over the course of her life.

"The brain injuries make things significantly worse," Ryan shared during a September 2026 episode of Mythical Kitchen’s Last Meals. "I had a pretty crazy, life-altering brain injury a few years ago, and I was out of commission for six months."

While Ryan described her first four concussions as "incidents," she said her fifth one was trauma caused by "sustained shaking over a minute of time."

Now, the former Disney Channel star needs to close her eyes to "think better."

"Quite often the world is really loud. It’s really too bright. There’s a lot going on," she explained. "The visual data that I'm taking in can be so distracting and so loud. Then, with the migraines—which are significantly worsened by that—it sort of is too much."

Brianna "Chickenfry" LaPaglia's Ovarian Cyst

"There was a half a liter of blood in my pelvic floor," Brianna shared in a TikTok video after the operation. "I have five incisions all over my stomach. They went in through my belly button with a camera so they could find all the blood."

I had a massive bleed and the doctors made it plain that my chances of surviving were precarious if they didn’t operate again. This time they needed to access my brain in the old-fashioned way—through my skull."Thankfully, Emilia shared, she's now "at a hundred per cent."

Snoop Dogg's daughter Cori Broadus is grateful for her family.Because after she suffered a "severe stroke" in January 2024, her loved ones rushed to be by her side."I texted them that I just had a stroke and sent them a picture," she told E! News correspondent Will Marfuggi in December 2024. "My kidneys were failing. It was a lot going on."Today, Cori is on the mend."I'm doing great," she added. "I just had a little bit of motor skills that I had to work back on. But other than that, I was fine."

I couldn’t walk for longer than five minutes at a time without having to lay down for hours, and hours and sleep. Everything I ate hurt my stomach,” the actress said on a September 2024 episode of the SHE MD Podcast. “It was this conflation of issues and diagnoses and different doctors telling me different things.”So Shailene—who chose to keep the exact condition private—set out to find answers. “I come from a very holistic background and study herbalism,” she added. “So I was very keen on, ‘I’m going to work with real MDs, [and] I’m also going to work with independent kind of healers.’ Just trying to search for some sense of comfort in my own skin.”It was a long journey—one that lasted for 10 years.“Throughout that decade, a lot of other things came from feeling so much discomfort physically,” the Big Little Lies star noted, “which was, ‘My gosh, if everything I eat hurts my stomach, I’m now suddenly afraid of food.’ And then going into the kind of mental f--ckery that can happen with that of body dysmorphia and confusion about identity and feeling safe in my own capsule, in my own skin, what that meant, and what that should be.”After tending to both her physical and mental health, Shailene is feeling much better.“It was a journey that ultimately physically resolved itself, and I am very healthy,” she shared. “I’m so happy to be able to say that."

Things have been quieter on the automaton bird front in recent days. The investigative journalism has been done, the fans have weighed in on either side, and Molly the bird has had her price upped from $15,000 to $15 million. (This honestly still could be afforded by Kelly Clarkson, who reportedly earns $14 million per season each time she does The Voice.) While feathers doubtless remain ruffled on both sides, an insider came out of the woodwork to talk about the daytime host’s response, and how her celebrity pals really factored in.

An insider spoke to popular scooper Rob Shuter this week about Birdgate, aka Ms. Clarkson’s claims she was treated like a Pretty Woman character after entering a Brooklyn store and inquiring about an automaton bird bracketed into the wall. Apparently, Ms. Clarkson is uninterested in apologizing after the incident, per the new report.

Kelly is perfectly happy. She doesn’t think she did anything wrong, and nobody around her is telling her otherwise. She’s living in a bubble of applause.

The insider went on to speak about the outsized response the singer has gotten from her fans, which range wildly from daytime viewers, to The Voice fans, and people who love her music. When her viral tweets and Instagram posts broke, some of her Voice co-workers sent support, including her former step mother-in-law Reba McEntire, who wrote, “Oh Kelly their loss honey.” Per the insider:

Kelly sees Reba [McEntire], Jennifer [Hudson], Blake [Shelton] and Pink defending her. Her fans are overwhelmingly supportive. Why would she apologize when everyone she trusts is cheering her on?

There is some difference between the faction defending the generally relatable Kelly Clarkson and the other faction calling her out for the attempted takedown of a small business, and the insider said this is doubtless due to their still being differences in how the singer thinks she “stood up for herself” while her critics thinks she’s a “millionaire” taking shots at an entity with less resources and power.

To be clear, I don’t think the small business Art of Play was ever looking for an apology. Owner (and popular children’s book author) Adam Rubin said late last week that he would invite Kelly Clarkson back to their store to see what it is all about. He called what happened a “misunderstanding” basically of epic proportions. Despite reach outs, the store reportedly hasn’t heard back.

So, with no apology on the horizon, all that’s left is for Pablo Torre to auction off that comparable bird automaton he purchased while in the store and doing his own investigation.

Palvin’s Victoria’s Secret ensembles included a flirty low-cut pink mini dress and matching undergarments, which the model teamed with oversized silver hoop earrings and mesh stilettos. Her second look included the brand’s famed jumbo wings, which Palvin wore off her back to complement a white bejeweled bodice and boyshort briefs.

Both looks were enthusiastically approved by Sprouse, 34, who proudly filmed his wife strutting her stuff on the catwalk while cheering her on.

Palvin said during a backstage interview with People that motherhood has proven to be a “fun” ride. “It’s like a rollercoaster,” she explained before addressing Sprouse’s role in the house. “Dylan’s great, you know, he always wanted to be a dad. #96. Inside Prime Culture, the Dance Music Management Company Turning Underground Talent Into Global Headliners

Alberto Bragado built Prime Culture to focus on culture over commerce, with the company now offering event production, A&R and agency services for a roster including Michael Bibi, PAWSA and ANOTR.

On a humid summer night at DC10 in Ibiza, the vibe inside the club is “controlled chaos.” But one person in particular maintains a serene presence amid the party’s banging kickdrum.

Understated in jeans and a t-shirt on the club’s sprawling backstage patio, Alberto Bragado is the founder of Prime Culture, the management company that works with PAWSA, the DJ in the booth tonight. The company also represents DJ/producers including English phenom Michael Bibi, Dutch duo ANOTR and other electronic acts carving out a distinct, and increasingly large, presence in dance music. With PAWSA and Bibi among his first management clients, Prime Culture is also strongly associated with Solid Grooves, the label co-founded by the English producers, which is also the name of the party happening here tonight.

The dancefloor is sardine-level packed, but it’s tame compared to the scenes that defined Bragado and Prime Culture’s earlier days on the island. After he started working with Bibi and PAWSA in 2014, they booked a Solid Grooves residency at the former Ibiza club, Privilege. Trying to save money during the season, the guys stayed together in a nearby villa, where they started hosting afterparties.

“At the beginning it was just us,” says Bragado. “Then some friends start coming, and then fans were arriving to the villa, and it became an actual afterparty.” When videos of this party went viral in 2018, “that created a name for us in Ibiza,” Bragado says. “We were these new kids that do the residency and have the villa party every Sunday.”

They knew they were onto something when, Bragado continues, “strangers were coming into the villa and telling us they were friends with the Solid Grooves guys.” Soon, other DJs were asking if they could come play, and aspiring attendees were jumping the fence to gain entry.

Named for the kind of culture it works to nurture and promote, Prime now employs nine managers who look after 33 artists including Carlita, Ben Sterling and Beltran. All in, the roster reads like the cool kids’ table at house and techno high school. Last year, Bragado and Prime Culture manager Michael Discenza expanded the business by creating Select Culture, a booking agency for rising management clients. Prime Culture now also has in-house event production and A&R departments to support its roster.

The hybrid structure is working: Bibi and PAWSA are both hard ticket and festival draws in the U.S. and Europe, where a 2024 headlining show by Bibi in London’s Finsbury Park drew 45,000 attendees and a 2025 show by PAWSA at the city’s Gunnersbury Park brought a crowd of 25,000. Meanwhile, ANOTR’s “Talk to You” (featuring 54 Ultra), debuted at No. 5 on Billboard’s Hot Dance/Electronic songs chart earlier this year, spending 29 weeks on the tally.

“The vision is for it to be something managers want to be part of not just for the salary,” says Bragado. “They’re their own bosses and can build a roster themselves. It’s a community of managers and artists more than a pyramid structure. Everyone has freedom.” This freedom extends to the artists, who don’t sign management contracts with Prime. “Other management agencies have three-year contracts; I don’t have that with any of my artists,” he continues. “Any artist can leave at any time.”

Born in Madrid, Bragado worked as a paramedic before getting into music almost by accident, when, at age 19, he helped an artist from the Dominican Republic book shows in Europe. Bragado advised this artist to just announce a tour and put Bragado’s phone number on the announcement so promoters could call him to set up shows, which they did. “We were using some contract I found on the internet,” Bragado says. But while he was green, he was also a fast learner, and the successful 20-date tour led to a run working with Dominican hip-hop artists in Europe.

Bragado had been going to Ibiza for fun since he was a teenager, “but I didn’t have any clue about electronic music,” he says. That changed when a Dominican artist came to Madrid and needed a studio space. Bragado connected this artist with Spanish DJ/producer Dennis Cruz, who had a studio in the city. Cruz told Bragado he needed a manager and Bragado took the gig, immersing himself in music by Euro final boss DJs like Marco Carola and Luciano — and feeling, in his words, like “maybe this has a future.”

Cruz was getting loads of requests from labels and promoters, but Bragado couldn’t do the work as extensively as he wanted given that he didn’t speak English. In 2014, he moved to London to learn the language, along with the ins and outs of the U.K. dance industry. This is where he met Bibi and PAWSA, who’d just founded their independent dance imprint Solid Grooves and were interested in releasing music by Cruz.

“They didn’t have a manager, so I was like, ‘What about getting together to do it?’” Bragado recalls. They accepted, and in 2015 Bragado created the management company SG Artists, named after Solid Grooves. The goal was to expand Solid Grooves events outside the U.K., which Bragado focused on while also signing rising artists. (“At the beginning I had a couple of different emails with different names, one for accounting, one for logistics, and it was all me,” he says with a laugh.) The first international dance show he booked was a club set for Cruz in Bulgaria. They made 500 bucks.

“I was also traveling with him and basically spending more money than I was making in commissions just to meet people and network,” he says. The 2016 Ibiza season was the first one Bragado attended as part of the Solid Grooves team, via Bibi and PAWSA’s residency at Privilege (the label had done residencies at clubs like Sankeys in seasons prior.) The following year, they hosted a huge Solid Grooves residency at the island’s open-air venue Benimussa Park, then returned to Privilege for a Sunday night residency in 2018 — the era when fans began swarming the Solid Grooves villa to get inside its buzzy parties.

“We were small, fully independent DJs,” Bragado says, “but we were already making noise.” Around this time, he changed the company’s name to Prime Culture.

Naturally, those knocking at the door also included DJs who wanted to be part of the company. Now, seven years later, Prime is home to an ecosystem of artists with similar sounds and aesthetics who often share stages and festival billings, a goal from the beginning. “Culture-wise, what we’re creating needs to all be a similar sound and vibe, because one of the key things is that the artists help each other,” Bragado says.

“Working with Alberto has played a huge role in our growth, both personally and in our career,” ANOTR says in a joint statement. “From the beginning, he understood our vision and helped us to develop ourselves as artists and never tried to change who we are or what we want ANOTR to be. Instead, he’s always helped us turn our ideas into something bigger and pushed us to think beyond what we thought was possible.”

“We support artists on their vision,” says Bragado. “If someone wants to do a new record label [or a new party] we always support them to have their own projects.”

To execute these projects, Prime has an in-house production team led by head of production Kelamo Masali, that helps artists develop and expand their event brands. These include Miguelle & Tons’ Two and a Half Cats, Dennis Cruz’s Botaniq, Bibi’s One Life series (launched after the producer announced in late 2023 that he was in remission from brain cancer), along with ANOTR’s No Art, which this year drew 25,000 attendees in Amsterdam in July and 20,000 in Manchester in May. With these shows, the idea is to extend artists’ influence beyond releases and traditional touring, with the production team also helping ensure artists’ visions are aligned with the show contracts they’re signing.

Meanwhile the in-house A&R team, led by head of music Stephanie Moran, helps develop a wide range of releases. Bragado advises that they’ll likely soon hire someone to facilitate studio sessions, with the idea to continuously fill gaps in artist services. Management agencies with such additional services are becoming more common across genres, although still relatively rare. What’s especially unique is Prime Culture’s in-house agency, Select Culture.

While headliner-level Prime artists like ANOTR and Bibi are represented by the big agencies, “some of the artists don’t want to be with a bigger agency because they get lost,” Bragado says. “With Select Culture, you get more focused attention.” He adds that having an in-house agency also saves artists money, because they’re not being charged compounding management and agency fees.

The first Select Culture office opened in June of 2025 in Miami to help the team focus on bookings in the U.S., a focus market amid dance’s current popularity surge in the States. “The U.S. scene has grown massively,” Bragado says. “Before it was just about EDM, and now I think house music has taken over a lot of the spaces and audiences EDM used to own.”

Earlier this year Bragado also established Select Culture Europe in partnership with David Nus and Javier Castro with offices in Madrid and Ibiza. Select Culture now operates globally and reps white hot names like Mau P (in Europe and South America), Max Styler (in Europe and MENA) and Mita Gami (in Europe, South America, Asia and Australia.)

“It’s growing faster than we were expecting,” says Bragado, who acknowledges that creating the agency got the attention of the majors. “We explained, because it was the truth, that at the beginning, it was just a platform for smaller artists, but let’s see in the future.”

Bragado says that so far, the secret of his success is simple: being honest and straightforward and “discussing without forcing. I think it’s important to not rush in, to be humble and to understand each artist’s situation… When you make choices based just on the numbers, there is a big part of the creative course of the artist’s work that you’re maybe choosing wrong.”

“What makes Alberto special is how personally invested he is,” says ANOTR. “It never feels like he’s just managing a career or making business decisions. He genuinely cares about the people he works with. He knows when to push us, and when to protect us.”

As Bragado frames it, the plan for Prime Culture is to continue growing horizontally (“That’s maybe why Prime is not a business that is the most attractive for a corporation to buy”), adding managers who can eventually become partners “so the vision doesn’t stop with one or two people” and creating projects that don’t just feel like business moves, but like actual culture.

While the scale has changed, Prime Culture’s M.O. is still, essentially, to get fans and artists so excited about these projects that they’re willing to jump the metaphorical fence to be part of them. Eight years in, the only difference is how many people are lining up outside.
