#98. Arnold Schwarzenegger Only Directed One Movie - And It Wasn't In The Action Genre

The career path of actor turned director is enough of a phenomenon in Hollywood that it became its own axiom, or at least wry joke. It only makes sense that an actor, after they've gained enough experience and clout, would wish to take the reins of a production themselves, as the creative life of an actor is, ultimately, one at someone else's behest. These new directors usually tackle material and genres they're highly familiar with. That said, it's not exactly an enormous rarity for an actor-turned-director to wish to branch out, either.

However, while there have been folks like Clint Eastwood, who started with a thriller (instead of a Western), the award for most surprising genre swing by an actor turned director goes to Arnold Schwarzenegger. When he made his feature directorial debut in 1992, it wasn't anywhere near the action genre which he became famous for as a star. It wasn't even sci-fi, which he had a long standing relationship with, too. Instead, it was a holiday romantic comedy, "Christmas in Connecticut," which is a remake of the 1945 film starring Barbara Stanwyck. As if that weren't odd enough, the movie wasn't released to theaters. Instead, it premiered on the TNT network in, of all months, April of '92. To date, it remains Schwarzenegger's only feature as a director, and is only the second of two projects he ever directed, the other being the 1990 episode of "Tales from the Crypt" entitled "The Switch." For better or worse (mostly the latter), Schwarzenegger's "Christmas in Connecticut" lives up to its status as a trivia stumper, as the star's work behind the camera is proof that he made the right choice to stay in front of it instead.

The original "Christmas in Connecticut," directed by Peter Godfrey, released in August of 1945 during the final days of World War II. As a result, "Christmas in Connecticut" is a thoroughly contemporary movie, whose events kick off when a war hero, Jefferson Jones (Dennis Morgan), gets caught in an erroneous marriage proposal to his hospital nurse. She in turn becomes convinced that her new beau will honor his commitment if he experiences domestic bliss, which she believes is best represented by the nationally popular lifestyle writer Elizabeth Lane (Barbara Stanwyck). However, Lane is actually not a Connecticut housewife, but a jaded, single New York City woman who made up her alter ego to boost readership. This all leads to a group of characters descending on a Connecticut farm for the holidays, where mistaken identities collide in farcical fashion.

For his remake, Schwarzenegger and writer Janet Brownell understand that the core elements of the story are its Shakespearean-esque farce and the false identities put forth by the various characters. Yet their attempts to update the 1940s setting to the early '90s are awkward at best, turning Elizabeth (Dyan Cannon) into a TV cooking show personality (who can't actually cook), and Jefferson Jones (Kris Kristofferson) into a reclusive mountain man who loses his cabin in a fire while performing a rescue of someone stranded in the woods. The characters of Elizabeth's blowhard boss and obnoxious suitor are combined into Tony Curtis' Alexander Yardley, and the whole thing hinges on a Christmas Day live broadcast which goes awry. In essence, the film plays like Schwarzenegger and Brownell gave up on "Christmas in Connecticut" and attempted to emulate John Hughes films and the ending of "Scrooged" instead, a tack change which fails miserably.

The irony of "Christmas in Connecticut" is that, despite its flaws, it still might've worked as a calling card for Arnold Schwarzenegger as director if he truly took a back seat to the movie he was making. However, by this point in his career, Arnold was a master of self-promotion and hadn't yet reached the apex of his hubris, something which happened the very next year with "Last Action Hero." Thus, while Schwarzenegger doesn't play a named character in "Christmas in Connecticut," he peppers himself throughout the film nonetheless. In one scene, the character of Tyler (Gene Lythgow) puts on sunglasses and says "I'll be back," a line which Schwarzenegger dutifully overdubs for him. Later, a character is watching "Twins" on TV, a moment which is followed soon after by Arnold turning up as an unnamed PA for Elizabeth's broadcast in the film. Though Schwarzenegger must have intended these cameos and references as cheeky Easter eggs, they end up as just another distraction in an already distracted movie.

An even further irony to the "Christmas in Connecticut" saga is that Schwarzenegger would eventually end up in a movie which did become a new holiday classic, playing the lead in Brian Levant's "Jingle All the Way" in 1996. While that counts as a somewhat related victory, it's still too bad that "Christmas in Connecticut" ended up as Arnold's only directorial feature effort. Perhaps he could've done something special with an action or a sci-fi script, or maybe a holiday or comedy film that wasn't an awkward remake. As it stands, his "Christmas in Connecticut" is destined to remain a curio, a film whose existence is more interesting than itself.

#99. The Simpsons Brings Back Beloved Character for First Time in a Decade

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon, now voiced by Sunil Malhotra, returned during The Simpsons' Oct. 18 episode, speaking for the first time since Hank Azaria left Fox's animated comedy in 2017 amid backlash.

Warning: This article contains spoilers for the Oct. 18 episode of The Simpsons.

One of The Simpsons' most iconic characters has finally returned to Springfield.

Apu Nahasapeemapetilon—the beloved Kwik-E-Mart convenience store clerk originally voiced by Hank Azaria—made a surprise appearance during the Oct. 18 episode of Fox's long-running animated comedy, speaking for the first time in nearly a decade thanks to new cast member Sunil Malhotra.

The season 38 pre-Halloween episode, titled "The Revengening," culminated with Apu revealing to the town he's been hiding in plain sight, albeit behind a spooky costume, since Azaria's 2017 departure from the series.

Apu's return was a complete shock to fans as Simpsons producers kept Malhotra's casting a complete secret—until now.

"When my agent called me about a Simpsons audition, I knew exactly what role it was for, and the idea actually made my stomach sink," the Grey's Anatomy alum told Variety in an interview published Oct. 18. "But admittedly, part of me was also curious."

But after Azaria—who is not of South Asian decent—willingly walked away from the role with an apology amid backlash over racial stereotyping, Malhotra thought good and hard about the opportunity to revive the fan-favorite character.

"It had been eight years since Apu had spoken on the show," the 50-year-old continued, "and it got me thinking: Did the writers’ room look different now? Could they bring him back in a way that acknowledged and apologized for past mistakes? Could I make the character my own, and reclaim him in some way? And could they achieve all of that in an unmistakably Simpsons way that didn’t disappoint fans?"

At first, Malhotra admitted he "was prepared to walk away" because to "be the butt of the joke wasn’t something I was willing to do." However, producers eventually put an end to his worries.

As Malhotra recounted, "It was the beginning of a deeply collaborative experience that I hope is equally satisfying for longtime fans of The Simpsons and for other South Asian kids who, like me, stopped watching at some point along the way."

Ultimately, The Simpsons crew was just happy to finally have Apu back with Homer, Marge, Lisa, Bart and the rest of the Springfield gang.

As executive producer Matt Selman told Variety, "We love this character, and wanted to bring him back in a smart, Simpsons-y way that allowed him to evolve. We’re excited by what Sunil has already brought to the role, and look forward to seeing more of Apu in the future."

Of course, this is hardly the first time The Simpsons has shocked fans with an unexpected twist. Keep reading for shocking secrets behind the making of the iconic TV series.

1. The Simpson family first appeared as a series of shorts in The Tracey Ullman Show in 1987 after creator Matt Groening passed on an initial offer to turn his Life in Hell comic strips into animated shorts. According to the creator, he hurriedly sketched the family while waiting in the lobby for his pitch meeting.

2. Groening named all the characters after his own family members, substituting Bart for his own name. Why Bart? It was an anagram of the word brat.

3. They soon became the most popular thing about Ullman and producer James L. Brooks, who'd recruited Groening, realized they should be their own series, ultimately negotiating a provision in the contract with Fox that prevented them from ever interfering with the show's content.

4. The family is yellow because Groening wanted something that would grab people's attention as they flipped through the channels. He told the BBC that "an animator came up with the…yellow and as soon as she showed it to me I said: 'This is the answer!' When you're flicking through channels with your remote control, and a flash of yellow goes by, you'll know you're watching The Simpsons."

5. The first full-length episode produced, "Some Enchanted Evening," did not broadcast until May 1990, as the first season's last episode, because of animation problems that delayed the show's launch from fall until December 17.

6. Groening drew each of the Simpson family members to be instantly recognizable in silhouette, leading to their distinctive hairstyles and head-shapes.

7. Oingo Boingo frontman and composer Danny Elfman was approached by Groening to create a "retro-style" theme for the opening sequence. The iconic piece of music, believed to be the most popular in Elfman's career, took him only two days to create.

8. The show's lengthy opening sequence was developed to cut down on animation necessary for each episode, however three elements change from episode to episode: Bart's chalkboard message, the music played during Lisa's sax solo, and the closing couch gag, the length of which varies based on the needs of that particular episode.

9. Groening chose Springfield as the show's setting because of how common a city name it is in America, appearing in at least 29 states. Despite revealing to Smithsonian Magazine in 2012 that it was named after Springfield, Oregon, near his hometown of Portland, he intentionally kept the fictional town's state obscure. "In anticipation of the success of the show, I thought, ‘This will be cool; everyone will think it's their Springfield,'" he told the magazine. "And they do."

10. The Bush family were not fans of the show. In October 1990, then-First Lady Barbara Bush called the show "the dumbest thing [she] had ever seen," prompting the show's writers to pen a response from Marge Simpson, who argued the family was trying their hardest. The First Lady then apologized.

In early 1992, then-President George H.W. Bush said, during a speech for his failed re-election campaign, "We are going to keep on trying to strengthen the American family, to make American families a lot more like the Waltons and a lot less like the Simpsons." The writers responded in the show's very next broadcast, a rerun, with an opening showing the family watching the speech as Bart replies, "Hey, we're just like the Waltons. We're praying for an end to the depression, too."

11. While the show has been a mainstay on Sunday evenings for much of its run, its initial success there, becoming the first Fox series to rank among the season's top 30 highest-rated shows in its first season, prompted the network to move it to Thursdays, airing opposite The Cosby Show, then the number one show. It would remain there until season six when it was moved back to Sundays.

12. Yeardly Smith, the voice of Lisa, is the only main cast member who regularly voices only one character.

13. Until the 17th episode of the second season, Fox and the production crew kept which characters the voice actors performed a secret, going so far as to close recording sessions while refusing to publish photo of the recording artists. With "Old Money," however, the network revealed which roles each actor played because the producers decided their cast should receive credit for their work.

14. Until 1998, the six main actors were only paid $30,000 per episode. After a pay dispute, in which the network threatened to replace them with new actors until Groening stepped in to support his cast, they were bumped to $125,000 an episode. After a month-long strike in April 2004, in which the cast stopped showing up to cast readings in the hopes of getting a bigger piece of the show's rising revenue, their salaries were increased to somewhere between $250,000 and $360,000.

15. In 2011, the show was almost canceled by Fox unless production costs were cut, forcing the cast to accept a 30 percent pay cut from their then-$400,000 per episode, reached through contract negotiations in 2008, resulting in their current pay of just over $300,000 per episode.

16. The "voice" behind Maggie's pacifier-sucking is none other than Groening himself. When the eternal-toddler spoke her actual first word ("Daddy!") in 1992, the show turned to Elizabeth Taylor.

17. When the album The Simpsons Sing the Blues was released in 1990, lead single "Do the Bartman" was widely believed to have been composed by fan of the show, Michael Jackson. Brooks claimed that it was actually written by Jackson's friend, Bryan Loren, who remains the sole credited songwriter. But in 1998, Groening admitted it was actually co-written and co-produced by the King of Pop, who could not receive credit for it because of contractual issues. When Jackson later guest-starred in an episode, he was credited under pseudonym John Jay Smith and his character's singing voice was performed by a soundalike, Kipp Lennon.

18. Jackson wasn't the only famous guest-star to perform under a pseudonym. In the second season, Dustin Hoffman played Lisa's substitute teacher Mr. Bergstrom. Unsure he wanted to be tied to a cartoon, he chose the name Sam Etic for his credit, a play on the word semitic.

19. The reason Krusty the Clown and Homer look so similar? "The satirical conceit that I was going for at the time was that The Simpsons was about a kid who had no respect for his father but worshiped a clown who looked exactly like his father," Groening explain. Early plans for Homer to be revealed to be moonlighting as the clown were considered to be too complicated for the show and scrapped.

20. A 2003 episode revealed Homer's email address to be ChunkyLover53@aol.com. The episode's writer, Matt Selman, registered the address beforehand and within minute of the show airing, the inbox had hit its message limit.

21. While Homer's "D'oh!" has been added to the Oxford English Dictionary, the expression appears in scripts simply as "annoyed grunt." Dan Castellaneta, the actor who's played him for three decades, says he's based the sound off of Jimmy Finlayson's "Doooooh!" in the Laurel and Hardy films.

22. While nearly everyone in The Simpsons is drawn with only four fingers, only one character gets an extra fifth digit: God.

23. The show has something of a knack for predicting the future. In the year 2000, the episode "Bart to the Future" mentioned Donald Trump had been President of the United States at one time and left the nation broke. In 1998's "When You Dish Upon a Star," 20th Century Fox was revealed to be a division of The Walt Disney Company, which famously happened 19 years later.

24. In 1992, Ullman sued Fox, claiming her show was the source of The Simpsons' success and she should share in the profits. The claim was ultimately thrown out of court.

25. In 1997, a life-size replica of the Simpsons' house was built in Henderson, Nevada for a contest sponsored by Fox and Pepsi. After decorators painstakingly recreated the 2,200-square-foot, four-bedroom home, the winner, a retired factory-worker from Kentucky, opted for a $75,000 cash prize over the home (which cost $120,000 to build) and it was sold in 2001 after it was stripped of its unique coloring.

26. The show has been dubbed into Japanese, German, Spanish, Portuguese, both standard French and Quebec French, and Arabic. For the latter, because of Islamic customs, Homer drinks soda instead of beer and eats Egyptian beef sausages instead of hot dogs. His name in the Arabic version is Omar Shamshoom.

27. The actors behind the French dubs of Homer and Marge, Phillipe Peythieu and Veronique Augereau, met during auditions and got married a decade later.

28. Homer is the only character who has dialogue in every single episode.

29. In 1999, Time included Bart in the Time 100, their list of the century's 100 most influential people. He was the only fictional character on the list.

30. If you were to watch every episode of the series broadcast over the last 30 years, it would take you over 14 full days.

Plus, the Oct. 18 episode also marked the vocal debut of Janina Gavankar (The Morning Show) as Apu’s wife, Manjula, adding even more South Asian representation to the cast.

#101. Gisele Bündchen, 46, Rocks Pink Lingerie at Victoria's Secret Fashion Show

Gisele Bündchen delighted fans by unexpectedly appearing in the 2026 Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show.

The model, 46, surprised fans with a pre-taped video appearance that captured her lying on a couch in pink lace lingerie paired with the brand’s signature pink-and-white striped bathrobe. The video was aired at the show just ahead of the Sunday, October 18 live event kicking off inside Los Angeles’ Sony Pictures Studios.

“Are you ready for the show?” Bündchen seductively asked the camera after it panned across her toned physique in the video, which was later shared by Bündchen via her Instagram Stories. The clip concluded with the model flashing a wide grin as she threw her hands up over her head and giggled.

Bündchen, who began walking as an Angel for the brand in 1999 and hung up her “wings” when her contract concluded in 2007, had clearly filmed the clip prior to allegedly injuring herself, as reported by Page Six one day prior to the live event.

The outlet published photos that depicted Bündchen sporting a moon boot and hobbling along a Florida parking lot on Friday, October 16. Despite the apparent injury, the model still maintained a glamorous silhouette with her signature caramel locks styled in waves with a black singlet and blue denim cut-offs.

The Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show was filled with other famous faces, including Kylie Jenner who made her Fashion Show debut for the brand in a $50 million bra fitted with 4,410 natural diamonds and a statement 75.54-carat $22 million yellow diamond. The reality TV star was cheered on in the crowd by boyfriend Timothée Chalamet and mom Kris Jenner.

Veteran Angel Miranda Kerr, however, declined to take part in the 2026 production, sharing an explanation via Instagram ahead of the event. “It meant so much to be invited to return this year, especially as it marks 20 years since my first show…. but I ultimately felt in my heart it was right to cherish this chapter as it was. Sending so much love and light to everyone in this year’s show!” she wrote on Saturday, October 17.

Bündchen’s appearance at the show comes amid the release of Lars Anderson’s new book about her ex-husband, Tom Brady. In Brady: An American Story and the Price of Greatness, the author claimed that a friend of the NFL great, 49, had revealed that he was absolutely “stung” when the model became pregnant “roughly two years after their divorce.”

Bündchen, who shares son Benjamin, 16, and daughter Vivian, 13, with Brady, married jiu-jitsu instructor Joaquim Valente in December 2025 after the pair welcomed a son in February that year. Bündchen and Brady finalized their divorce on October 28, 2022, after 13 years of marriage.

For Brady’s part, he also shares son Jack, 19, with his ex Bridget Moynahan.

#102. Alfonso Gomez-Rejon To Direct Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa’s New Disney+ Series ‘Afterlife With Archie’

EXCLUSIVE: Alfonso Gomez-Rejon (Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, Hunters) will direct the pilot of Afterlife with Archie, which was greenlit for a TV series adaptation on Disney+ in July. Gomez-Rejon will also direct the second episode and will serve as executive producer of the episodes.

Based on the bestselling comic book series by Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa and Francesco Francavilla, Afterlife with Archie turns the all-American town of Riverdale into a zombie-overrun apocalypse — where the only thing scarier than the undead is trying to survive your teenage years. When a supernatural spell from a certain teen witch backfires, unleashing an army of the possessed dead upon Riverdale, Archie and his friends must fight to stay alive, testing the friendships, romances and loyalties that have always held them together.

Afterlife with Archie is executive produced by Aguirre-Sacasa and Jimmy Gibbons via Muckle Man Productions and its overall deal with WBTV; Greg Berlanti, Sarah Schechter, and Leigh London Redman via Berlanti Productions and its overall deal with WBTV; and Jon Goldwater for Archie Comics Studios. Watch on Deadline

In addition to his directing work on the film Me and Earl and the Dying Girl and the Prime Video series Hunters, Gomez-Rejon is also a frequent collaborator with Martin Scorsese, including the upcoming Aldeas: A New Story, a new documentary featuring Pope Francis’ last on-camera interview. Additional credits include the Benedict Cumberbatch film The Current War. Gomez-Rejon also received an Outstanding Directing for a Miniseries or Movie Emmy nomination for American Horror Story: Coven.

The director currently has work lined up on the Apple TV series Stowaway, starring Oscar Isaac as Juan Carlos Guzmán; the film The Fortress of Solitude; and the TV adaptation of Edna Ferber’s book Giant at Amazon. He is repped by CAA, Untitled and JSSK.

#103. 5 Prematurely Canceled Western TV Shows That Deserved A Second Chance

Many great TV shows have been canceled after only one season, and many terrible ones have suffered a similar fate. That's no different for TV Westerns, which were so prevalent in the mid-20th century they might as well have been the only thing on TV. Still, no matter how popular the genre was, there were always going to be those shows that never managed to catch on and ultimately fell by the wayside while others galloped their way to success.

It's not always clear why some projects became beloved classic Western TV series while others very quickly failed. Why did a show about a mysterious cowboy such as "The Virginian" catch on when another show about a mysterious cowboy, like "The Loner," didn't? And why did so many small screen Westerns with solid casts and interesting premises simply fail to garner the kind of ratings they needed to stay on the air? What we do know is TV history is littered with swiftly-canceled Western shows, many of which more than deserved a second chance.

Here, we've assembled five examples. While some of these might not have been the finest sagebrush sagas to grace the small screen, they all had something promising to them and, given a second chance, might have been able to earn their place in the pantheon of legendary TV Westerns.

By the mid-'70s, the Western was fully in its revisionist era. Clint Eastwood had become the poster boy for the genre's evolution into a more cynical and deconstructionist version of itself that ultimately marked the end of its pop culture dominance. Meanwhile, networks had begun the decade by carrying out the so-called "rural purge," cancelling shows with a rural setting en masse. The legendary "Gunsmoke" wasn't even immune and was abruptly canceled in 1975 after two decades on the air. A year later, "The Quest" ventured into this precarious TV terrain.

NBC's Western series debuted in September 1976 with Kurt Russell and Tim Matheson in the lead roles of formerly estranged brothers Morgan and Quinton Beaudine, respectively. The show follows the pair as they scour the Old West in search of their sister, Patricia, who was taken captive alongside Morgan eight years prior. While Morgan was raised by the Cheyenne and Quinton had a more traditional upbringing in San Francisco, the fate of their sister remains undetermined. On their travels, they meet former bounty hunter turned trail boss Tank Logan (Brian Keith), who hires the boys to help him with his cattle drives.

A pilot episode of "The Quest" aired as a TV movie in May 1976 and fared well in the ratings, prompting NBC to green-light a series. But the show struggled. For one thing, it ran opposite ABC's "Charlie's Angels," which ultimately sealed its fate, and "The Quest" was canceled after one season. In fact, it was pulled after just 11 episodes, despite the fact Russell and Matheson had great chemistry and the show was an all-around well-made entry in the small screen Western canon. It should have lasted longer, and perhaps if it debuted a decade prior, it would have.

After "Star Trek: The Original Series" was canceled in 1969, it took a while for William Shatner to lead another show. Though he appeared in multiple TV movies, small screen guest spots, and in several movie projects, Shatner's first leading role in a TV series after "Star Trek" came with 1975's "Barbary Coast." It was short-lived.

The show starred Shatner as government agent Jeff Cable, who's tasked with investigating the various illicit dealings that take place in the titular section of 1870s San Francisco. Cable, who operates out of a casino in the district, is a master of disguise, and is assisted in his investigations by his pal and casino owner Cash Conover (Doug McClure).

It was a "Wild Wild West"-style spy adventure in the Old West, though in fairness it was more realistic than Robert Conrad and Ross Martin's beloved series. Shatner was clearly enjoying the opportunity to don his various disguises, but he and McClure (who replaced Dennis Cole after he portrayed Conover in the pilot) didn't exactly have the best chemistry. The show also didn't get off to the best start when Shatner broke his ankle on set and production had to stop for 10 days. Things didn't seem to improve for "Barbary Coast," and ABC pulled the plug after 13 episodes.

Still, given time, the show and its stars could very well have come into their own. Though networks were moving away from rural shows at the time, "Barbary Coast" was set in an exciting and dynamic section of San Francisco and incorporated a spy element that meant it was, at the very least, offering more than your standard small screen Oater.

"Nichols" has to be one of the most delightfully misguided shows in TV history. This offbeat 1970s Western starred James Garner alongside "Superman" star Margot Kidder in a show that tried to have it both ways and was rewarded with a swift cancellation.

Garner plays Frank Nichols, the sheriff of a small town also called Nichols that was founded by his own family. After leaving the Army, Frank returns to Nichols with the intent to settle down and live a quiet life far away from the violence of his military career. But he's blackmailed into taking on the sheriff job by the matriarch of the town's new ruling dynasty.

The show was set in 1914, which was significantly later than standard Western TV shows that typically unfolded during the immediate post-Civil War era. This was seemingly an attempt to update the genre during the "rural purge" of the early 1970s. The thing is, the Nichols of 1914 isn't all that different than your typical Old Western town. The only thing this updated time period really did was allow Garner's sheriff to ride a motorcycle rather than a horse.

That might sound like a show destined for failure, but "Nichols" was sort of charming. Garner and Kidder, who played the local barmaid Ruth, had some great chemistry, and there was a self-awareness to both Garner's sheriff and the show as a whole. Sadly, it was canned after one season, ending with an amusingly off-the-wall episode in which Nichols is shot dead, only for his twin brother (also played by Garner) to show up sporting a mustache. Imagine how that second season would have gone...

A show featuring one of the best Western actors of all time defending his ranch from various foes intent upon ending a longstanding family dynasty? That sounds a heck of a lot like "Yellowstone." Unfortunately, Sam Elliott's forgotten Western series "The Yellow Rose" aired long before Taylor Sheridan's neo-Western captured the public's attention, and only ended up lasting one season.

Elliott plays ex-con Chance McKenzie, who arrives at the eponymous ranch after gaining his freedom. His father, Wade Champion, previously won the land on which the ranch is built from his neighbor, Jeb Hollister (Chuck Connors of "The Rifleman"). When he passed away, Champion left the ranch to his sons Roy (David Soul) and Quisto (Edward Albert). But Chance wants his share of the property, too, and arrives in the series premiere to join Roy, Quisto, and the rest of the family.

We then witness McKenzie and co. battling to keep hold of their father's ranch in a soapy melodrama clearly designed to capitalize on the popularity of "Dallas," which had been running since 1978. "The Yellow Rose," which debuted in 1983, seemed to have what it needed to succeed in that regard, and certainly wasn't lacking in legendary Western actors with both Elliott and Connors involved.

Unfortunately, the ratings just weren't good enough, and NBC canceled the show after one season of 22 episodes. But there must have been something to it, as the network aired "The Yellow Rose" again in 1990, perhaps in the hopes audiences would respond differently. Alas, it would take until 2018 before those audiences were ready for a soapy Western show about a family defending their ranch, and by that time, Sheridan was poised to strike. Perhaps a "Yellow Rose" remake might fare better now...

When we talk about short-lived TV shows, we're usually talking one-season wonders. But "Wildside" has to be one of the shortest-lived Western shows in TV history. The ABC series ran for six episodes between March and April 1985 before it was pulled off the air in what is one of the most disappointing cancellations on this list.

"Wildside" had a great cast and an interesting premise, but wasn't even given a chance to come into its own. William Smith, who'd previously led the classic '60s Western series "Laredo," stars as Brodie Hollister, a former outlaw who's an expert marksman. In his past, Hollister was part of a five-man group of outlaws, four of whom decided to clean up their act and settle down in the relatively peaceful town of Wildside, California. The group is made up of Hollister (who, after leaving his lawless ways behind, became a horse breeder), John D'Aquino's Varges de la Cosa, Howard Rollins' Bannister Sparks, and Terry Funk's Prometheus Jones. All of them seem to be upstanding members of society, but when trouble arrives in Wildside, they reteam to defend their community.

Smith's casting was inspired. The actor was known for playing villains and therefore easily exuded the aura of a man with a shady past. Meg Ryan also appeared in this underrated Western series, playing Wildside's newspaper editor, Cally Oaks, who forms an attraction to Hollister's son, played by J. Eddie Peck. The whole thing was a solid show with a unique premise that could have been great had it been given more time. Sadly, ABC put it up against "The Cosby Show," which proved too formidable a foe for Hollister and his band of reformed outlaws.

#104. Seth Rogen Trusted Animated ’Tangles’ Would Resonate Because of Its ’Specificity’

Seth Rogen has made projects about the end of the world and anthropomorphized grocery store items, but the new hand-drawn, black-and-white animated film “Tangles,” a drama about a woman returning to her small conservative town to take care of her mother who has Alzheimer’s disease, might be closest to in his heart. In conversation at the Middleburg Film Festival this weekend, the producer shared how the specific approach that director Leah Nelson and her co-screenwriters Sarah Leavitt and Trev Renney was more of a selling point than a deterrent.

“To me, animation is a medium and it is my instinct to trust the creative ambitions and instincts of the people that I work with and to not question them too much, honestly. And if anything, I have tried to train myself to really go on the journey with people’s creative instincts, even if they are not my own or even if they seem like you could argue against them,” said Rogen. “This film being an animated film is the perfect example of that. You probably could have talked them out of this. You probably could have argued there are surreal sequences [that] you could probably do in live-action if you really wanted to. There’s visual effects, you can make a wave come into a room. It’s not impossible.” Related Stories Léa Seydoux Became Fearless After the Controversies of ‘Blue Is the Warmest Color’ — She’s Doing It Again with ‘Gentle Monster’ ‘La Bola Negra’ Earns $277,500 in Limited Release as Netflix Reports Box Office Results for the First Time in History

The opportunity for Rogen and his wife, director Lauren Miller Rogen, to produce the film came about from the advocacy work they’ve done for Alzheimer research. The couple met Nelson and Leavitt, who wrote the graphic novel that the film is based on, “Tangles: A Story About Alzheimer’s, My Mother and Me,” at a charity event, and stayed in touch with them to develop the film adaptation, and fundraise for it over time.

Talking more about the film taking what some may see as an unconventional approach to the material, even from an animation perspective, Rogen said, “Truthfully, they came to us wanting it to be animated. It was based on a graphic novel. They had a look, they had a vision. And rather than try to poke holes in that, we all chose to support it. And rather than say, ‘Why does this have to be animated?’ We all thought, ‘Wow, very interesting. What an interesting approach to this.’ It’s more unique, it’s more specific.”

He continued, “The more I make things, the word ‘specificity’ is the thing that I am telling the people I work with the most to seek and to try to create in their own work. What makes it specific to you and to this? What makes it different [from] what anyone else would do to tell this story? What makes it distinct? And so all those things, animation, that’s specific, black and white, that’s specific. Hand drawn, that’s specific. And I think in art, the more specific art is, the more it seems to resonate.”

Rogen used examples of other famous artists working in different mediums to support his theory. “Andy Warhol isn’t the best painter. He’s one of the most specific painters. Jackson Pollock you can argue is not even a good painter, but it’s unbelievably specific. You see it, you know who did it right away. And that’s to me the key of specificity. And I think with this, you see one frame of it, you know what it is,” he said.

Speaking again about “Tangles,” the producer said, “You could put 10 movies on the screen. If this was one of them, the specificity of it is what would make you instantly recognize it. And to me, that has become, as I’ve worked more and more, something that I’ve really looked to and encouraged those who I work with to pursue, is not just creative ambition or clarity or any of that. All those things as well, but also what can you do to make this specific? What can you do? What are all the things you could do, all the parameters you can put on it that will set it apart from anyone else’s version of this were they to do it?”

“Tangles,” which includes the voices of Julia Louis-Dreyfus, Abbi Jacobson, Bryan Cranston, Beanie Feldstein, and Rogen himself, premiered at the Cannes Film Festival in May, and was eventually acquired by IFC in August, just in time to mount a Best Animated Feature Oscar campaign.

Verity has been one of the upcoming 2026 movies that I was most looking forward to watching. I didn’t love the book, but the film adaptation sparked my curiosity. It was one of Anne Hathaway’s must-watch 2026 movies. The film is the salacious, semi-erotic thriller that I wanted and expected.

It has some major changes from the Verity book, but I think it’s a pretty faithful adaptation. In fact, I think some parts of the book work better in movie form, including its discussion about being a writer.

Warning: Verity spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

Verity is a pretty engaging and entertaining audiobook. It’s definitely worth listening to before seeing the movie, but the story gets even stronger when you see Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, and Josh Hartnett play Verity, Lowen, and Jeremy. Hathaway does such a good job playing Verity as this dubious figure that you remain unsure of what’s real, what’s fake, and most importantly, what’s the truth.

The Verity ending becomes so much stronger with Hathaway’s performance. Initially, you’re sure she’s some evil woman who kills for what she wants, but then seeing Verity’s reaction to Jeremy, you aren’t too sure if she’s as evil as she has portrayed herself in the manuscript.

Additionally, Dakota Johnson plays Lowen as a bit of a dubious character as well. We aren’t sure if we can trust everything she says either. She’s so seduced by Verity’s life. She may be telling the reader a story that makes her look better. The elements of the unreliable narrator always existed in the Verity identity, but they sing on screen. Don’t trust any of these characters and their accounts of things.

I didn’t draw a connection between Jeremy as a stand-in for the number one fan until seeing the Verity movie. He adores Verity when he first meets her, but then loses interest and even finds someone new to obsess over (Lowen). I think many authors experience having a big first fan who loves and adores them, only to eventually lose interest or fade away. They may even become a fan of someone with a similar writing style or subject matter. And transfer their parasocial obsession to the new subject. Fan love is often fleeting.

Verity’s desperation to keep Jeremy could be a metaphor for how some authors start to lose fans or readers and go through extreme measures to keep them. For most authors, that may mean writing stories to appease their readers more than themselves. Verity highlights the dangerous game between fans and a subject.

They need each other but shouldn’t be desperate to hold on to one another. Sometimes letting fans move on is the best way for authors to stay true to their art. That comes across better in the movie than in the book, or at least I drew the connection better in the movie.

Art is someone’s child. It’s their creation, and they bring it into their world, one way or another. Artists don’t always love what they create. For example, a successful first novel can sometimes be more of a burden than a blessing.

People have expectations based on it. Verity sees her children as a curse, and that’s sometimes the consequence of art. It becomes something regretted more than loved.

I have been a life long lover of pop culture, especially television, turned that passion into writing about all things entertainment related. When I'm not writing about pop culture, I can be found channeling Gordon Ramsay by kicking people out the kitchen.

#106. Amelia Earhart Plane Search: Investigators Share Major Update

After satellite images of an object in the Pacific Ocean were believed to be connected to Amelia Earhart's missing plane, researchers shared an update on their expansive expedition.

The search for Amelia Earhart's missing plane has continued to sputter.

After researchers traveled to the uninhabited South Pacific island of Nikumaroro to search for the pilot's missing aircraft after satellite images showed a mysterious shape—dubbed the Taraia Object—submerged in a nearby lagoon, they confirmed that the expedition found no conclusive evidence about its whereabouts.

"We can say now, after the conclusion of our work, that the Taraia Object did not or does not represent the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's Electra aircraft," the Archaeological Legacy Institute's executive director Rick Pettigrew said in an Oct. 18 YouTube video. "Instead, we think it's most likely that the object was a collection of debris that accumulated here."

Pettigrew—whose team worked with researchers at Purdue University—noted that, unfortunately, the mystery has been "ongoing for 90 years, and the mystery continues."

As for what was seen in the 2020 satellite imagery that sparked the investigation?

Evidence gathered at the Taraia Peninsula, according to an Oct. 18 Purdue press release, confirmed that the "visual anomaly" was "likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit."

"The fragment's reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer," the release added. "Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand."

But that doesn't mean the expedition to find Earhart's plane—which disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in 1937 while she attempted to fly around the world—was fruitless.

"At the same time, the evidence for the castaway hypothesis, which brought us here, remained very, very strong," Pettigrew explained. "We think that it's very likely that Amelia and her navigator Fred Noonan did, in fact, end up here on Nikumaroro Island."

"We accomplished our main goal, which was to come here and test that hypothesis," he continued. "We followed our game plan. We did the analysis."

Purdue's general counsel Steve Schultz couldn't help but praise the team for taking the investigation to new heights.

"Unfortunately, we weren't able to find that smoking gun, but we're again proud of what we accomplished," he added in the YouTube video. "We leave Nikumaroro knowing more than what we did when we came here."

"Amelia herself said, ‘Adventure is worthwhile in itself,’" Schultz said. “We've lived that out this week with all the trials and tribulations that we had, the things that we've had to overcome, and yet be able to follow our game plan and follow the evidence to the end. We're very proud of that, and we leave fulfilled in that sense."

#108. Before Clayface, Tom Rhys Harries Was In A Little-Discussed Fantasy Movie With Patrick Stewart

There are five films in the "Dragonheart" film series. Yes, seriously. And yes, Tom Rhys Harries — the star of DC Studios' Batman-adjacent horror movie "Clayface" – plays a lead in the fourth of them, "Dragonheart: Battle for the Heartfire," opposite Patrick Stewart, who played the voice of Draco the dragon. No one talks about this movie (or any of the other "Dragonheart" sequels or prequels, either).

Some readers may recall Rob Cohen's original 1996 film "Dragonheart" with clarity. Dennis Quaid stars as Sir Bowen, a knight in the 10th Century who has sworn to hunt down and slay all the dragons. His quest is successful, and the bulk of the movie concerns Bowen's relationship to Draco (Sean Connery), the last living dragon. It's a fun flick, it made a decent chunk of change, and it was nominated for Best Visual Effects at the Academy Awards. Most folks rank it among the best movies about dragons ever made.

What many readers may not know is that "Dragonheart" has one straight-to-home-media sequel and three straight-to-home-media prequels. "Dragonheart: A New Beginning" was released in 2000. That was followed by the prequel film "Dragonheart 3: The Sorcerer's Curse" in 2015, "Dragonheart: Battle for the Heartfire" in 2017, and finally, "Dragonheart: Vengeance" in 2020. A different celebrity voiced the dragons in each of these films, with Robby Benson, Ben Kingsley, Patrick Stewart, and Helena Bonham Carter taking on various draconian roles.

Prior to "The Battle for the Heartfire," Harries had accrued several movie and TV series credits, having appeared on shows like "Parade's End," "Jekyll and Hyde," and "Midsomer Murders." A "Dragonheart" film was merely another tick on his resume. Meanwhile, for Stewart, it was likely an easily acquired paycheck, employing only a script, a recording booth, and a willingness to growl.

The story of "Dragonheart: Battle for the Heartfire" is, as many high fantasy stories are, incredibly complex. Tom Rhys Harries plays a character named Edric, one of a pair of twins, whose sister Mehgan is played by Jessamine-Bliss Bell. These kids are the grandchildren of characters named Gareth and Rhonu, who are played by Julian Morris and Tamzin Merchant in "Dragonheart 3." Merchant returns in "Heartfire," while Valeriu Bazu takes over the role of Gareth.

Those characters had a son named Walter (Turlough Convery), who, in turn, fathers the central twins in "Heartfire." Through a complex dragon-human magical interlinking that is common in the "Dragonheart" films, the twins are born with patches of dragon scales and mild superpowers. Edric is strong, and Mehgan is able to manipulate fire. Edric's heart is also magically bound to the dragon Drago (Patrick Stewart), which is bothersome, as Edric, when invited to sit on his grandfather's throne, proves to be a less-than-stellar king. He's arrogant. Meanwhile, Mehgan, raised separately, is full of hate and bitterness following an accidental act of childhood arson.

It should be noted that arrogant royals are a common enough feature in the "Dragonheart" movies. In the original "Dragonheart" film, Draco places half of his heart into a young prince, saving his life and magically binding them together (thus, when one dies, so goes the other). However, the young prince grows up to be a terrible tyrant that must be defeated, putting Draco's life at risk.

Here, though, we're meant to root for the initially arrogant Edric. The rest of the plot of "Heartfire" involves Vikings, a battle between Edric and Mehgan, and an extended period with Edric on the lam.

Gradually, Edric is humbled, and Mehgan, now in a position of power, becomes targeted by the vicious Thorgrim (André Eriksen) and his assistant Sable (Marte Germaine Christensen). Throughout the movie, the twins reveal their past, including the fact that they weren't raised together, and other dark secrets besides. That synopsis might make the film sound complex, but all that matters is that the twins reconcile and the villains are all defeated.

There aren't a lot of reviews for "Dragonheart: Battle for the Heartfire" out there. Common Sense Media praised the film's clarity but snickered a bit at its theatricality. Elsewhere, Nick Rogers of the Midwest Film Journal ranked all five of the "Dragonheart" movies and surprisingly put "Battle for the Heartfire" at #1, comparing the film favorably to "Game of Thrones." As he put it:

"With a duel for command, 'Dragonheart: Battle for the Heartfire' is the most overtly 'GoT'-like, but it avoids painting Edric or Mehgan as evil. Instead, they're equally vulnerable to influence, folly and tragedy, albeit along differing trajectories."

Actual moral ambiguity? Clarity of storytelling? These are signals of basic quality in any movie, and it's nice to hear that a non-theatrical "Dragonheart" sequel, one released 21 years after the original film, can possess some actual acumen.

As for Tom Rhys Harries: the early critic reactions to "Clayface" have been largely positive, and the film itself looks pretty scary. No dragons, though.

Three years after it was first announced that a Harry Potter TV series was in the works, it’ll finally make its way to the streaming schedule this Christmas. With that, a new cast is entering the Wizarding World, and following in the footsteps of Emma Watson as Hermione Granger is Arabella Stanton. The show's casting director put a lot of thought into tapping Stanton for the role, and there was even the cute element from her audition that proved to be very important for her being cast. (And it makes so much sense.)

Back when Watson first auditioned for HP, she proved on set she was born to play Hermione. That was because she memorized everyone’s lines and started mouthing them. In the case of Stanton for the TV adaptation, casting director Lucy Bevan spoke on the HBO Max special, Finding Harry: The Craft Behind the Magic, about what was “crucial” for HBO’s perfect Hermione. See what Bevan said:

So, right off the bat, I love hearing Arabella Stanton talk. Just like the Hermione actress who came before her, she’s got a very refined way of speaking. Even when the child star said one of her character’s iconic “Leviosa” lines, it sounded flawless. No wonder Audible had Stanton record for Harry Potter’s audiobook as the Muggle-born student.

Not only is Hermione Granger a real bookworm in the J.K. Rowling series, but she’s also an 11-year-old student with her childlike quirks. So I love the fact that Bevan says it was Stanton's snort during her audition that essentially helped land her the role:

So this is Arabella’s audition. So she did the poem Invictus. So we got her in to do a scene where she’s talking to her parents about Harry and Ron, and she sort of got the giggles and did a little snort. And that’s the take we used to show [the producers] that she’s playful. So Arabella’s snort was quite crucial in the casting process.

That’s the cutest thing! I’m glad the casting team chose to keep those giggles in the audition, as even that small snort can do a lot for Stanton's performance. While Hermione is supposed to be the logical one of the trio, it’s good they’re allowing her to be playful as well, like many of the other Hogwarts students.

On the surface, these may seem like small details, but they'll help the HBO present a more accurate depiction of the books. As seen in the new Harry Potter trailer scenes, Hermione can be occasionally awkward and anxious. Considering we didn’t get to see so much of that side in the movies, the team behind the TV series clearly wants to show us a side of the brainy witch that exists in the book series.

Relatively speaking, we've still only seen just a snippet of Arabella Stanton's take on Hermione. Still, I'm confident that she'll grow into the role perfectly, just like Emma Watson. If everything goes accordingly, that "crucial" snort will go down as a key piece of behind-the-scenes Potter lore.

Hold out your wands for Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, which premieres on HBO on Christmas Day and will also be available to stream with an HBO Max subscription that same day. In the meantime, use the service to check out the OG films to see Emma Watson's performance.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#110. All 4 Big Bang Theory TV Shows, Ranked

"The Big Bang Theory," the CBS sitcom about a bunch of nerds and a girl who hangs out with them for some reason, which was created by Chuck Lorre and Bill Prady, is still one of the most popular half-hour comedies in recent memory. Long after it wrapped up its original run in 2019 after 12 seasons and the same number of years, people are still tuning into "The Big Bang Theory" on HBO Max (its exclusive streaming home as of this writing). It's also spawned a series of spin-offs, which isn't all that surprising. Are they all worth watching, though?

Your mileage may vary, and drastically. I'm not going to pretend that "The Big Bang Theory" is my all-time favorite sitcom, but I also won't pretend that the show doesn't have its charming moments and doesn't feature a pretty incredible cast, nearly all of whom have produced some stunning post-"Big Bang" work since 2019 to boot. As I write this, there are three spin-offs of "The Big Bang Theory," bringing the total number of shows in its small-screen universe to four — so which one reigns supreme, and which is the worst of the bunch?

Technically, the CBS sitcom "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage" is a spin-off of a spin-off; both George "Georgie" Cooper Jr. (Montana Jordan) and his eventual wife Mandy McAllister (Emily Osment) began their narrative on "Young Sheldon." We'll return to that prequel eventually, but first, let me be clear: "Georgie & Mandy's First Marriage" is a dreadful, mean-spirited slog that's honestly unbearable to witness. "Georgie & Mandy," obviously, centers around the titular couple's first marriage — it started airing in 2024 and is still running, so as I write this, we don't know what brings an end to said marriage — and also brings Mandy's parents Audrey and Jim (Rachel Bay Jones and Will Sasso) into the mix, chiefly because Mandy and Georgie live with them as they raise their daughter CeCe.

Despite game guest appearances from "Young Sheldon" stars Zoe Perry and Annie Potts (reprising their roles as Mary Cooper and Connie "Meemaw" Tucker), among others, "Georgie & Mandy" is laboriously paced, full of dated and awkward jokes, and saddled with a laugh track that has no place on any sitcom, network or otherwise, in the mid-to-late 2020s. Not a single character feels like a real human with any interiority, and it's honestly sort of embarrassing that a show with this poor level of quality is even airing on television. That said, it's a huge ratings juggernaut, so what do I know?

When I first heard about the HBO Max series "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" — the only non-prequel spin-off to "The Big Bang Theory" thus far — I got my hopes up, and I did so on the record right here at /Film. To be fair to Past Nina, I wasn't totally delusional. Not only did the HBO Max of it all suggest more creative freedom than any show in "The Big Bang Theory" yet (all of the rest originated on network TV, which is much more restrictive), but the concept, in which beleaguered and constantly downtrodden comic book owner Stuart Bloom (Kevin Sussman) found himself in a multiversal battle to save the larger universe, seemed solid. Add in comedy powerhouses like Lauren Lapkus, John Ross Bowie, and Brian Posehn returning to reprise their "Big Bang Theory" roles as Denise, Barry Kripke, and Bert Kibbler, and I thought showrunners Zak Penn and Chuck Lorre had a hit on their hands.

Unfortunately, the reality of "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" was more of a fail than a pass. Sussman is a genuinely hilarious performer — honestly, all of them are — but stocking a show with secondary and even tertiary "Big Bang Theory" characters just doesn't really work in practice, and the narrative's constant zigs and zags turned out to be more frustrating than fun. Maybe the show can course-correct in its confirmed second season, but as it stands, it's just not the best "Big Bang Theory" show.

On some level, it makes me feel absolutely insane that Chuck Lorre — at least, this is how I imagine it — walked into the CBS offices one day and pitched, "What if Sheldon, but young?" Still, there's no question that "Young Sheldon," which casts "Big Little Lies" alum Iain Armitage as a young version of Jim Parsons' idiosyncratic physicist Sheldon Cooper, is the second-best "Big Bang Theory" show with a bullet. Armitage does an excellent job playing Sheldon "but young" — I'm being flip, as he's a child prodigy who attends college at age eleven and graduates at fourteen with major academic distinctions — and he's joined by Zoe Perry as his mom Mary Cooper, Lance Barber as his gruff but loving father George Cooper Sr., the aforementioned Montana Jordan as Sheldon's older brother Georgie, and Sheldon's twin sister Melissa (Raegan Revord), known as Missy.

"Young Sheldon" wisely dispenses with the laugh track and uses a single-camera approach instead of the multi-cam setup utilized by "The Big Bang Theory," and beyond that, it delves into some seriously deep emotional topics (we know Sheldon's father passes away in "The Big Bang Theory," but even with this inevitability, the arc surrounding George Sr.'s death is pretty gutting). Still, it's just ... not the best "Big Bang Theory" show. Only one show could take that spot, and you know what it is.

The original iteration tends to be the best version, and that's true of "The Big Bang Theory," which proved to be lightning in a bottle when it started airing in 2007. In the pilot, socially awkward dorks and California Institute of Technology employees Sheldon Cooper (Jim Parsons this time) and Leonard Hofstadter (Johnny Galecki) introduce themselves to their bubbly new neighbor Penny (Kaley Cuoco), and history is made. Before long, the show brings Sheldon and Leonard's coworkers and friends Howard Wolowitz and Raj Koothrappali (Simon Helberg and Kunal Nayyar) into the fold, and by Season 3, Penny has two female cohorts: Mayim Bialik's Amy Farrah Fowler and Melissa Rauch's Bernadette Rostenkowski.

Sure, not every aspect of "The Big Bang Theory" ages well, and Penny's character didn't exactly start off strong (though the show eventually course-corrected, and frankly, Penny ended up with the best character arc of basically any series regular). Still, the chemistry between the regulars is completely undeniable, and even when "The Big Bang Theory" falters, it's still the best group in its small-screen universe.

"The Big Bang Theory" and "Stuart Fails to Save the Universe" are streaming on HBO Max, and "Young Sheldon" is available on HBO Max and Netflix.

#111. Justin Hartley's Colter Finds New Love Interest on 'Tracker' After Changes

Tracker just introduced Justin Hartley‘s newest — and potentially most significant — love interest after several changes in season 4.

During the Sunday, October 18, episode of the hit CBS series, Colter (Hartley) was seen fixing up his car by visiting a store specializing in spare parts. There he shared a few loaded moments with Jenna Nova (Gillian Bolt).

The duo bonded while looking for a bench that Colter could use to restore his dad’s truck. Jenna made the first move by asking Colter out to dinner, which he accepted. Later in the episode, he told Jenna over the phone that he wasn’t sure when he was coming back to town when she called with news about a possible car bench.

Jenna told Colter he only had two weeks to claim the item — and he subtly implied that he would make sure they would have their date before the two weeks are up.

The surprise connection comes after executive producer Elwood Reid told Us in August that Colter would meet someone new, adding, “One of the things I think we’re trying to do this year is open up life outside of the office. With Colter, we’re going to see the buds of a relationship forming.”

According to Reid, the show is dropping hints at something larger.

“We don’t know what it is yet. So it’s someone who Colter is pursuing — and what does that look like? Then can we get a much larger story out of that?” he continued. “That’s one thing that I think is unique to this season, which is we just never see Colter in a social and possibly romantic situation outside of the Billie universe.”

Though Colter has a connection with Billie (Sofia Pernas), nothing is off the table.

“This is much different. … Then the other thing, which is just an overall theme of the show, is how can we test and challenge Colter morally and physically,” Reid added.

He continued: “Many TV shows — long-running network shows — have characters who become infallible and become superheroes. There’s nothing wrong with that. But I think that one of the strengths of Justin as an actor is he has access to this emotional component or dynamic that a lot of leading men tend not to have. What does it look like when he fails or makes a mistake and that costs somebody their life or doesn’t get a result? Those are the things that I’m excited about getting into this year.”

The hit CBS series, which premiered in February 2024, introduced fans to survivalist Colter, who travels the country to help solve various missing persons cases. Colter’s job hasn’t allowed him to explore a serious relationship in the past — but that could change. (The show has also kept shaking things up with cast changes — and a relocation to Los Angeles in season 4.)

“We’re not just jumping right into it. We’re just showing the buds of it. This is the seed we’re planting, but what would happen if that relationship got leveraged against him somehow or that person or somebody close to that person got into a situation that needed Colter’s help?” Reid noted to Us. “Would that blow the relationship up? Would that deepen the relationship?”

Reid also pointed out that Colter might not be “in any position to have any kind of long-term relationship.”

“We don’t want him to be a guy that just rolls into town and romances somebody and then leaves the next day,” he said. “I do think he has a bit of a code and [we’re] playing with that a little bit. But with an actor like Justin, it’s just being able to see him flex that muscle a little bit because he is very charming. … Colter is a team leader, so he doesn’t want to show that weakness, but could we find somebody that he could open up to a little bit?”

Tracker airs on CBS Sundays at 9 p.m. ET before streaming the next day on Paramount+.

#112. Jason Segel Marries Kayla Radomski in Intimate "Storybook Wedding"

Jason Segel and Kayla Radomski officially tied the knot in a “storybook wedding” after two years together. The Shrinking star’s new wife shared a glimpse into their nuptials on social media.

How Jason Segel married Kayla Radomski? Long story short, it was happily ever after.

#113. 5 Star-Studded TV Shows That Were Canceled After A Few Episodes

Ever since Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson delivered two of the best performances of their careers in 2014's "True Detective" Season 1, the boundary between movie and TV star has all but crumbled. Now, A-listers don't think twice about leading prestige streaming dramas, and in many cases, that has led to some of the best TV shows of the 2010s and 2020s.

But not every big name actor has had success on the small screen. In fact, TV history is full of star-studded shows that struggled to foster much of an audience, mostly because they were summarily yanked off the air before they even had a chance to do so. Networks will often give new shows a chance to build a following, but in some cases, they pull the plug at the first sign of trouble, even if there's a big name top-lining the project.

If you look back at your favorite actor's filmography, chances are they may have led some sort of obscure TV series you never heard about. Here, we've rounded up a few examples which demonstrate how even the most well-known actors are no guarantee of a show's success or safety.

I will resist the temptation to make a joke at the expense of this show's title. "Emily's Reasons Why Not" was based on Carrie Gerlach's novel of the same name and starred Heather Graham as lovelorn Los Angeles book editor Emily Sanders. The show was supposed to follow Sanders as she put a new dating rule into practice: she can only break up with a guy if she can list five reasons to do so. Unfortunately, we never saw much of that play out, as "Emily's Reasons Why Not" lasted just a single episode, which, according to the New York Times' Alessandra Stanley, had to do with the fact "Heather Graham was so off-putting" in the series.

A single installment of this "Sex and the City"-style sitcom aired on January 9, 2006 and brought in 6.2 million viewers. Meanwhile, "Desperate Housewives" was comfortably bringing in 23.7 million viewers. Evidently, this simply wasn't good enough for ABC, which had heavily promoted the show ahead of its debut. According to a contemporaneous E! Online report, the network completely shuttered production on the show following the end of filming on Episode 6. Executive producer Gavin Polone told the outlet, "When the audience stays away, in this super-competitive environment, quick decisions are made. That's the television business."

In the end, none of the other episodes ever made it to air, which judging by the critical response, that was probably for the best. Dana Stevens of Slate described it as "another disappointing role for Graham," who she noted had "struggled to find a place on the big or small screen" ever since her role in "Boogie Nights." "Emily's Reasons Why Not" didn't do much to help.

Today, it's hard to imagine a network green-lighting a show called "We Are Men." Back in 2013, however, that's exactly what CBS did when it ordered 10 episodes of writer Rob Greenberg's single-cam sitcom. But only two of those episodes ended up airing.

That certainly wasn't a reflection of its cast. The show starred Christopher Nicholas Smith, Tony Shalhoub, Jerry O'Connell, Kal Penn, and Rebecca Breeds, all of whom did an unsurprisingly admirable job in a sitcom that didn't exactly have the most appealing premise. Beyond its talented cast, this was a sitcom about a dude whose wife stood him up at the altar, whereafter he makes friends with three other divorced guys. It's like Ross' divorced men's club from "Friends" brought to life, except it's not very funny.

Greenberg had previously won Emmys for his producing and writing work on "Frasier." That, along with a solid cast, seemed to bode well for "We Are Men," which ultimately debuted on CBS in September 2013 and lasted only two episodes before CBS dropped the axe. Hey, that's double the time "Emily's Reasons Why Not" stayed on the air.

The critical reception to this short-lived sitcom was absolutely atrocious. A 4% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes should give you some idea of how reviewers felt, but just in case, consider Verne Gay of Newsday's assessment: "[More like] We Are Morons." That surely makes it a contender for one of the worst sitcoms of all time. And to think, Kal Penn went from "House" to "How I Met Your Mother" to this...

Before "The Office," Steve Carrell starred in a short-lived sitcom with none other than Tim Curry. "Over the Top" was a silly little show about an actor who falls on hard times and moves into a hotel owned by his ex-wife for some reason. It was pretty dire stuff, and only lasted three episodes before ABC decided it could no longer inflict the show on the small audience that was watching.

Curry played Simon Ferguson, who, after being fired from a popular soap opera, finds himself on the verge of becoming fully washed up. So, he moves into the Manhattan hotel which is run by a woman named Hadley Martin (Annie Potts). It seems Ferguson was once married to Martin for 12 days, and decides that he needs to take up residence in her hotel, where she lives with her two children. A young Steve Carrell plays Greek chef Yorgo Galfanikos, who's used frequently throughout the three episodes of the show that did air.

As delightful as Curry's presence is, the rest of this show was about as generic as you can get, with rote sitcom humor failing to set "Over the Top" apart from the competition. 11 episodes were shot, but only three ended up making it to air. Some messy behind-the-scenes drama involving a relationship between the show's executive producer and ABC's Entertainment President was speculated about as a factor in the show's bungled launch. But in the end, it just wasn't very good, and critics were absolutely relentless in their condemnation of Curry and Carrell's collaboration.

"The Simpsons" star Hank Azaria auditioned twice to become a main character on "Friends," but ended up in a guest role as Phoebe Buffay's (Lisa Kudrow) on-again-off-again boyfriend David. While Azaria landed nicely on his feet by voicing multiple beloved characters on "The Simpsons," it seems he always had ambitions to front a successful sitcom. Unfortunately, he never really realized those ambitions, despite trying numerous times.

The closest he came was with his recurring role on Fox's "Herman's Head," which ran for three seasons. Otherwise, there's "If Not for You," a '90s sitcom that lasted one season and starred Azaria alongside Elizabeth McGovern. Then there was "Imagine That," which was even more short-lived.

Azaria stars as Josh Miller, a TV comedy writer who uses his Walter Mitty-esque fantasies as inspiration for his writing. Throughout the show, he was supposed to deal with an overbearing boss and a fraught marriage to his wife, Wendy Miller (Jayne Brook), but "Imagine That" was pulled after just two episodes. Today, the show is basically lost media. Six episodes were produced, but they're nowhere to be found — though judging by a Reddit thread, every now and then the pilot resurfaces.

Critics would probably rather it didn't. As The Washington Post's Tom Shales put it: "'Imagine That' traps the versatile Hank Azaria in a smutty-minded sitcom about a spineless comedy writer who doesn't get enough sex at home."

Kelsey Grammar will forever be sitcom royalty for playing Dr. Frasier Crane on both "Cheers" and its equally beloved spin-off, "Frasier," but the man is certainly no stranger to sitcom failure and swift cancellations. Grammar's forgotten 2009 sitcom "Hank" was pulled off the air after just five episodes, which you'd think would be a wake-up call for the actor. Perhaps these multi-cam live-studio-audience sitcoms were becoming old hat in the age of "The Office" and its mockumentary format? Well, the message didn't quite sink in, and five years after "Hank," Grammar returned with another sitcom, and this time he brought Martin Lawrence along for the ride.

"Partners" sees Grammer and Lawrence play Allen Braddock and Marcus Jackson, respectively, two Chicago lawyers with very different backgrounds and professional experiences. Braddock worked for his father's law firm, but was fired and needs a place to set up shop on his own. Luckily, he meets Jackson, who runs a law firm out of his basement, and the two go into business together, thereby establishing the "sit" of this sitcom as a fairly rote odd-couple-type deal.

Unfortunately, neither critics nor audiences were interested. "The show itself is practically an afterthought," wrote Variety's Brian Lowry, who went on to describe how "watching these two comedy veterans trying to keep such a leaky, woefully flat vehicle afloat is more depressing than nostalgic." Unsurprisingly, then, "Partners" didn't last long. The show premiered on August 4, 2014, with FX committing to just 10 episodes with the option to order 90 more if the show did well. It did not, and was cancelled after its 10-episode first season. Sadly, Grammer didn't learn his lesson, and returned to the business of delivering "more depressing than nostalgic" fare with his short-lived "Frasier" revival in 2023.

#114. Emma Slater Claps Back at Fan, Defends Alan Bersten Replacing Val Chmerkovskiy

Dancing With the Stars’ Emma Slater clapped back at a fan who questioned why her boyfriend, Alan Bersten, is stepping in for Val Chmerkovskiy amid his one-week benching.

“Alan is going to dance for Val? Alan? Alan was eliminated,” the fan said in a Saturday, October 17, TikTok clip, to which Slater, 37, responded, “Yeah that’s what happens, we all step in for each other.”

Slater’s public interaction comes after Us confirmed on Saturday that Bersten, 32, will dance a Viennese waltz with Jenna Dewan during the Monday, October 20, episode of the reality TV dancing series after the actress’ pro partner, Chmerkovskiy, 40, was benched for making controversial social media comments about judge Carrie Ann Inaba.

Bersten, who went public with his romance with Slater in April 2025, and partner Giada De Laurentiis faced off against Chmerkovskiy and Dewan, 45, during season 35 of DWTS, however Bersten and De Laurentiis, 56, were eliminated during week 2. (Slater remains in the current competition with her own celebrity partner, Jackson Olson.)

Slater’s comment on the TikTok post was one of a string of social media viewpoints that defended Bersten’s momentary return to season 35. “Who did you think was gona step in? Channing Tatum?” wrote one fan, referring to Dewan’s ex-husband, 46, and Step Up film costar, while another wrote, “Well obviously an eliminated pro would step in … there’s nobody else to do it.”

Not everybody is thrilled with Bersten’s return, however, with former DTWS pro Gleb Savchenko shading the decision during a recent TikTok livestream. “Alan, I think he’s Alan. I mean, he’s just not up to the level of dancing, like, period,” Savchenko, 43, told fans. “[The] quality, the technique. He’s a good dancer, I guess, for TV but if we talk about art? Like creating art? He’s like, eh.”

He added, “I don’t have anything against the guy, just, why Alan? Who else is there?”

A spokesperson for BBC Studios shared a statement regarding Chmerkovskiy’s suspension with Us on Saturday. “The well-being of everyone who works on Dancing With the Stars is non-negotiable,” the statement read. “Val’s social media post was inappropriate and does not reflect the values or standards expected of anyone connected with the show. As a result, he will not participate in next week’s show.”

Chmerkovskiy’s post in question was sparked as a form of defense over his wife and fellow DWTS pro, Jenna Johnson, following criticism she received from Inaba, 58, over her lift with partner Harry Shum Jr. Johnson during Super Bowl Night earlier this month.

“She’s trippin talking to her like that,” Chmerkovskiy wrote in the comments section of a TikTok video about the routine before a separate now-deleted social media comment from him read, “You almost saw Fresh Prince enter the ballroom last night.”

The comment was in reference to the moment Will Smith slapped host Chris Rock at the 2022 Oscars, notoriously shouting, “Keep my wife’s name out of your f***ing mouth.”

#115. Tom Hiddleston Got A Note On Thor's Set That Made One Loki Scene A+: ‘The Results Are In The Film Forever’

Like so many Marvel Cinematic Universe fans, I’ve watched Tom Hiddleston expertly play the role of Loki for a while. It’s honestly wild to think he’s been playing the Asgardian trickster-turned-God of Stories for over 15 years now. Of course, his tenure in the MCU began with 2011’s Thor (which is streamable with a Disney+ subscription). Hiddleston’s work in the movie is excellent and, before a major scene, he apparently received a key note, which I’d say is a major reason why the moment is so great.

Before Loki ever died multiple deaths across various timelines or became a member of the Time Variance Authority, he was a prince who was jealous of his brother, Thor. Hiddleston’s character eventually stepped into villain territory after learning he was the son of Frost Giant king Laufey. That discovery culminated in a tense confrontation between Loki and his adopted father, Odin. Hiddleston recently watched and reflected on the filming the scene and remembered what director Kenneth Branagh told him before filming the big moment:

I remember it like it was yesterday. Ken [Branagh] had said to me, ‘When you say tell me,” say it really quietly. And then if he doesn’t hear you and he doesn’t tell you, demand that he tell you and don’t take no for an answer.’ And so that extraordinary explosion, when I say, ‘Tell me,’ there had been this silence on the other side of the camera, as Tony didn’t say anything. And I just screamed.

That guttural scream was definitely effective for me when I first saw Thor years ago, and it still strikes a chord today. It’s perfectly executed by Hiddleston and, ahead of that, Branagh seemed more than aware of how such a delivery would be crucial while portraying Loki’s frustration and desperation. Good on the Belfast helmer for giving that note to his actor. Of course, given the Oscar winner’s storytelling prowess, the notion of him delivering such an insight isn’t surprising. Hiddleston also said this when discussing the scene with BAFTA:

What happened, as a result of that, in the take, there was a palpable emotional reality that was taking place, as I say, in the moment. I couldn’t have cultivated it. I couldn’t have brought it in from yesterday. And the results are in the film forever.

I understand exactly what the Life of Chuck means in regard to not having been able to draw that emotion from other sources. For a scene like that, such an emotion is quite specific, and I’m glad he and Branagh hit the right note. While the God of Thunder’s first solo film may not be super high on the list of best MCU films, it’s still a solid and fun entry in the canon due to moments like the scene between Loki and Odin. Check out Hiddleston watching it in the Instagram post below:

Having initially auditioned for Thor, Hiddleston credits Tim Burton’s Batman for his desire to play a villain in a superhero movie. The character, of course, ended up becoming much more than a bad guy and is now arguably as beloved as any MCU hero. With that, it was quite emotional when Loki’s journey seemed to end with the conclusion of his eponymous TV show’s second season. However, we’ve since learned that the antihero will return in the upcoming Avengers: Doomsday.

Tom Hiddleston has promised that the forthcoming superhero flick won’t undo Loki’s new status, which gives me comfort. I’m also hopeful that Hiddleston will get a scene or two filled with some genuine catharsis not unlike that confrontation scene he got a note on all those years ago. Fans can see how Loki’s journey continues when Avengers: Doomsday opens in theaters on December 18 amid the 2026 movie schedule.
